21091-the-life-of-william-ewart-gladston:
John Morley, himself a leading Liberal politician, wrote this three-volume life of William Ewart Gladstone, published in 1903. Volume One covers the years 1809 to 1859, from Gladstone's birth to the middle of his career. Morley worked from the vast Gladstone papers kept at Hawarden.

He also drew on thousands of letters from Gladstone's many correspondents and on journals from other sources. The volume traces a young Tory who became a Peelite and then a rising Liberal leader. Speeches, budgets, church questions, and party fights fill the story. Morley's access made this the standard life of Gladstone for years.
agassiz-essay-on-classification-1859:
Louis Agassiz published his Essay on Classification in 1859, in the English edition of his 1857 work. Agassiz, the Swiss-born Harvard naturalist, was then America's most famous scientist. The essay states his system: species are fixed forms in the mind of a Creator, classed by a divine plan.

Agassiz sorted animals by body plans he called branches, and he argued that classification reveals thought, not descent. The book appeared the same year as Darwin's Origin of Species, and it became the great anti-Darwinian statement of special creation. Agassiz's students filled American museums and universities. Modern readers meet in the essay the strongest case the losing side made, by its most gifted champion.
andronomy-or-magneto-physiognomico-crani: Andronomy, or Magneto-physiognomico-craniology, 1859. The magnetic system. This book preserves that work. Later readers can locate it. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Writers of history may cite it later.
antarctic-treaty-1959:
Twelve nations signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington in 1959, setting the whole southern continent aside for peace and science. The signers included rival Cold War powers and states that claimed slices of Antarctic land. They agreed to freeze the quarrel over ownership and keep soldiers and weapons off the ice.

The articles ban military bases, weapons tests, and nuclear explosions on the continent. They guarantee free scientific research and open inspection of all stations by other parties. No new land claims may be made while the treaty lasts. Many more nations have joined since, and the system remains one of the most successful arms control agreements ever written.
appreciation-phrenologique-de-monsieur-t: Appréciation phrénologique de Monsieur Triat, 1859. The Triat appreciation. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
arxiv-2512-00459:
Hybrid mesons mix quarks with excited glue, and some carry quantum numbers no ordinary meson can have. Christian Farina and Eric Swanson compute strong decays of two light exotic hybrid mesons in 2025. The states studied have exotic quantum numbers forbidden to simple quark-antiquark pairs.

Their model builds hybrid structure from the QCD Hamiltonian in Coulomb gauge with a single constituent quasigluon. Decay patterns are the fingerprints experiments use to identify new particles. Predictions like these tell collider and spectroscopy experiments which channels to watch for the first confirmed exotic hybrids. Exotic quantum numbers are a guarantee that any confirmed state is genuinely new physics. Hadronic decays are how such short-lived states announce themselves to detectors.
arxiv-2512-00659:
Aligning two sets of rotations sounds simple until time alignment is missing and axes are unknown. Anik Sarker and Alan Asbeck present a fast, robust method for rotation pattern alignment in 2025. Their approach is invariant to permutation and sign, the two ambiguities that plague the task.

Calibration and registration in robotics and sensing often hit exactly these obstacles, along with outliers. A correspondence-free method skips the fragile step of matching individual rotations first. Reliable alignment underpins camera calibration, motion capture, and spacecraft attitude estimation, where a wrong rotation quietly corrupts everything downstream. SO(3) is the group of three-dimensional rotations, the native space of the problem. For folks who tune rigs in the field, the gain is time. Two sets of spins can be lined up fast, with no need to pair them off one by one.
arxiv-2512-01059:
Anantha Padmanaban Krishna Kumar tests whether smaller vision transformers can work better in a 2025 paper. Scaling laws suggest bigger models usually win, but accuracy and training behavior do not always rise with size. Kumar studies one standard model, ViT-B/16, trained on the ImageNet-1K image dataset.

Two simple parameter-reduction strategies are applied to its MLP blocks: sharing weights and reducing width. Each removes about a third of the baseline parameters. The comparative study measures how performance changes as rank and size shrink. If leaner models match or beat the original, training and deployment costs fall for everyone.
arxiv-2512-02059:
Grand unified theories try to merge the forces of nature into one scheme, and hints of them may hide in unexpected algebra. M. Adeel Ajaib's 2025 paper studies nilpotent matrices, matrices that vanish when raised to some power, that produce the Schrödinger equation when written in first-order form.

Ajaib carries out a rigorous search for all such matrices and finds they fall naturally into group-theoretic patterns reminiscent of grand unification. No unified structure was assumed at the start; the organization emerges from the algebra itself. Whether coincidence or clue, the fingerprints suggest the quantum equation carries more symmetry history than its usual form reveals.
arxiv-2512-02259:
The Apache Software Foundation's libraries run much of the world's software, from Log4j to Tomcat and Struts, which also makes them prime targets for attackers. Derek Garcia and four co-authors present CVE Breadcrumbs in 2025, a way to track known vulnerabilities through the versioned history of Apache libraries.

Incidents like Log4Shell showed how a flaw in one ubiquitous component can endanger thousands of downstream systems. Following a vulnerability across versions shows which releases carry it and where fixes landed. That trail helps security teams decide what to patch first in a sprawling dependency tree.
arxiv-2512-02559:
Bárbara Muniz, David Plaza, and Claudia Rojas-Andías prove a structural fact about a small but rich algebra. The algebra is the spherical Hecke algebra of type G2, tied to an affine Weyl group. Its Kazhdan-Lusztig basis is a special basis used to study symmetry and representation theory.

The authors show each basis element splits into atomic pieces, an atomic decomposition. As a side benefit, they give a new algorithm for generalized Kostka-Foulkes polynomials in this type. Concrete decompositions like this make hard algebraic objects easier to compute with and compare, both by hand and by machine. Small cases done with care often crack the big ones open in time, and this one is no odd case out.
arxiv-2512-02759:
Aref Farhadipour, Teodora Vukovic, and Volker Dellwo match faces to voices in languages the system never saw. Cross modal verification asks whether a face and a voice belong to the same person. The FAME2026 Challenge tests this under multilingual strain, with unseen and unheard languages.

The Zurich team compares two designs. One is a dual encoder trained from scratch with contrastive and orthogonal losses. The other adapts the ImageBind foundation model with small LoRA updates. Knowing which approach travels across languages helps build media tools that work worldwide. Tongues the tool has not heard are the true test, since real world use will not stay in two or three tongues.
arxiv-2512-02959:
Dmitry E. Pelinovsky and Rudi Weikard construct breathers, wave packets that ride on a periodic wave without spreading. On an elliptic wave background, a breather superposes a soliton and a periodic wave traveling at different speeds. The two interact periodically in space and time.

For the defocusing modified Korteweg-de Vries equation, building general breathers stayed open for years. The elliptic background ties to genus two hyperelliptic solutions at a degenerate edge. Bright and dark breathers both appear in their construction, enriching the known wave families for this classic nonlinear equation. Wave forms that hold their shape on a wavy sea are the gems of this field. Each new one found by proof adds a gem that tests can chase in tanks.
arxiv-2512-03059:
Electric buses paired with solar power could clean up city travel. Jiaju Qi, Lei Lei, Thorsteinn Jonsson, and Dusit Niyato study bus charging in this 2025 work. The hard part is to keep costs low while no bus runs out of charge.

Real life adds shifting solar output, changing power prices, varied trip times, and few charge points. The authors use a layered form of deep learning that learns charging plans under set limits. Safe plans matter for transit fleets that want low carbon trips. Good timing can also cut bills for bus firms. Transit planners reading it gain a view of the trade-offs behind each charging choice.
arxiv-2512-04059:
Scientists who hunt signals in noisy fields, from brain scans to sky maps, first find peaks, then ask which peaks are real and where they sit. Alden Green and Jonathan Taylor build inference for that two-step reality in a 2025 statistics preprint. The catch is selection: confidence statements made after choosing significant peaks must account for the choosing.

Their method first tests each peak against a null hypothesis of no signal. Peaks declared significant then receive confidence regions locating the nearby true peak and bounding its height, valid post-selectively. Their assumptions pair a smooth signal with noise of constant variance, in a high-curvature asymptotic regime. There they prove control of both false discoveries and of regions missing their true peak. An intermediate result uses the Kac-Rice formula to approximate the intensity of the peak process, second-order accurate near true peaks.
arxiv-2512-04159:
New particles at the tera-electronvolt scale should, by rights, have shown up already in flavour-changing processes, unless something shields them. Admir Greljo, Ajdin Palavrić, and Ben A. Stefanek ask how little shielding is actually needed, in a 2025 particle physics preprint. Full flavour universality is stronger than the data demand.

The authors identify the minimal continuous symmetry that must survive approximately: a product of an SU(2) acting on quarks and a U(1) factor. With only a few symmetry-breaking spurions, each around a percent in size, the framework still reproduces the observed fermion mass hierarchies. That gives the Standard Model flavour puzzle a fresh angle. Within effective field theory, the setup structurally protects generic TeV-scale new physics from flavour bounds. The allowed space of collider scenarios grows beyond minimal flavour violation and U(2) frameworks, with richer patterns of flavour violation.
arxiv-2512-04259:
People ask ChatGPT for code every day and ship much of what it returns. But studies of its security usually test code generated on demand for the study itself. Kobra Khanmohammadi and colleagues revisit the question with real-world material in a 2025 preprint on software security. Their dataset is code that actual users requested, in the wild.

The study evaluates that code for both correctness and security, and examines what users were trying to do when they asked. A further experiment tests whether common prompt engineering strategies improve matters, using real-life prompts. The findings back the earlier synthetic studies: the generated code is frequently insufficient on security. The authors also observe that users rarely ask how secure the code they request actually is. That pairing, weak code and unasked questions, is the paper's real warning.
arxiv-2601-06859:
Maryam Raouph and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with computing natural magnitudes in the photometric systems of astronomical plates using gaia DR3. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Accurate photometric calibration of astronomical photographic plates remains a fundamental challenge in astronomy.

Especially when bridging historical photographic data with modern observations due to. The mismatch of spectral sensitivities of photographic plates and passbands of modern calibration catalogs. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07259:
Research by D. Allard and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with what can be learnt from UHECR anisotropies observations. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Recent measurements have revealed several anisotropy signals in the arrival directions of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs).

At large angular scales, the Pierre Auger Observatory has reported a significant dipole modulation in right ascension. While at intermediate angular scales, localized flux excesses have been identified by both the Auger and Telescope Array collaborations. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07359: Shezheng Song and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers seeing right but saying wrong. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have show strong capabilities across a variety of vision-language tasks. However, their internal reasoning often exhibits a critical inconsistency: although deeper layers may attend to the correct visual regions. Final predictions are frequently misled by noisy attention from earlier layers. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07459:
Himanshu Patil and colleagues presented work on Video Question Answering at a 2025 computer vision conference in Mandi, India. VideoQA systems answer questions about video, which helps make audio-visual content searchable and easier to use. Fields from education to entertainment and surveillance rely on such tools. The paper appeared as a 2026 preprint.

Large visual language models drive most current VideoQA, but they are costly to run. To save compute, they usually take a fixed set of frames sampled evenly from each video. Even sampling can miss the moments a question is actually about. The authors instead select frames based on the query itself. Readers interested in efficient video understanding get a clear statement of the trade-off and one way around it.
arxiv-2601-07659:
Alberto Tabarelli de Fatis and colleagues predict a new regime for light inside superconducting circuits. They study superconducting transmission lines as a platform for a quantum fluid of microwave photons. The photons travel along the line rather than sitting in a cavity. Strong photon-photon interaction comes from the natural nonlinearity of Josephson junctions built into the line.

The authors predict this interaction is strong enough, at realistic parameters, to reach a strongly interacting photon regime. In their picture the photons move from coherent behavior toward fermionized behavior, where they act almost like particles that cannot overlap. Such a fluid would let physicists study many-body quantum physics with light. The work speaks to quantum optics and superconducting device scholars. It offers target parameters for experiments.
arxiv-2601-07959:
Rohith Reddy Gangam and colleagues study matchings that stay stable when preferences change. The setting is the two-sided stable matching of Gale and Shapley, used for markets like residency placement. Given two preference instances on the same agents, a matching is robust if it is stable under both. Their 2026 preprint develops this notion of robust stable matchings. Preferences in real markets shift between rounds and years.

A robust matching avoids rematching everyone when tastes move a little. Stability under both instances is a strong demand, so existence is not obvious. Characterizing such matchings helps market designers plan for change. It also speaks to fairness, since churn harms participants who planned around a match. The paper serves theoretical computer scientists and market design economists. It adds a durability criterion to a Nobel-cited framework.
arxiv-2601-08259: Yinqiu Liu, Ruichen Zhang, Dusit Niyato, and co-authors survey agentic AI for next-generation networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that agentic systems promise to turn language models into autonomous operators. Chatbots that only talk would give way to agents that act on the network. The gap lies between abstract reasoning and physical actuation, which the authors call tool intelligence. Tool engineering is their name for building that bridge well. The paper maps what networks need before agents can be trusted with real operations.
arxiv-2601-08859:
Bruno Saraiva and six co-authors build a tool that gives code a face users can click. Science code oft needs many set values to run. In plain code, a user must type those values and know code terms. Each lab tool looks unlike the next, and set values are lost when a run ends. That loss hurts repeat work.

Their tool is called EZInput. It makes the same click form in many code homes, from a note page to a full app. Set values are saved, shared, and used again with ease. A reader who writes science code gets a way to cut dull input work. It also helps peers run the same code with the same set up.
arxiv-2601-08959:
Md Mashrur Arifin, Maqsudur Rahman, and Nasir Eisty build a tool to spot bad apps on Android phones. New bad apps hide well, and past apps give no true guide. One strong trick turns app code into an image and lets a sight net read it. But past work oft skips app text facts, such as what rights an app asks for.

The team joins image facts with text facts in one deep net. They also test how image type and size shift the score. That test was oft left out in past work. A reader in phone safety gets a fuller spot tool. It reads both the look of code and the words an app shows to the store.
arxiv-2601-09059:
Santiago Martinez Novoa and Nicolas Rozo Fajardo build a team tool for health talk in more than one tongue. Their task was part of a shared health AI test in 2025. Talks come in Indic tongues. The tool must sum them and answer asks in them. Few tools do such work well in low resource tongues.

Their chain has three stages. First, talks are turned to English. Next, a small distilled model sums and answers. Last, results turn back to the source tongue. Each stage is lean, so the chain can run on a fair budget. A reader in health tech gets a plain chain that may serve clinics where staff and sick folk share no one tongue.
arxiv-2601-09359:
A team from Collaborative Research Center 1625 tells how they run data for a vast joint hunt in stuffs. The hunt seeks a firm base for how mixed solid faces act at atom scale. Labs in the hunt make thin film sets, take marks of more than one kind, and run sims. Each lab makes data in its own form, at its own pace.

They use ontology forms, shared word frames that say what each term means, to tie the sets. One tongue for all sets lets a search cross labs and tools. A reader in data work gets a field tale of how to run data for a hunt too big for one lab's own plan.
arxiv-2601-09659:
Miguel de Carvalho revisits a little-known 1930 note by Kolmogorov about what a mean should be. His 2026 arXiv paper connects the Kolmogorov superposition theorem with regular means. Kolmogorov's axioms for probability are famous; his axiomatic frame for means is not.

That frame yields one functional form covering the arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic means, among others. The paper explores how this unifying concept works. A single form behind many averages clarifies why each mean suits its own task. It also rescues a neat idea from an overlooked corner of a great mathematician's work.
arxiv-2601-09859:
Anant Mehta, Xiyuan Wei, Xingyu Chen, and Tianbao Yang ask whether open CLIP models can be improved cheaply. Their 2026 arXiv paper offers an optimization framework for self-supervised fine-tuning of CLIP. CLIP is a cornerstone of multimodal learning, joining images and text.

The usual way to do better is to train from scratch on billions of samples, at prohibitive cost. The authors ask a different question: can existing open weights be lifted across downstream tasks with self-supervised data alone? A yes would let small teams improve flagship models. Fine-tuning recipes matter wherever budgets are tight.
arxiv-2601-10059:
Shuowei Ma, Qianfan Wang, Lvzhou Li, and Fei Shi cut the cost of reading a quantum state. Full state reads grow too fast as a system grows. No lab can run that many tests on a large state. A part read is a cheaper path.

A part read finds all small group shares of the state. Few test sets can do that job. The team gives a best such read for qudits, which are units with more than two states. They also give the best order in which to run the tests. That order saves time while the read stays sharp.
arxiv-2601-10259:
Dikai Liu, Yifeng Xiong, Marco Lops, Fan Liu, and Jianhua Zhang study masks for a rig that must sense and send in turns. Such a rig is named ISAC. It shares one radio for both jobs. In half duplex form, it can send or sense at one time, not both.

A mask sets which time slots send and which sense. The team work out the mean reply of such masks in range and Doppler terms. Doppler terms track speed from tone shifts. They give a closed form for that reply. The form helps pick masks that sense well and send well.
arxiv-2601-10659:
A 2026 arXiv preprint studies counterdiabatic driving, a trick for steering quantum systems fast without errors. The test bed is the Landau-Zener model, a two-level system swept through an avoided crossing. If the sweep is slow, the system stays in its state and jumps vanish. Fast sweeps break that calm.

An extra control field can be designed so the combined system acts calm at any speed. The paper treats the harder case where the gap at the crossing is random. Random gaps arise in real devices with flaws and noise. A control that works despite them would help builders of quantum hardware run fast, clean operations.
arxiv-2601-10759:
Kai Ming Ting, Ye Zhu, Hang Zhang, and Tianrun Liang compare two ways to describe data for clustering. Density distribution has been the default lens since the early days of statistics. It says where points pile up thickly. Mass distribution takes a different view of the same points. The authors test the two lenses head to head.

They show that density has a built-in flaw: a high-density bias, no matter which clustering algorithm is used. Clusters in sparse regions can be swamped by dense ones. The finding reframes a step most data work takes for granted. Practitioners who group data, from images to genomes, get a reason to rethink their basic descriptor.
arxiv-2601-11059:
Projesh Nath Choudhury, Shaun Fallat, and Chi-Kwong Li study semigroup automorphisms of total positivity. Totally positive matrices, and their nonnegative kin, have all minors of the right sign. They connect to analysis and mechanics, through classic works by Schoenberg, Gantmacher and Krein, and Lusztig. Totally positive matrices form a set that stays closed when matrices are multiplied.

That set sits inside a larger family of invertible matrices. The authors study the maps that preserve this set's structure. Automorphisms reveal a structure's true symmetries. For total positivity, those maps govern which changes keep every minor's sign, a property with uses from data work to cluster algebras.
arxiv-2601-11359:
Wenhui Tan, Ruihua Song, Jiaze Li, Jianzhong Ju, and Zhenbo Luo pick frames for video AI. Their 2026 preprint is named Think-Clip-Sample, a slow-fast method. Multimodal large language models have advanced video understanding fast. Long videos still strain them, for two clear reasons.

Compute cost caps how many frames a model can read. Poor frame choice wastes that small budget on bland shots. The team's method picks frames in a slow-fast rhythm. Slow thought plans where the key content may sit. Fast sampling then grabs frames that match the plan. Better frames mean better answers on long videos. The work came from Renmin University and Xiaomi teams.
arxiv-2601-11459:
Brian Keith defines a young field called Interactive Narrative Analytics. The 2026 preprint joins narrative extraction with human sensemaking. News collections are now vast beyond any reader's grasp. Overload and misinformation make true stories hard to find.

The field pairs two kinds of tools in one loop. Computational methods pull narrative structures from big sets. Interactive visual analytics then let people explore them. Human interpretation stays in charge of what stories mean. The mix aims at sensemaking, not just fast sorting. Analysts can test how a story forms and spreads. The preprint sets out the field's scope and promise.
arxiv-2601-11759:
Álvaro Castañeda and Gonzalo Robledo wrote a guide to linear systems that change with time. Such systems are called nonautonomous, since their rules shift as time runs. A key trait is exponential dichotomy, a split of paths into fast growth and fast decay kinds.

They link that trait to its spectrum and to results on smooth shifts of such systems. The book aims to be a friendly first read on the field. It also spreads the pair's own work in this frame. Students of dynamics gain a clear path into a hard topic.
arxiv-2601-12359:
Anirudh Sekar and five co authors look at a weak spot in large language models. Bad prompts can slip in through side paths such as email or user content. Once inside, they can push a model past its safety rules. The model may then give harmful or wrong output that its makers did not intend.

Their guard watches for drift in embeddings, with no need for past shots of an attack. The name of the method stresses that it is light and cheap to run. The team notes that even the best models stay open to such prompts. Fixes tied to one model are slow and narrow, so a broad guard has clear worth.
arxiv-2601-12459:
Enrico Massa and Davide Astesiano present a take on Mach principle within a geometric theory of gravity. Mach principle holds that local inertia comes from the rest of the universe. In their approach, neither inertia nor free fall is assumed at the start. The motion of any local system grows out of its links with all else.

Those links can be direct or indirect, but none are left out. The result is a consistent relativistic form of the old idea. Work of this kind tests how far Mach vision can be pushed in modern gravity. It also clarifies what a theory must give up or keep to honor that vision. Cosmology gains a cleaner base for its core claims.
arxiv-2601-12659:
Ruiqi Wang and seven co authors work on drone based wireless networks for future 6G systems. Fleets of unmanned aerial vehicles can serve users from the air in a downlink setup. Their high mobility makes design hard, though. Beamforming and flight trajectory must be optimized together, a coupled problem.

Classic numerical methods for this problem suffer from high latency. Standard deep learning often ignores how interference patterns shift as drones move. The team propose a two layer reinforcement learning approach for the joint design. Learning based control can react fast once trained. Handling interference topology is key to scaling to many drones. The work serves non terrestrial networks in next generation wireless.
arxiv-2601-12859:
Luca Schaufelberger, Aline Hartgers, and Kjell Jorner generate conformers of cyclic molecules with flow matching. Cyclic molecules are ubiquitous in chemistry and biology. Their restricted flexibility gives structural pre organization that is key to function. That trait matters in drug discovery and catalysis, where shape decides binding.

Reliably sampling the conformer ensembles of ring systems remains challenging, though. Rings cannot flop freely, so naive sampling misses valid shapes or wastes effort. The team work in Cremer Pople coordinates, a classic system for ring puckering. Flow matching in those coordinates respects the geometry of rings by construction. Better ring sampling would sharpen virtual screening of drug candidates.
arxiv-2601-13159:
Tom Baumbach studies a plane form of the log Minkowski task. That task asks when a set of cone volumes can come from a real shape. Here the shapes are polygons, flat forms with straight edges. Each polygon is marked by the set of its out face unit arrows.

Baumbach takes a fixed finite set of such arrows that spans the plane. He marks the hull of the closed set of all cone volume lists from such polygons. The hull is the least bent set that holds them all. Such marks help staff who work on shape from data, a field where a list of sums must be tied back to a true form.
arxiv-2601-13259:
Francesco Pedrotti studies when a random walk settles fast and when it cuts off sharp. Plus curve has long been known to give strong gains for Markov chains. Those gains span smooth effects, bounds on spread, mix time caps, and of late the cutoff act, a sharp drop from far to mixed.

Pedrotti asks how far those gains reach when curve is less than plus. He uses a join of entropy and Wasserstein tools, a way to track both spread and shift. He also treats weak local focus, where mass piles up less than the ideal. From that he draws a rule for when cutoff still holds. The work widens a core kit in chance theory.
arxiv-2601-13359:
Asen Dotsinski and Panagiotis Eustratiadis jailbreak open language models with a plain prefix trick. Guard work grows as open models gain skill. Auto jailbreaks such as GCG work well but burn huge compute and need deep craft. A cheap path, if one lives, is a risk all guards must know.

Their trick is called sockpuppetting. It slips a set accept string in front of the model's out put. That head start can tip the model to go on with a bad reply it would else refuse. No search or tune is used. For safety teams, a low cost trick that works is a call to test guards as real foes would.
arxiv-2601-13459:
Arpan Ghosh and co-authors test if young stars that eat fast also blow more ionized gas. Young stellar objects grow by pull of gas in, called accretion. They also lose mass in jets. The tie of in flow to out flow is a core ask in star birth.

Their test set is the Coronet Cluster of young stars. The team ran a joint survey in near infrared light and in centimetre radio waves, at more than one epoch. In five of twenty six stars they catch a hydrogen line that marks in flow. Those five also show radio signs of out flow. Such joint data ties the two acts star by star, not just in bulk.
arxiv-2601-13859: A team led by O. C. Feulefack studies a spin qubit in a parabolic quantum wire in 2026. A bichromatic field, with two drive tones, acts on the qubit. Their theory shows a synthetic gauge field in this setup. Its strength can be tuned by how tight the wire holds the spin. The field leads to Floquet topological effects, patterns that repeat in time. The team shows how topological protection can guard qubit states from timed shakes.
arxiv-2601-13959:
Shikher Sharma and Simeon Reich build an algorithm for equilibrium problems on curved spaces in 2026. Hadamard manifolds are curved spaces with a key negative-curvature trait. Monotone equilibrium problems on them model games, flows, and balance points. Their method is a Bregman regularized proximal point algorithm.

A Bregman function shapes the regularization term that steadies each step. On Hadamard manifolds, that term is in general nonconvex unless curvature is zero. The team develops the method with that flaw in view. Sound solvers on curved spaces aid data science on non-flat data.
arxiv-2601-14059:
Andrea Gilot, Axel Bergström, and Eva Darulova add floating-point support to a program verifier in 2026. Stainless is a deductive verifier for a subset of Scala. It now gains automated verification for floating-point numbers, the first such support of its kind. The subset includes polymorphism, recursion, and higher-order functions.

They follow the KeY verifier's approach to axiomatise math functions. They go further by supporting all functions from Scala's math API. They also verify the axioms against the actual implementation in Stainless. Verified float code matters for finance, science, and control systems.
arxiv-2601-14159:
Panagiotis-Eleftherios Eleftherakis and a large team test CFD codes across many GPU types at scale in 2026. Heterogeneous supercomputing with GPUs is now central to high-performance computing. Computational fluid dynamics is a de-facto HPC workload with heavy demands. Performance portability means keeping near-optimal speed across distinct accelerators.

Their Multi-Partner Project analyzes multi-GPU portability for CFD simulations. Codes that slow down on new hardware waste costly machine time. The study spans several partners and their distinct systems. Results can guide how CFD teams write code for the next machines. The tests run at scale, not on toy grids. That scale is what makes the port costs real for HPC teams.
arxiv-2601-14759:
Syed Luqman Shah and co-authors improve channel estimation for wireless systems in this 2026 paper. Accurate channel estimation with low pilot overhead and computational complexity is key to efficiently utilizing multi-antenna wireless systems. Pilots are known signals sent so receivers can measure the channel. Fewer pilots mean more room for real data.

The field is evolving from purely statistical descriptions toward physics- and geometry-aware propagation models. This work focuses on incorporating channel information in that newer spirit. Their method improves GPR-based CSI acquisition via a spatial-correlation kernel. GPR is Gaussian process regression, and CSI is channel state information. The gain is room. Each saved pilot is a slot that can carry pay data in its place. Readers get sharper channel knowledge at lower pilot cost.
arxiv-2601-14959:
Xinyu Peng, Han Li, and co-authors work on filling in missing frames in video. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with video frame interpolation, which builds new frames between existing ones. Most methods treat a video as short separate chunks, such as triples of frames.

That frame-by-frame habit can cause flicker and motion flaws across a clip. The authors propose a holistic, video-centric approach instead. Their method, named Local Diffusion Forcing for Video Frame Interpolation, works with the whole video in view. It aims for smoother motion and steadier frames over time.
arxiv-2601-15159:
Giulio Nesti and Luca Pezzè study a ring of superfluid stirred by a moving barrier. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with ring-shaped superfluids, which recent experiments probed with weak links or impurities. The authors push the theory beyond the regimes tested so far.

They study a one-dimensional potential that rotates around the ring at a set speed. They ask when dynamical instability sets in. Both the tunneling regime and the hydrodynamic regime come under study. The result speaks to how long a circulating superfluid flow can stay stable over long stretches of time.
arxiv-2601-15259:
Florian Kogelbauer proves that a kinetic equation admits solutions outside the usual fluid picture. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with the linear BGK equation, a model of gas flow with a density-dependent twist. Most known solutions behave like a fluid at large scales.

Kogelbauer shows that non-hydrodynamic solutions exist in any number of dimensions. For any Knudsen number, a measure of how rarefied the gas is, he builds a starting state with odd behavior. Its mass density loses energy at a rate that blows up as the Knudsen number shrinks toward zero.
arxiv-2601-15359:
Hollis Williams computes with a pair of equations used in a famous unproven claim about black holes. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with the generalized Jang equation, coupled to a conformal flow of metrics. A recent result by Jaracz frames the work.

Jaracz showed that no global solutions meet the conditions needed to prove the Penrose conjecture this way. The proof found a breakdown: the Jang slope fails at finite radius. Williams studies the coupled system numerically. His investigation traces how that breakdown unfolds inside the coupled equations themselves in detail.
arxiv-2601-15459:
Sarvin Ghiasi, Majid Roshanfar, and co-authors teach surgical robots to feel a crash coming. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with multi-arm robots in laparoscopic surgery. Several arms work in a tight space, so collision detection and distance estimates are vital for safety.

The framework joins three tools. Analytical modeling states the arms' geometry. Real-time simulation tests the motion as it happens. Machine learning, trained from simulation, predicts collisions and minimum distances. Together they aim to keep multi-arm surgery both safe and efficient for the patient and for the whole surgical team.
arxiv-2601-15859:
Lina Felsner and six co-authors make a new kind of X-ray image in a 2026 arXiv paper. X-ray dark-field imaging shows fine tissue structure in a way plain X-rays do not. It gives clues that standard scans miss. But dark-field data are scarce. That scarcity hampers deep learning models, which need large datasets. The team builds the first frame of its kind. It makes dark-field images from standard chest X-rays.

Their tool is an uncertainty-guided progressive GAN. Maps of doubt steer the build toward detail that can be trusted. Growth in stages builds the image step by step. Fake dark-field data could unblock model work in this young field. Hospitals cannot easily collect paired scans. A sound tool gives researchers data to train and test methods now.
arxiv-2601-15959:
Kevin N. Hainline and a large team list candidate galaxies from the universe's first era in a 2026 arXiv paper. The sample belongs to JADES Data Release 5. It holds 2,081 sources selected at photometric redshift above eight. The fields are GOODS-S and GOODS-N. Together they cover 469 square arcminutes of sky. At redshift eight and beyond, light left its sources within the first few hundred million years.

Photometric selection picks candidates by their colors across filters. Spectroscopy must later confirm the true distances. A large, clean candidate list is the funnel's wide end. Later JWST time winnows it to confirmed early galaxies. Each confirmed case tests how fast galaxies assembled after the Big Bang. The catalog serves observers planning those follow-ups.
arxiv-2601-16159:
Celsa Pardo-Araujo and three coauthors weigh how oft core burst stars leave a magnetar. Their 2026 preprint deals with the death bursts of big stars. Magnetars are dead stars with huge fields. Their fields can reach ten to the four teen times Earth scale in Gauss. Such stars may drive the most bright bursts seen far off.

Those bright acts span super bright bursts, gamma bursts and fast radio bursts. The team asks what share of core bursts make a magnetar. That share ties burst rates to births of these rare stars. A firm share helps read burst counts from far space. The work links star death counts to burst counts.
arxiv-2601-16559:
Roberto Pegurri and coauthors guess car net states ere they shift with a twin. Their 2026 preprint deals with car to all links, called V2X. Safe car apps need nets that act ere change hits. Past twins oft just ape the net as it now stands. A twin that can guess next states could warn cars in time.

The team tests guess twins on a live V2X twin set up. Tests check if next state guesses hold true in real runs. True guesses let nets shift load ere jams form. That shift is key for safe linked car fleets. The work moves twins from ape to guess tools.
arxiv-2601-16659:
Jamie Duell and Xiuyi Fan work on plain-language reasons for machine calls. A counterfactual reason tells what change would flip a call. A loan tool, say, might cite a higher wage. But models get fresh training all the time. Old reasons can break with each fresh train. Their 2026 preprint seeks reasons that hold up.

Their method gives reasons with two firm traits. First, the new case must earn a firm, sure call. Next, small model shifts must not shake that call much. The authors call such reasons safe in chance terms. Banks and clinics need reasons they can trust over time. This work points to ways of proof for such trust.
arxiv-2601-16759:
Alda Andrade, Mónica Martins, André Ferreira, Tarcísio Araújo, Luís Lopes, and Victor Alves share a new photo set for gut care. The set holds scope shots from a test called ERCP. That test lets docs see and treat bile and pancreas ducts. AI could help docs read such shots fast. But free photo sets for this test are rare.

Their 2026 preprint fills that gap with a large, cleaned set. Each shot was picked and checked with care. Labs can now train tools on the same base. Shared sets make tool tests fair and clear. They may speed safe AI help in gut clinics.
arxiv-2601-16859:
Georges Skandalis and Alain Valette weigh the cost of moving mass on a graph. Their graph is a net of points joined by set-length paths. The cost norm gauges the least work to shift loads. Loads sit at points, and paths bear the moves. Their 2026 preprint sets out traits of that norm for fin graphs.

Shortest-path gaps set the space for their math. The team ties the cost norm to the graph's shape. Such ties help in chip layout and net design. They also feed pure work on normed spaces. Small graphs here stand in for big real nets.
arxiv-2601-17159:
The STIS Cycle 30 team reports a year of checks on a Hubble scope tool. STIS is a light-split tool on the Hubble Space Telescope. Its marks must stay true for science to hold. The team's 2026 report covers late 2022 to late 2023. Nineteen set check plans ran in that span. Each plan's aims, shots, and results get a short brief.

Past years' marks set the bar for each check. Gaps twixt aim and mark get flagged with care. Notes point to deep reads for each plan. Such reports keep a famed scope's facts on firm ground. All Hubble users lean on that ground.
arxiv-2601-17359:
Payel Santra, Partha Basuchowdhuri, and Debasis Ganguly extend their work on query performance prediction. The classic task flags which queries will do well or poorly for one ranking model. Their new frame flips the task. For one query, it asks which ranking model will serve it best. That is a finer and harder call.

They call the framework Breaking Flat. It judges prediction at a grain the old tests miss. Search systems hold many models with mixed strengths. Picking the right model per query could lift results for all users. The framework gives teams a way to test that pick. It moves QPP from a score to a choice tool.
arxiv-2601-17659:
Shan Gao generalizes the Aharonov-Bohm effect beyond its classic form. The classic effect shows a phase shift from potentials in field-free regions. It is well established for static magnetic fluxes. Time-varying fluxes are less settled and still debated. Gao extends the analysis to those changing cases. The work tests how far potential-based effects reach.

A general form would unify static and dynamic cases. It could also settle claims that split the field. Quantum sensors use phase shifts as their core signal. Clear rules for dynamic fluxes guide their design. Gao's study speaks to foundations and devices at once. It asks what potentials do when nothing stands still.
arxiv-2601-17759:
Mengxin Wu, Ziye Chen, Guang Yang, and Mingshu Zhao report a surprise in the physics of light. Their 2026 preprint is about extended self-similarity, a tool used to find scaling laws in complex systems. The tool was built for systems ruled by nonlinear effects. The team shows the same scaling can appear in a system with purely linear physics.

Their test case is light moving through a multimode optical fiber. Many light paths mix inside the fiber and form a speckled pattern at the far end. The pattern comes only from steady, linear interference between the paths. Finding the scaling law here widens where the tool can be used, and it sharpens what the law really means.
arxiv-2601-18259:
L. Moral-Almansa and co-authors take a chemical census of two starless cores in a nearby filament. Their 2026 preprint studies the B213/L1495 filament. Starless cores are cold clumps of gas that have not yet lit a star. How their chemistry evolves as they near the protostellar stage is not fully understood. Detailed chemical characterizations of such sources are needed to chart that path. The team studies two cores in depth.

Each molecule found is a clue to age, density, and history. Comparing two cores in one filament controls for the wider setting. The results feed models of how stars and their planets inherit their chemistry. Starless cores are the quiet start of the star formation story.
arxiv-2601-18359:
Jendrik-Alexander Tröger, Christina Steinweller, and Stefan Hartmann study how doubt spreads through models of glue that hardens with heat. Epoxy resins set by a mix of heat and chemical change, and the set shifts the shape and strength of the part. A full model needs many linked rules, and each rule brings its own set of tuned facts.

Those facts come from tests, step by step, and each step adds its own small doubt. By the end, the doubt in the last guess may be much larger than teams think. The authors track that growth so that a plant can know how much trust a model earns. Such care counts when a glued part must hold a load in a car, a plane, or a bridge.
arxiv-2601-18659:
Ingo and colleagues share McSAS3, a fresh take on a tool that reads how stuff is built from the spread of a beam. When a beam of light or neutrons hits a sample, its spread holds marks of the size and form of the bits in-side. The tool runs that spread back-wards by dice rolls to guess the mix of bits that made it. The new take is built to slot into auto flows that grade streams of data.

It can still be run by hand on one batch at a time. A screen face comes with guides, worked cases, and films that show each step. The first take was prized for its fair guesses with few set rules. A fresh take that fits auto flows could bring that gain to big labs. There, beams run day and night and staff cannot grade each spread by hand.
arxiv-2601-18859:
Chiara Mingarelli sets a hard cap on how loud the joint hum of all black hole pairs in space can be. Each pair that spirals in gives off waves in space. All pairs at once make a hum that tools strain to hear. That hum can't be free of bounds: it is made from mass, and mass is in short store. Each bit of mass can be turned to waves at most once.

Mingarelli turns that plain fact into a scale law that caps the hum at each tone. The cap holds for all pairs, of all sizes, with no need to know their counts. If a hum is heard past the cap, it can't be from black hole pairs in the plain way. It would point to a new source, such as waves from the birth of space. The cap thus gives hear tools a sharp check.
arxiv-2601-19059:
Ryan LaRose and ten co-authors price out a quantum computing task from core biology. The reaction they study, the breaking of ATP and its kin, drives metabolism, cell signaling, and even cancer drug work. To judge what a quantum machine would need, they cost three known quantum algorithms for finding a molecule's lowest energy.

The three are the variational eigensolver, quantum Krylov methods, and quantum phase estimation. Each trades circuit size, shots, and runtime in its own way. A hard cost count on a real reaction helps labs and funders tell which quantum chemistry dreams are near and which are far.
arxiv-2601-19159:
Qian Chen and Benoît Collins price a test that tells whether a quantum state has a hidden split. The test uses semidefinite programs, a class of optimization tools, arranged in a ladder of ever sharper checks. The property under test, called k-block positivity, links to whether quantum states can be separated.

The pair use a symmetry cut based on rectangular Young diagrams to tame the cost. They tie the cost to the sizes of certain symmetry groups and give an exact formula for it. Their formula also shows why the ladder stops early in one special case, a neat closure.
arxiv-2601-19659:
Mao-Lin Luo and five colleagues teach AI models new tasks without erasing old ones. Continual learning is hard because training on new data tends to overwrite what came before. For pretrained vision-language models, three goals compete. The model must keep its original knowledge, retain the tasks it already learned, and stay flexible enough to learn more.

Their method, KeepLoRA, adapts the model with small low-rank updates. A residual gradient adaptation steers those updates to protect earlier knowledge. The authors present it as a simple approach that balances the three goals well. Models that learn continually could stay useful for years instead of being retrained from scratch. The work targets vision-language systems used in changing real-world settings.
arxiv-2601-19759:
A. R. M. Wolfert writes on how group preferences get combined into one choice. Preference aggregation sits at the heart of multi-objective design and group decision-making. It picks the alternative that best fits a shared purpose in complex social and technical settings. Preferences are subjective, tied to context, and express the free choice of the people involved.

The paper argues for aggregation methods that respect the uniqueness of each person's ordering. A method that flattens real differences can pick options nobody truly wants. Design teams and public bodies both lean on such aggregation daily. Getting it right shapes products and policies alike. The work examines what a faithful aggregation should preserve.
arxiv-2601-19859:
Oscar Fontanelli and Wentian Li model a common shape in real data: the beta rank function. Rank distributions often decay as power laws on both sides of a smooth peak. The beta rank function captures that two-sided shape. It is used wherever data deviate from pure power laws, from word frequencies to city sizes.

The authors introduce a two-step generative process that produces data following this distribution exactly. Their derivation runs through redistribution dynamics across two scales. A generative story matters because it hints at what real processes create the pattern. Rank functions with a mechanism behind them are more than curve fits. The work connects a descriptive tool to an analytic origin.
arxiv-2601-19959:
D. Belitz and T. R. Kirkpatrick comment on a claim about ferromagnetic quantum phase transitions. Clean metallic ferromagnets were once expected to show a quantum critical point. It is now known they generically avoid it, turning first-order instead. The cause is soft modes in the underlying Fermi liquid, which create long-ranged correlations between magnetic fluctuations.

The comment addresses a paper on the instability of that critical point and the symmetry of the ferromagnetic ground state. Comments in physics sharpen claims by testing their logic against established results. The authors bring the soft-mode theory to bear on the disputed points. The exchange helps settle how quantum ferromagnetism really behaves at zero temperature.
arxiv-2601-20059:
Christian Iliadis and five colleagues present the 2025 evaluation of experimental thermonuclear reaction rates, the rates that govern nuclear burning in stars. The work sets out the formalism for estimating these rates for astrophysical use. It stresses modern statistical methods, such as Monte Carlo sampling and Bayesian models.

The authors also cover resonance energies drawn from nuclear mass values, and indirect estimates of particle widths. They show how rates are matched to statistical-model results at high temperature. Reliable rates feed directly into models of how stars live and how the elements form, so a careful shared evaluation anchors much of astrophysics.
arxiv-2601-20459:
Mugdha Khedkar and three colleagues study the trouble Android developers have with data disclosure. Law requires developers to report accurately what data their apps collect, through the Play Store's Data Safety Section form. Large codebases make that reporting hard, since data practices hide across many parts of an app.

The authors take an empirical approach, examining developers' experience with the form. Where reports go wrong, users are misled about privacy and regulators are misinformed. Understanding the friction points can guide better tooling and clearer forms, so honest reporting becomes the easy path.
arxiv-2601-20659:
Sara Candussio wrote this master's thesis at the University of Trieste in the 2023/24 academic year. Its subject is the robustness of large language models. In plain terms, it asks how these models can cut down on false or made-up outputs. Such errors are often called hallucinations. The work was supervised by Luca Bortolussi, with Gabriele Sarti as co-supervisor.

Candussio builds what she calls a dialectic pipeline. The word dialectic points to a back-and-forth between opposed views. Her aim is to use that exchange to raise output quality. The thesis argues that checking and improving outputs is key to safe large-scale use of these models. It is a full thesis text, framed for a degree in data science and scientific computing.
arxiv-2601-20959:
Arjun Bagchi and three co-authors explore string theory with the tension turned off. Their 2026 paper concerns tensionless, or null, strings. The tensionless limit probes the very high energy regime of string theory. That contrasts with the well-studied point-particle limit, which reduces to Einstein gravity. A tensionless string sweeps out a null worldsheet in the target space. Hence the second name, null strings.

The authors review the lives of these unusual objects. A worldsheet is the surface a string traces as it moves. When that surface is null, light itself can travel along it. The physics becomes both stranger and more symmetric. Such limits often reveal hidden structure in a theory. The paper maps what is known about null strings. It serves theorists hunting for the deepest form of string theory.
arxiv-2601-21359:
Luan Pham tackles root cause analysis for failures in complex systems without a map of how parts connect. Finding the true source fast stops damage from spreading. Methods that lack a dependency map often blame the part with the highest anomaly score.

That rule fails when a small delay at the source grows into a huge anomaly downstream. The loudest alarm is then far from the real fault. The author proposes a graph-free method built to handle that growth effect. It aims to point engineers at the true origin, so fixes land where they will actually stop the failure.
arxiv-2601-21659:
A.S. Bratus and O.S. Rozanova write the governing equation for a diffusion process that switches between regimes. In their model, the states are spread continuously along a segment rather than sitting at a few points. An advection term, which carries states along, can be included or left out.

The authors propose an integro-differential equation for the density of states. They show a constructive method for solving the starting-value problem. For some starting distributions, the solution can even be written in closed form. Regime-switching models appear in finance, biology, and climate, where the rules of motion change with hidden states.
arxiv-2601-21759:
Meet Doshi, Vishwajeet Kumar, Yulong Li, and Jaydeep Sen adapt text retrievers to new domains by choosing training data with influence scores. General retrievers train on a big eclectic mix of corpora and tasks. How that mix should be sampled for a new target is an open choice.

Common rules sample evenly, by size, or by expert hunch. The authors instead estimate each source's influence on the target task. Sampling by influence spends the training budget where it helps the new domain most. Smarter sampling could make domain search tools strong without giant new labeled sets.
arxiv-2601-21959:
Yu-Wei Chen, Raghu Pasupathy, and Jordan Awan design hypothesis tests that keep data private. Their framework is Gaussian differential privacy, a strict standard for how much a test may reveal about any one person's data. They treat simple hypotheses and one-sided and two-sided tests under monotone likelihood ratio conditions.

Their method builds on a private estimate of the mean, with clamping bounds chosen from the data itself. The authors show its risk matches the best possible private rate, up to logarithmic factors, making the test near-optimal. Their 2026 preprint matters for medical and social research, where analysts must test claims about sensitive data without exposing the people behind it.
arxiv-2601-22059:
J. Renner, J. J. Gómez Cadenas, and S. R. Soleti build a virtual version of a medical scanner. Positron emission tomography is a powerful imaging method, but designing and evaluating new scanners is slow and costly. The work splits into detector design and simulation, image reconstruction, and image interpretation.

Their 2026 preprint presents AIRPET, a virtual PET environment that ties those stages together in software. A faithful simulator lets engineers test scanner designs before building hardware, and lets reconstruction algorithms be graded against known ground truth. That speeds the cycle of improvement for machines used in cancer diagnosis and brain research, where better images change real treatment decisions.
arxiv-2601-22159:
Naufal Suryanto and a large international team build a language model specialized for cybersecurity. Security operations need assistant models that support many kinds of work, from reading threat reports to guiding incident response. General models lack the depth and currency that defense work demands.

Their 2026 preprint introduces RedSage, a cybersecurity generalist large language model. A specialist trained and evaluated on security knowledge could help analysts triage alerts, explain vulnerabilities, and draft responses faster. The dual-use stakes are obvious. The same knowledge that defends networks can attack them. A public specialist model raises governance questions. The field must answer them alongside capability.
arxiv-2601-22259:
Da In Kim, Wei Siang Lai, and Kelly Zhang bring a new kind of table model to survival analysis. That field asks how long it takes for an event, such as death or failure, to occur. Their 2026 preprint notes a snag: many records end before the event takes place.

The team recast the task as a chain of yes-or-no questions over time slices. That shift lets table models, built for rows and columns, do the job. The method covers both fixed traits and traits that change with time. It opens a strong new tool to health and risk work.
arxiv-2601-22359:
Hsiang Hsu and a large team show that erased data can still haunt a model when inputs are tweaked. Machine unlearning aims to strip one user's data from a trained model without a full retrain. Their 2026 preprint notes that past proofs of erasure use clean inputs only.

When inputs get small, hostile tweaks, the erased trace can show through. They call this leftover trace residual knowledge. The gap matters for privacy law and for user trust. Their work sets a sterner test for claims of true erasure. Builders will need guards that hold under attack.
arxiv-2601-22459:
Joan Hernàndez Tey and Emanuele Cozzo read the time ties of spread on layered networks to tell its mode. On multiplex networks, a contagion may hug one layer or roam across all of them. Their 2026 preprint derives a closed-form mean-field account of those time ties.

The ties encode which mode the spread sits in. That gives watchers a dial they can read from data alone. The work fits disease, rumor, and fault spread on real layered systems. Early mode reads can guide where to act first. It is a neat link from math to watch-keeping.
arxiv-2601-22559:
Siu Chin shows that a neat identity for the harmonic oscillator opens an exact model of the Monte Carlo sign problem. The sign problem plagues simulations of fermions, particles that refuse to share a state. His 2026 preprint applies the identity to fermions in any number of dimensions.

The result is a rare case that can be solved in full. With exact answers in hand, scholars can see what the sign problem truly does to energy reads. That view can guide fixes for the general case. The work is a small, sharp window into a big wall.
arxiv-2601-22659:

That parallel lets SVMs serve as estimators with known traits, not just black-box scorers. It can also yield forecasts of choice from the fitted model. The work joins machine learning and econometrics in a clean way. Each field gains a tool from the other.
arxiv-2601-22859:
Chuanzhe Guo and a large team present MEnvAgent, a system that builds test setups for coding tasks on its own. AI agents for software work need tasks that can be checked by running code. Building those runnable setups by hand, across many programming languages, is slow and scarce work.

MEnvAgent automates the construction of environments in many languages at once. That makes it possible to generate large numbers of tasks with known, checkable answers. Better task supply means coding agents can be trained and judged on firmer ground. Automated construction also keeps the environments verifiable, since each generated task can be executed and checked by design.
arxiv-2601-23059:
Antonio Vitale and three co-authors test whether code comments help machines fix bugs. Automated bug fixing turns a broken method into a corrected one with language models. A common prep step strips comments from code before training, on the assumption that they add noise.

Their empirical study checks that assumption directly. If comments guide fixes, removing them wastes a useful signal about intent. The answer shapes how training data for coding models should be cleaned across the field. Removing comments before training is standard practice, so the study's verdict could change preprocessing habits across the field. The work is empirical throughout, measuring real fixing performance with and without the comments present in code.
arxiv-2603-01759:
Zichen Tian, Yaoyao Liu, and Qianru Sun tune the fine-tuning knobs of large models automatically in this 2026 work. Their test bed is remote sensing, where training a model from scratch fails for lack of data. Parameter-efficient methods update few weights, yet their fixed settings can badly cap results on new image types.

Their method, MetaPEFT, adds adaptive scalers that adjust module influence while fine-tuning runs. Three levers move together: where modules insert, which layers they touch, and how fast each learns. arxiv-2603-01859:
J. Pawlowski, P. Lydzba, and M. Mierzejewski extract conserved quantities of a quantum system from just a few of its states. A single energy state can already reveal if a system is integrable or chaotic, past work showed. The team shows those integrals can also be estimated from a small set of states. As system size grows, the needed share of states shrinks toward zero. A cousin model with fragmented Hilbert space breaks the pattern, since most states are needed there. That split marks a rare deep difference between true integrability and mere fragmentation of the state space.
arxiv-2603-01959:
Mehran Shakerinava, Behnoush Khavari, Siamak Ravanbakhsh, and Sarath Chandar map exactly what diagonal state-space models can and cannot track. Their 2026 work studies sequential state-tracking, where a model must follow a changing state step by step. Diagonal state-space models are fast and parallel, yet their expressive limits were unclear.

For a single layer with complex diagonal dynamics, non-Abelian group tracking proves impossible at finite precision. Non-Abelian means step order matters, a trait of many real state systems. With more layers, the reachable groups are exactly those with a layered series of Abelian factors. That places the model family precisely inside the solvable groups of algebra. Experiments add a warning: multi-layer models often fail to learn even the tracking they can express.
arxiv-2603-02459:

Classic inequalities for polynomials, tied to Marcinkiewicz and Zygmund, anchor the field. The survey generalizes those results to functions in arbitrary finite-dimensional spaces.

Norms come from general probability measures, not just uniform ones. Discrete sums must approximate them faithfully for every function in the space. The authors emphasize recent advances, especially their own research line. Main proof ideas and techniques are highlighted, not just final statements. The survey complements three recent surveys on the same topic. Readers gain a map of where sampling theory stands now.
arxiv-2603-02859:
Zuzana Haniková tests whether an alternative logic of sets can capture the idea of feasible numbers. Her 2026 paper works inside Vopěnka's Alternative Set Theory, a framework often used to model vague notions. The target is Yessenin-Volpin's view that only numbers small enough to handle in practice fully count as numbers.

She tries to model Dummett's weakly infinite totalities, collections that behave as finite from some angles and endless from others. Dummett treated their coherence as the test case for the whole feasible-number idea. The verdict here is negative: the set theory captures some features of feasible numbers, but not all. Haniková stresses that one failed route does not settle the broader debate over ultrafinitism.
arxiv-2603-02959:
Julio Silva-Rodríguez and Ender Konukoglu stretch a handful of labeled medical images much further with unlabeled ones. Vision-language models adapt well to new tasks from few examples, but rare disease classes often get too few labels and drag accuracy down. Their 2026 method targets exactly that low-shot squeeze in medical imaging.

A fast semi-supervised solver spreads pseudo-labels, guided by the model's text side, from labeled to unlabeled images during adaptation. The unlabeled pool helps cover classes that annotation budgets miss. The authors report labeling effort cut by at least half in low-shot settings while keeping adaptation efficient. arxiv-2603-03059:

Design schools are adding these tools to the curriculum, yet learning to judge them critically means using them more, with little way to count the environmental cost. His 2026 paper views the problem through human-computer interaction research.

Three directions follow. Contextual eco-feedback would show students the footprint of their AI use as they work. Participatory scoping would let affected stakeholders help set the terms of adoption. Treating data centers as a shared study topic would tie the tool back to the built world architects shape. The paper argues generative AI is a socio-technical process, not just a new drawing tool, and education must engage it critically.
