The embrace between Havana and the bloc grew closer month by month that year. The short paper tracks the tightening in trade, arms, and public statements as analysts recorded it that spring.
cia-0000135859: A CIA meeting record from 1 July 1952, now declassified, deals with a conference with a person whose name is deleted, held in the summer of 1952. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136159: On 6 April 1954, the agency filed a cable, now declassified, on transmitting messages verbatim, word for word with no paraphrase, for PRINCEP and ONTRICH. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136259: Press file in the declassified files, dated 6 May 1954, covers a Guatemala press digest covering the fifteenth through the seventeenth of June, filed in May. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136359: Messages numbered 17, 18, and 19 from the SECANT base are transmitted in this June 1954 LINCOLN cable, and they show confusion after the pact. One sender has learned of the pact but says the Zacapa road system is in danger and the troops are not aware of junta authority. Another reports the liberation army demoralized by the latest news, disgusted officers, and a request for a plane. Victory, on the ground, looked like disorder.
cia-0000136559: Filed in the Spanish texts of Brigade 2506, this document is dated 4 November 1960. That week produced a dense cluster of brigade records in this release. The brigade itself was a CIA-trained unit of Cuban exiles preparing to invade Cuba. The catalog assigns this item no subject heading. It survives in Spanish as released, and it is identified here by its date and its place in the brigade's papers.
cia-0000136759: A Spanish document dated 3 January 1961, filed with the 2506 Brigade papers in the CIA's declassified release. The brigade was training that week for the invasion of Cuba, still a secret plan. The catalog record gives this item no subject. It survives in the original Spanish, part of the early-January run of brigade records, and is identified here by its date and collection.
cia-0000136959: Prepare for the worst while PAGE is inside Guatemala, headquarters advises in May 1954. Frank Wisner signed the cable. LINCOLN made the correct decision in returning PAGE. A calculated risk can still win big results. His knowledge, ability, and relationships are the prize. Difficulties around the CALLIGERIS effort are growing. One step is urged. The station should plan embassy action now. The plan would cover PAGE's arrest or disappearance. His stay should be as short as possible.
cia-0000141159:
Declassified CIA cable traffic from November 1961 deals with two linked tasks after the failed Bay of Pigs landing in Cuba. Headquarters tells a station that a security officer and an associate will arrive on 4 November 1961, on Pan Am flight 551. The two men already hold rooms at the Gran Hotel, and the station is asked to meet them there.

The same cable turns to the crew of B-26 number 933, an armed bomber painted with Cuban markings. Its wreck had been found in jungle near the Bocay River in Nicaragua. The station is told to remove the remains, hold them under control at Managua, and wait for orders on final handling.
cia-03177759: November 13, 1957 brought the day's intelligence bulletin. Washington's leaders got the global roundup. The Cold War's November routine. It retains its place in time. This file preserves that declassified paper. Kept for study. Scholars will consult it.
cia-03179259: December 15, 1959: the bulletin carried the day's intelligence. The pre-holiday briefing for senior readers. The Cold War's December memo. Later readers can locate it. This declassified bulletin lasts, the file remains, the document lasts. It is kept for study by scholars.
cia-06557559: TERRORISM REVIEW, a CIA publication. The terror survey. This file preserves that declassified review. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
cia-06628559: THE POTENTIAL FOR POLITICAL VIOLENCE IN ARGENTINA, ETHIOPIA, AND THAILAND, MARCH, a CIA assessment. The violence forecast. This file preserves that declassified paper. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
copyright-renewals-1959: This Library of Congress catalog lists the copyrights renewed across America in 1959 — books, music, plays, and films whose owners claimed another term of protection. Such records were the working tools of publishers and studios managing their libraries of rights. Today they serve historians tracing which works survived in print and which slipped away.
coriolanus-pg2259: Volumnia's plea breaks him in this edition: the proud warrior, marching on Rome with the Volscians, yields to his mother's kneeling. "O mother, mother! You have won a happy victory for Rome, but for your son a mortal one." Pride's tragedy, stark and Roman.
countess-kate-pg3259: Charlotte Yonge's Countess Kate: a Victorian girls' classic. The spoiled heiress reformed. Wholesome and charming. A beloved tale, the spoiled heiress reformed, yonge's girls' classic, wholesome and charming, a beloved tale, the heiress reformed, Victorian girls' classic.
cyril-commentary-luke-pusey-1859:
Cyril of Alexandria preached on the Gospel of Luke through a full church year at Alexandria, and 156 of his sermons survive. The Greek text is mostly lost, so the sermons come down in Syriac. R. Payne Smith translated them into English from a Syriac manuscript, and Oxford published his work in 1859.

Sermon by sermon, Cyril walks his flock through the parables, healings, and passion of Luke. He reads each scene for doctrine, above all for the unity of Christ, and then for the shaping of a Christian life. The set is one of the great sermon courses of the early church. It shows Cyril the pastor, not just Cyril the fighter.
darwin-origin-of-species-1st-ed-1859:
Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in London in 1859. The first edition states his case as he first made it, before six rounds of change. He argues that all life forms descend, with changes, from shared ancestors.

Darwin shows how breeders shape pigeons and stock by picking traits. Nature, he says, does the same work far more slowly. Species that fit their place live and breed, and the rest die out. Few books have changed science, or thought about life, our place in it, so much. He had stacked facts from farms, pigeons, and wild shores.
dee-true-faithful-relation-1659:
John Dee, Elizabeth's astrologer, spent years recording conversations with angels through the scryer Edward Kelley. Meric Casaubon printed those records in 1659 as A True and Faithful Relation. Casaubon meant the book to discredit the pair; instead he preserved the source text of Enochian magic for all later ages.

Day after day, the diaries log spirits speaking through Kelley's shew-stone. Letters, calls, and whole angelic languages arrive in session. Dee's patience and Kelley's performances make strange, gripping reading. The volume is Elizabethan England's oddest spiritual diary. Occultists still mine it as scripture, while historians read it as a window on two remarkable, entangled minds.
dickens-tale-of-two-cities-1859:
Charles Dickens published A Tale of Two Cities in 1859, set in London and Paris. Its first line, it was the best of times, is famed around the world. The French Revolution drives the plot, with the guillotine as its grim refrain throughout.

Lucie Manette frees her father from eighteen years in the Bastille in Paris. Charles Darnay, her husband, is twice tried for his life in both capitals. Sydney Carton, a wastrel lawyer, swaps places with Darnay at the scaffold in Paris. Madame Defarge knits names of the doomed into her cold register of hate. Sacrifice and resurrection give the swift tale its lasting moral weight and fire.
erckmann-chatrian-the-man-wolf-1859:
Erckmann-Chatrian tell of a lord cursed as a wolf in The Man-Wolf and Other Tales, in English from 1876. The pair were famed tale smiths of France. Their chief tale is set in a great house in the Black Forest. A guest hears of a white wolf that plagues the line, and of a wild dame of the woods whose fate is bound to the curse of the house.

Rich air and slow dread fill the tale. The mate tales deal with dreams, ghosts, and doom in the same grave tone. The book is the theme in fine dress. Its craft sets it past pulp.
europmc-pmc10088059:
Lee and co-workers report that contact points with the endoplasmic reticulum control the behavior of membraneless organelles, in a 2020 study. The endoplasmic reticulum is a membrane network inside cells that helps move ions and molecules. Membraneless organelles are droplets of proteins and RNA with no skin of their own.

The team found an unexpected interface between the network and these droplets. That contact shapes how droplets form, move, and break apart. The finding adds a new control layer to cell organization. That layer matters for health and disease alike.
europmc-pmc10838959:
Kumar and a large team review tiny cell-made sacs as tools for diagnosis and therapy in this 2024 paper. Extracellular vesicles are nano-sized sacs, meaning sacs a few billionths of a metre wide, that cells release into body fluids. They carry proteins, gene messages, and fats between cells. Blood holds many of them, though sorting them from other blood particles is hard.

Because their cargo mirrors the state of the cell that made them, these sacs can flag disease early, the authors say. In cancer, testing sacs in blood could spot tumours sooner and without surgery. Loaded with drugs, sacs could also deliver cargo to chosen cells. The review ranges over cancers, brain diseases, and diabetes. The authors see wide promise, paired with a need for better sorting methods.
europmc-pmc11153159:
Pirnay and a large multinational team report outcomes for 100 personalised virus treatments of stubborn infections in this 2024 study. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect and kill bacteria. Personalised phage therapy picks phages matched to a patient's own germ. Trials of off-the-shelf phage products had disappointed, so the team reviewed tailored cases instead.

The 100 cases ran from 2008 to 2022 across 35 hospitals in 12 countries, coordinated by a Belgian consortium. Lung, skin, and bone infections were most common. Treatment used 26 phages and six defined cocktails, sometimes pre-adapted to the target germ. Clinical improvement was reported for 77.2 percent of infections, and the target germ was cleared in 61.3 percent. Skipping antibiotics alongside phages cut the odds of clearance sharply, their analysis found.
europmc-pmc1247559:
Xia and co-authors tested which particle chemicals damage cell power stations in 2004. Diesel exhaust particles were split into chemical fractions. The question was whether particles or their cargo cause oxidative stress. Cell tests compared three fractions.

The quinone-rich polar fraction proved most potent. It generated more reactive oxygen and dropped membrane voltage. It also shrank mitochondrial mass and triggered cell death programs. In isolated mitochondria it pried open a leak pore directly. Redox-cycling quinones copied that pore effect. Xia pins ultrafine particle toxicity on specific chemicals. Mouse liver cells were used for the pore tests.
europmc-pmc1283159:
Aranzana and colleagues tested genome-wide association mapping in a model plant in 2005. The plant Arabidopsis thaliana mostly self-fertilizes. It exists as inbred lines that can be typed once and tested repeatedly. The team sampled 95 lines with genome-wide data.

Traits tested were flowering time and pathogen resistance. False positives ran extremely high due to population structure. Despite that noise, known major genes were found for every trait. Those recoveries prove the approach can work in this species. Aranzana also warns structure correction is essential for human studies. Linkage patterns in this selfing species run unusually long.
europmc-pmc1397859:
Does living near a burger joint make people heavier? Jeffery and co-authors asked that question in 2006, using a phone survey of 1,033 adults in Minnesota. They recorded height, weight, and how often each person ate out. They also mapped how close homes and jobs sat to fast food places.

Eating fast food often went with a high fat diet and a higher body mass index, a simple score of weight for height. Yet living or working near fast food places showed no link to weight or to eating there. Jeffery suggests weak measures may hide a link, or sheer spread of outlets may not drive obesity on its own.
europmc-pmc1475659:
A sensor that spots flu may also make flu worse. Le Goffic and co-authors tested that idea in mice in 2006. The sensor, TLR3, detects viral RNA in lung cells. Mice lacking it were infected with influenza A and compared with normal mice.

Mice without TLR3 made fewer swelling signals and drew fewer killer T cells into the airways. Oddly, their lungs held more virus, yet they survived better. Le Goffic concludes the sensor drives much of the harmful swelling that makes flu deadly. The work warns that a strong immune reply can harm the host more than the germ itself.
europmc-pmc1513259:
A vaccine made of short germ pieces only works if a person's immune tags can grab them. Bui and co-authors built a tool in 2006 to forecast who a vaccine would cover. Human immune tags, called HLA, come in over a thousand forms. Each form grips a unlike set of pieces.

Their algorithm uses HLA frequency data for each ethnic group. It computes the share of people who should respond to a given piece set. Builders can test designs before trials and widen coverage where it lags. Bui offers the tool free as a web application, aiming to curb ethnic bias in vaccine reach.
europmc-pmc1769359:
Parents' ratings of a child's quality of life must be trustworthy when children cannot answer. Varni, Limbers, and Burwinkle tested parent proxy reports in 2007 in 13,878 parents of children aged 2 to 16, using the PedsQL survey.

Missing answers ran at just 2.1 percent, showing the survey is feasible by proxy. Most scales in each age subgroup cleared the 0.70 reliability bar for group comparisons. Total scores neared or passed the higher bar. Varni concludes proxy reports are reliable and valid in each age band, backing recent FDA guidance that asks for such subgroup proof.
europmc-pmc1780059:
Doytchinova and Flower built VaxiJen in 2007, a free web server that predicts which proteins might work as vaccine parts. An antigen is a protein piece that the immune system can learn to attack. Older tools hunted antigens by lining up sequences, which misses new proteins with no close known match.

Their method skips alignment entirely. It turns each protein sequence into a fixed set of numbers based on the main traits of its amino acids, using a transform called auto cross covariance. Models trained on sets built from 100 antigens already known and an equal count of non-antigens covered bacteria, viruses, and tumors. In checks the models scored between 70 and 89 percent correct. VaxiJen was the first server of its kind.
europmc-pmc1794559:
Carpenter, Sabatini and colleagues introduced CellProfiler in 2006, free open-source software that measures cells in microscope images. Modern microscopes can gather thousands of cell images in a day from drug or gene screens. Scoring those images by eye had become the bottleneck that slowed whole experiments.

CellProfiler lets researchers build an analysis pipeline by chaining modules, each doing one step such as finding cell borders or measuring brightness. It counts and measures many features at once, including the size, shape, and location of labeled cell parts. Unlike a human scorer, it applies the same rules to every image and can run through large screens unattended. The authors describe it as the first free system of its kind built for flexible, high-throughput cell image analysis.
europmc-pmc1976759:
Hobson and Denekamp measured in 1984 how fast the lining of blood vessels grows inside tumors compared with normal tissues. Fast vessel growth feeds tumors, and earlier single-dose labeling hinted that tumor vessel cells divide far more often. Their method gave rats of labeled thymidine, a DNA building block, every eight hours for a week.

Five experimental mouse tumors were compared with placenta and with normal tissues. Continuous labeling confirmed the large gap: tumor vessel lining had potential doubling times between 2.4 and 13 days, and placenta was at least as fast. Normal vessel lining turned over vastly more slowly, an estimated 47 to 23,000 days. That slowness held even in gut and skin, whose surface cells renew quickly, so vessel growth is set by the tissue's tumor status, not by local cell turnover.
europmc-pmc2064959:
Vazeille and colleagues compared two chikungunya virus strains in mosquitoes in 2007. In 2005 and 2006 a major outbreak hit La Réunion island, spread by the mosquito Aedes albopictus. The team fed virus to eight mosquito collections from La Réunion and three from Mayotte. One strain carried alanine at position 226 of a surface protein. The later strain carried a valine change there, called A226V.

The later strain spread through mosquitoes at least twice as fast as the earlier one. It also produced nearly 100 times more viral RNA copies in infected females. Virus reached the salivary glands within two days, ready for transmission by biting. La Réunion mosquitoes proved as efficient as other known vector species. The findings support that a highly competent local mosquito drove the outbreak.
europmc-pmc2124559: A medical paper on catalase in human tissues and its variations in disease. The enzyme, tracked. This article preserves that biochemistry. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2124759: A medical paper on the catalytic activity of blood and red blood cell counts. The blood's chemistry. This article preserves that hematology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2125159: A medical paper on the relation to the blood of the poliomyelitis virus. The virus in blood. This article preserves that virology. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. Readers can find it here.
europmc-pmc2125259: A medical paper on the blood supply of the kidney and the vagus nerve's influence. The renal blood. This article preserves that physiology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
europmc-pmc2125359: A medical paper on the mechanism of the curative action of antipneumococcus serum. The healing serum. This article preserves that immunology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2128159: A medical paper with studies on experimental pneumonia, acute respiratory production in monkeys. The monkey lungs. This article preserves that research. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128559: A medical paper on the behavior of leucocytes during regeneration and thyroid-induced changes. The busy white cells. This article preserves that hematology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2131359: A medical paper on the extent of the capillary bed of the heart. The heart's tiny vessels. This article preserves that cardiology. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2140859: A biology paper on the swelling of isoelectric gelatin in water, equilibrium conditions. The swollen gel. This article preserves that biophysics. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2362859:
Culig and co-authors built a new cell model of prostate cancer resistance in 1999. Advanced prostate cancer is treated by cutting male hormone supply or blocking its receptor. Tumors often escape, and the drug bicalutamide normally blocks that receptor, called the androgen receptor.

They grew hormone-sensitive prostate cells without androgen for 87 generations, creating a subline named LNCaP-abl. The new cells carried about four times more receptor, and their resting receptor activity ran 30 times higher than the parent cells. Bicalutamide flipped roles in them: instead of blocking, it stimulated growth and switched the receptor on. In mice, bicalutamide sped growth of the new tumors while testosterone slowed it. The receptor gene itself had not mutated, showing resistance can arise without new gene changes.
europmc-pmc2592359:
Coppé and colleagues discovered in 2008 that senescent cells, cells that have permanently stopped dividing, broadcast a rich cocktail of secreted signals. Senescence protects against cancer by halting damaged cells, but what those cells release was poorly mapped. Using antibody arrays, the team measured secretions from human cells driven into senescence by DNA-damaging stress.

The cocktail, named the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, built up over several days and mixed inflammation and malignancy signals. It appeared in normal and tumour cells alike, and in prostate tumours of patients treated with DNA-damaging chemotherapy. Fed to premalignant cells, the secretions pushed them toward invasion. Two factors, IL-6 and IL-8, drove most of that push. Cancer-causing RAS amplified the effect, while losing the p53 suppressor did the same, revealing how p53 guards neighbouring tissue.
europmc-pmc2635959:
Davies and co-authors tracked harmful drug effects in hospital patients in a 2009 study of twelve wards. They followed 3,695 patient stays over six months in 2005. Every suspected bad reaction to a medicine was logged and judged for cause, severity, and whether it could have been avoided.

In total, 545 stays, about one in seven, included at least one bad reaction. Half of the reactions were judged avoidable, fully or in part. In 147 patients the reaction itself kept them in hospital longer. The medicines linked most often were water pills, strong opioid painkillers, and blood thinners. In detailed checks, the one clear risk factor was simply how many medicines a patient took. Each added drug raised the risk further.
europmc-pmc2671559:
Kaufmann and colleagues mapped in 2009 the genes switched on by SEPALLATA3, a master flower-building protein in Arabidopsis. Flowers form through homeotic genes that tell each ring of organs what to become. SEPALLATA3, from the MADS family of switch proteins, is needed for every organ type, yet which genes it directly controls was largely unknown.

The team fished the protein off the genome in two ways, using sequencing and gene chips, and found it bound at thousands of sites. Most strong sites stayed bound even in a mutant lacking another master switch, which makes only sepals and petals. The target list tied SEPALLATA3 to many growth and hormone pathways, with repeated links to auxin, the plant growth hormone. Gene readings backed the picture. Plants with a jammed version of the switch responded differently. The protein, it seems, tunes auxin response so young flower organs can grow out.
europmc-pmc2688759:
Mann and colleagues showed in 2009 that Staphylococcus aureus, a germ behind many hard-to-treat device and wound infections, uses the DNA of its own dead as building glue. In the slimy cities these bacteria build, called biofilms, some cells burst and spill their DNA. That loose DNA, named eDNA, helps the film stick and stand.

Two gene systems pull in opposite directions. One, cid, promotes the bursting; another, lrg, restrains it. Mutants lacking the restraint stuck harder and held more DNA in their matrix. Mutants lacking the bursting system failed to mature into the film's tower shapes. A third player, the bacterium's own DNA-chewing enzyme, trims the glue back, and its loss made films thicker and richer in DNA. Timed self-destruction, the authors argue, is not waste but construction, and the trimming may later help the film shed cells to spread.
europmc-pmc2698859:
Bahadori and colleagues reviewed in 2009 the economic cost of asthma across 68 studies from four decades of literature. About 300 million people live with the disease, and its price tag ranks among the highest of all illnesses. The review separates direct costs, such as care and drugs, from indirect ones, such as lost work.

Hospital stays and medications were the twin engines of direct spending. On the indirect side, missed work and school days formed the largest share, ahead of lost future earnings from illness and early death. Total costs climbed with the patient's age, with other diseases present, and above all with severity: a few poorly controlled patients account for a huge slice of spending. Despite good preventive inhalers existing, costs keep rising. Better patient and doctor education plus regular follow-up, the authors argue, are the brakes available now.
europmc-pmc2732559:
Donlan reviewed in 2002 biofilms, communities of microbes that attach to surfaces and enclose themselves in a self-made polymer matrix, a slime-like scaffold. Most microbiology had treated microbes as free-floating cells grown in rich broth. Biofilm cells differ from floating kin in matrix production, slower growth, and distinct gene activity.

Formation involves attachment shaped by the medium, the surface, and the cell coat, then growth into a structured community that favors gene exchange between cells. Cells also signal each other through quorum sensing, which can trigger detachment. Biofilms matter for public health through infections on medical devices and in the body, so understanding their life cycle should guide new control strategies.
europmc-pmc2738459:
Lanciotti and co-authors reported in 2007 laboratory-confirmed chikungunya virus infections in travelers returning to the United States from India during 2006. Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus that causes acute joint pain, fever, and rash, and it is native to Africa and Asia. Huge epidemics hit Indian Ocean islands and southern India in 2005 and 2006, with over a million cases in India alone.

Among travelers tested, thirty-five infections were confirmed, thirty-three in people returning from India and two from Réunion Island. Diagnosis used antibody tests, virus isolation, and genetic tests on early blood samples, since virus circulates for only a few days. The cases show how explosive overseas epidemics reach United States clinics through travel.
europmc-pmc2790859:
Finn and co-authors tested a cell-cycle drug called PD 0332991 against forty-seven human breast cancer cell lines grown in the lab in 2009. The drug blocks two enzymes, CDK4 and CDK6, that push cells toward division by acting on a brake protein called Rb.

Cell lines of the luminal type, which respond to the hormone estrogen, were hit hardest, while basal-like lines resisted the drug. Sensitive lines carried more Rb and cyclin D1 protein and less of a blocker called p16, and their growth stalled in an early cell-cycle stage. The drug also worked well alongside tamoxifen and trastuzumab, and it restored tamoxifen response in resistant lines.
europmc-pmc2806359:
Stöver and Müller built TreeGraph 2 in 2010, a free editor for drawing family trees of species, called phylogenetic trees. Researchers now run several analyses on the same data, and the support values they produce often conflict. Comparing those values branch by branch by hand is slow and error prone.

The program merges support values from different analyses onto one tree and marks where they clash. Users can attach unlimited data to each node or branch, import values from spreadsheets, and let line width or color follow any chosen value. Whole branches can be copied between files, and finished trees export in formats ready for journals or slides.
europmc-pmc2811159:
Gilley and Coleman showed in 2010 that a fast-vanishing protein called Nmnat2 is what keeps healthy nerve fibers alive. Axons, the long fibers that carry nerve signals, wither quickly once cut off from the cell body. A rare mutant protein that slows this decay hinted that a natural survival factor must be shipped down the fiber nonstop.

Briefly blocking Nmnat2 production made uninjured axons break down on their own, the team found. The natural protein is short-lived and must be replaced constantly by fresh supply from the cell body. When supply stops, the fiber's self-destruct program wakes. Because raising Nmnat2 levels is a drug-friendly idea, the authors name it a target for diseases where axons die back.
europmc-pmc2814859:
Hollenbach and co-authors compared two look-alike leukemia drugs head to head in human cell lines in 2010. Azacitidine and decitabine are both used for blood disorders and are often treated as the same kind of drug, since both strip chemical tags from DNA. The team measured shared and split effects across several readouts.

Both drugs depleted the tagging enzyme and damaged DNA, but decitabine matched azacitidine at doses two to ten times lower. At higher doses azacitidine cut cell survival and protein building more, while decitabine mainly stalled cells late in their cycle. Gene activity patterns barely overlapped. The split fits chemistry: azacitidine slips into RNA as well as DNA, while decitabine enters DNA alone.
europmc-pmc2873959:
Noren Hooten and colleagues profiled in 2010 how tiny regulatory RNAs in blood cells change as people age. These microRNAs, short strands that tune gene activity, help set lifespan in worms and flies, but their human pattern was unclear. The team measured over eight hundred of them in blood immune cells from young and older adults.

Most microRNAs faded with age rather than rising. Nine dropped clearly in older people, and five of those nine are already tied to cancer growth. The genes those RNAs normally keep down, including a growth signal hub and a DNA repair protein, rose with age as expected. Lowering one RNA in cells was enough to lift its target, which supports a real cause link and a possible blood test for aging.
europmc-pmc2898859:
Liu and Wu estimated in 2010 how much of the world's liver cancer is caused by aflatoxin, a poison made by molds growing on maize and nuts. Liver cancer kills more people than almost any other cancer, and it strikes developing countries far harder. The team combined data on toxin levels in food, how much people eat, and rates of hepatitis B, a virus that multiplies the toxin's danger.

Of roughly six hundred thousand new liver cancers a year, they attribute between twenty-five thousand and one hundred fifty-five thousand to aflatoxin. That is up to about a quarter of all cases, with deep uncertainty in the range. Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, and China carry most of the burden, where moldy food and hepatitis B overlap.
europmc-pmc2911859:
Häuser and co-authors pooled in 2010 the trials of aerobic exercise for fibromyalgia, a state of chronic widespread pain. Twenty-eight trials compared exercise with usual care, and seven compared types of exercise head to head. In all, the trials covered nearly twenty-five hundred patients. Outcomes were pain, fatigue, low mood, fitness, and quality of life.

Exercise beat usual care on every outcome. Pain, fatigue, and low mood each eased by a small but real amount. Limits on quality of life shrank, and fitness rose. Pool-based and land-based programs both worked, and no type won the head-to-head trials. Gains were clearest while the programs kept going. The pooled numbers give doctors firm effect sizes to cite when they prescribe exercise.
europmc-pmc2924359:
Estes and a large team produced in 2010 direct visual proof that gut microbes leak across the bowel wall in SIV infection, the monkey analogue of HIV. Chronic HIV keeps the immune system pathologically activated, and that activation predicts decline better than virus levels do. Leaked microbial products from the gut were the prime suspect, backed only by indirect blood evidence.

Examining tissues from chronically infected rhesus macaques, the team found microbial constituents deep in the gut lining, the draining lymph nodes, and the liver. The leaks mapped onto visible breaks in the epithelial barrier, with local immune responses gathered at the breach sites. Damaged gut integrity thus feeds the systemic activation that wears the immune system down, making barrier repair a legitimate treatment goal beside antivirals.
europmc-pmc2965659:
van Wijk, Stam, and Daffertshofer warned in 2010 that comparing brain networks of different sizes with graph theory can mislead. Graph measures offer a neat language for brain connections, yet they shift with node count and link density alone.

Fixing thresholds to equalise size can force weak links in or throw real ones out. Normalising against random look-alike networks can, counterintuitively, worsen bias for popular measures such as clustering. The authors survey fixes from network science and social research, and try estimating the size effect directly from data so genuine differences in brain wiring stand out.
europmc-pmc3037559:
Sullivan and coauthors compared in 2010 the genomes of ocean viruses that infect photosynthetic bacteria, set against their freshwater and land relatives. These viruses, among the most common genes found in seawater, carry tools for building new viruses and copying DNA. The team lined up twenty six full genomes from diverse hosts and waters.

All shared a core set of building and copying genes in the same order. The ocean set added its own shared genes, including some tied to light harvesting, nutrient stress, and nitrogen handling during infection. Genes for phosphorus use matched the waters the viruses came from, not the host they were grown on. No single gene cleanly split viruses by host type, suggesting the groups blur through cross infection. The maps give a yardstick for reading virus DNA gathered straight from the sea.
europmc-pmc3069059:
Lee, Lessler, and Stuart tested in 2011 whether trimming extreme weights improves a common technique for making compared groups fairly matched. The technique, propensity score weighting, reweights people so treated and untreated groups look alike on background traits. A few huge weights can dominate results, and cutting them down is a popular fix whose value was unclear.

In simulations, trimming clearly helped when the matching scores came from the usual regression model, cutting both bias and noise. With modern tree based methods, trimming added nothing, and those methods alone matched the best trimmed regression results. The catch is that the best trimming level is hard to know in advance. The authors advise analysts to invest in building the matching model well, rather than leaning on after the fact trimming to rescue a weak one.
europmc-pmc3087759:
Signorini, Segre, and Polgreen tested in 2011 whether chatter on Twitter could track flu during the 2009 swine flu pandemic in the United States. Twitter then carried tens of millions of short messages a day, and illness talk was buried in that stream. The team built methods to pull out tweets that signaled real sickness, public worry, or both, and to follow them over time.

Estimates of flu like illness built from the tweet stream matched official reported disease levels closely as the pandemic rose and fell. Separate measures captured surges of public concern that did not always move with case counts. The authors argue such streams can supplement slow official reporting, giving health officials a near real time sense of both spread and mood. Their study was an early proof that social media can serve as a public health sensor.
europmc-pmc3098059:
Zhu and coauthors released in 2010 a software package that explains, in bulk, the binding site lists produced by genome wide protein binding experiments. Such experiments, called ChIP-seq and ChIP-chip, return thousands of enriched DNA stretches with no labels attached. Working through them in a genome browser one by one is impractical at that scale.

Their package annotates whole lists at once inside the R statistics environment. It reports the nearest genes and their distances, draws summary charts, tests whether overlaps between experiments are larger than chance, and pulls the DNA sequences around sites for further study. Users can supply their own annotation sources, keeping the tool flexible across species and platforms. It also links each site to the known functions of neighboring genes. The package is free through the Bioconductor project, the standard home for such tools.
europmc-pmc3145159:
Jakob Zinsstag and colleagues traced the idea that human and animal health form one system in a 2011 paper in Preventive Veterinary Medicine. From early history through European universities to modern comparative medicine, healers have repeatedly noticed the bond. A twentieth-century thinker coined one medicine for it; practice later widened the frame to one health, adding social and ecological context.

Evidence now grows that joint approaches beat separate human and animal services, and training courses, ministries, and world bodies increasingly adopt them. Ecosystem thinking widens the lens further, treating health as a property of whole social and natural systems. The authors argue the remaining silos between professions are the main obstacle, and sketch what a modern systems theory of health needs.
europmc-pmc3154959:
Kirstin Mittelstrass and colleagues mapped sex differences in blood chemistry and their genes in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Men and women differ in disease rates, symptoms, and drug responses, yet most studies pool the sexes. Using samples from more than three thousand adults, the team measured over a hundred blood metabolites and scanned genomes separately by sex.

Most metabolites differed significantly between men and women. Genetic control also differed: one gene region governing an amino acid breakdown product showed a strong effect pattern unique by sex. The results show cell regulation runs partly differently in male and female bodies, right down to single genes. The authors insist future studies should design and read results with sex split in mind.
europmc-pmc3378559:
Foulongne and colleagues took a census of viruses living on healthy human skin in 2012, using high-throughput DNA sequencing. Skin bacteria had been studied for years, but its viruses stayed largely unexplored. Samples came from the normal-looking skin of five healthy people and one patient with Merkel cell carcinoma.

The surface carried a rich viral mix, including many polyomaviruses, papillomaviruses, and circoviruses. The survey also turned up new papillomavirus and circovirus genomes. Within known skin polyomaviruses, variety proved very low. The results support a standing viral flora on healthy skin, not just passing germs, and raise questions about its role in skin growths.
europmc-pmc3397359:
Belouzard, Millet, Licitra, and Whittaker reviewed in 2012 how coronaviruses break into cells using their spike protein. These enveloped RNA viruses must merge their coat with a cell membrane to deliver their genome. The spike both grabs a receptor on the cell and drives that merger.

Different coronaviruses trip the spike's shape change in different ways: receptor binding, acidic surroundings, or cutting by enzymes. The review compares the spike with other viral fusion proteins and marks what is shared and what is special. Those special traits shape which species and tissues each virus can infect and how severe it becomes. The map helps anticipate how new coronaviruses might jump hosts.
europmc-pmc3420959:
Dahlem and co-workers laid out simple methods in 2012 for making targeted mutations in zebrafish with engineered cutting proteins called TALENs. Zebrafish are prized for studying gene function, but knocking out chosen genes had been hard. A TALEN can be built to cut DNA at almost any preselected spot, and sloppy repair of the cut leaves small mutations.

The team tested four such cutters against different genes. Nearly every injected embryo gained targeted mutations, sometimes in half its genome copies, and most adults passed them to offspring. A melting-based test detects the new mutations cheaply. Off-target damage stayed minimal. From design to mutant embryos takes about two weeks using free tools, they report.
europmc-pmc3427559:
Woolhouse, Scott, Hudson, Howey, and Chase-Topping took stock in 2012 of all virus species known to infect humans and how new ones keep emerging. The count stood at well over two hundred species, the first found in 1901, with three or four added each year. The team asked how much of the pool remains hidden.

Extending the discovery curve suggests plenty of human viruses await discovery, though a slowdown in new families hints at limits. More than two thirds of human viruses also infect other animals, mostly mammals and sometimes birds. Only about half of animal viruses that can jump into people can then spread between them, and fewer still cause major outbreaks. New emergences look inevitable, so the authors call for a global watch system.
europmc-pmc3443459:
Todd, Luzina, and Atamas reviewed in 2012 the molecular machinery behind pulmonary fibrosis, the slow scarring that stiffens lungs. Its idiopathic form is the most common and severe, with median survival around three years and no proven therapy. Thirty-five years of literature have piled up without pinning down the drivers, so the review organizes the suspects.

Three broad arenas get separate hearings: inflammation and immune mechanisms, oxidative stress and its signaling, and clotting-related pathways. Running through all three are transformed fibroblasts churning out matrix, dying air-sac lining cells, and the matrix piling up between them. The authors stress the pathways interlock in real patients even though they are reviewed apart. The map shows where a therapy might break the cycle.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d259:
A Chinese summary record, printed in translation, covers President Roosevelt's conversation with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek at Cairo on the evening of 23 November 1943. Since no American record of the talk survives, this account is the volume's main source for what the two leaders settled between themselves.

Roosevelt holds that China should stand as one of the Big Four, deciding world questions on an equal footing. On Japan's emperor, Chiang says the Japanese people should choose their own form of government after the war. The two agree that Manchuria, Taiwan, and the Pescadores must return to China, and Chiang proposes joint trusteeship for the Ryukyus. He declines the lead role in occupying Japan, offering Chinese support under American command instead.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d359: According to the President's Log, Soviet foreign minister Molotov called on President Roosevelt at Tehran on 28 November 1943, after Stalin had left. An editorial note in the volume records the call. No record has been found of the remarks the two men exchanged. The editors note that the call was probably short. It may have been limited to an exchange of courtesies. Roosevelt's talk with Stalin ended at four o'clock, when the next meeting began. Elliott Roosevelt's book mentions the call briefly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d459: Where the wartime file runs thin, the editors step in at Document 459. Their editorial note forms part of the Cairo-Tehran volume. Notes in this series explain background and identify the people named nearby. They also tell readers where a related paper can be found. The summit record behind the note comes from Cairo and Tehran in 1943. Three Allied governments coordinated their war there. The note keeps their paper trail intelligible.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d559:
President Roosevelt wrote to Congressman Jan Mruk on March 6, 1944. A letter from a president to a single member of Congress belongs to the domestic side of wartime leadership, where foreign policy met voters and their letters. It appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Congressmen wrote to Roosevelt often on behalf of constituents with family, property, or roots in the war's path, and the President's replies carried policy into American homes. Mruk represented a New York district with deep Polish-American ties, at a moment when Poland's future, argued over at Tehran, weighed on many Americans. For readers, the letter shows summit diplomacy echoing into ordinary politics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d59: Roosevelt answered Churchill on October 26, 1943, and the letter is Document 59 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Same-day replies kept the two capitals in step while their ministers finished in Moscow. The catalog record supplies the parties and the date only. In the published series the letter stands near the end of the Moscow sequence, with Cairo four weeks away and Tehran five.
frus-1944-quebec-d159:
H. Freeman Matthews recorded a delicate telephone exchange with the British Embassy on August 29, 1944. He first told Michael Wright that the president had deferred the French mission question until the forthcoming high-level meeting. Then Donald Maclean called back, brandishing a copy of the Joint Chiefs' letter suggesting no military objection to the British request.

Matthews checked with Admiral Leahy and held the line. The chiefs' letter conveyed views on the military aspect only, he told Maclean, and could not modify the president's decision to defer. The editors' note adds a quiet ending: despite the anticipation, the subject was in fact never raised at the Quebec Conference.
frus-1944-quebec-d259:
The secretaries' note in C.C.S. 520/6, dated September 14, 1944, transmits the approved directive on strategic bomber control. Executive responsibility for the bomber forces in Europe was vested jointly in the Chief of the Air Staff, RAF, and the Commanding General, United States Army Air Forces. Bottomley and Spaatz were designated their representatives on the spot, providing control and local coordination through consultation.

The directive states the bombers' over-all mission: the progressive destruction and dislocation of the German military, industrial, and economic systems, and direct support of land and naval forces. Attacks would follow the objective priorities Eisenhower had established unless the two commanders judged changes necessary. The German Air Force, its fighting effectiveness substantially reduced, was no longer a primary objective; Germany's war economy was.
frus-1944-quebec-d59:
H. Freeman Matthews of the State Department wrote to Ray Atherton, the American ambassador in Canada, on September 6, 1944. Matthews directed European affairs work at the department. The letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Writing to the ambassador in the host country six days before a conference meant arranging the department's part on the ground: staff, papers, and contact with the Canadians. Atherton's Ottawa embassy was the conference's local base. For readers, the letter shows the State Department planting its flag in Canada ahead of the leaders, in the practical way that makes diplomacy function.
frus-1945-50-intel-d159:
Minutes record the Sixth Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board on 28 June 1946. It stands as document 159 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time.

Minutes trade color for proof: they may skip the tone of a talk, but they pin down its outcome. Later fights over who agreed to what often end with a page like this one. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d259:
On 17 February 1948, the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan) sent a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett). The State Department prints it as document 259 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d359:
Dated 19 January 1949, this letter runs from Robert Blum of the Office of the Secretary of Defense to Allen W. Dulles. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 359 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Reform of the CIA was in the air, with the Dulles survey under way and each agency guarding its own role.

Letters between senior men often carried the real weight of a matter, since a signed letter put the writer's name and office behind the words. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d59:
General Malin Craig, chief of the War Department's operations division, wrote to the members of the Lovett Committee on 18 December 1945. An operations chief writing to an intelligence study group crosses staff lines. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Craig's view mattered because operations consumes intelligence: the men who plan campaigns know what they need to know. His memorandum brought the user's voice into the Lovett group's work at a late stage. Readers can watch the War Department still feeding views into the study even as the secretaries neared agreement. The overlap of committees, letters, and minutes in December is the volume's picture of a government deciding by accumulation.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d159:
Stettinius urged a fast reply to Stalin on 29 December 1944, before Moscow recognized the Lublin Committee. His memorandum to the President is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Stalin's answer of 27 December was the trigger.

In that answer, Stalin refused the President's request to hold off recognition of the Lublin body as Poland's provisional government. He went further, suggesting that Washington and the other allies do the same. Recognition is expected on 31 December, Stettinius warns. The answer should be in Stalin's hands before that date, even though the President returns only tomorrow. A draft reply is attached, drawn along the lines of the British stand in Churchill's telegram of 16 December.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d259:
Admiral King turned to the Kurile Islands in a Joint Chiefs paper of 11 December 1944. His memorandum, J. C. S. 1176/2, is titled “Operations in the Kuriles” and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. King commanded the fleet and served as chief of naval operations.

The paper grows out of the staff studies on Russian entry into the Pacific war. King agrees that the time has come for more concrete action in developing plans for the northwest Pacific. His own line is to broaden the base of operations and keep the Japanese spread out. Diversionary strokes, above all those that stop Japan from massing her air power, will help most. The Kuriles, the island chain running north from Japan toward Kamchatka, are weighed in that light.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d359:
Staging American bombers near Vienna and Budapest came before the Joint Chiefs at Yalta on February 7, 1945. Admiral Leahy laid out a staff paper on using the Fifteenth Air Force in that area. The planners advised asking the President to seek Stalin's agreement. Bases in the Budapest area would host elements of the force.

The chiefs found no objection and backed the paper. The item sits oddly at Yalta, where Germany's fate led the agenda. Yet it mattered: Soviet armies were overrunning the very ground American planes hoped to use. Even airfields needed the alliance's permission by February 1945.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d459:
Bohlen's note on the last plenary session, February 11, 1945, centers on credit for the voting plan. The communiqué was debated in detail, he records, and most talk dealt with language. The Soviet side suggested one change: the communiqué should not say the accepted proposal had been put forward by the President.

Stalin said he had no objection to the President, or any American official, stating publicly that the American proposal had been adopted. But such a reference, he felt, did not properly belong in a communiqué. The Soviet suggestion was adopted. The note, filed in the Bohlen Collection, shows vanity and diplomacy being balanced line by line.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d59:
President Roosevelt cabled Ambassador Harriman on 16 January 1945 with a personal request about food at Yalta. The short top secret message appears in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It shows the President planning his daily routine weeks before the talks began.

Roosevelt wants his own mess set up ashore, with his own stewards and cooks. The point is to keep his usual diet during the conference. Supplies would come from the ship Catoctin. He asks Harriman to arrange it without offending the Russian hosts, a small detail that reveals how carefully the trip was stage-managed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d159:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded a conscience-clearing talk with the President in an extract dated June 18, 1945. The extract is document 159 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Grew had drafted a statement calling on Japan to surrender unconditionally, meant for release when Okinawa fell.

Truman liked the idea, Grew writes, but decided to hold it until the Big Three could discuss it. Grew says he spoke up so his conscience would be clear. He had left out no step that might save the lives of thousands of American fighting men. That held so long as Japan was still rendered powerless for the future. The President asked him to put the subject on the summit agenda. The debate fed into the surrender demand the Allies issued from Potsdam in July.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d259:
A briefing paper fixed the American line on Europe's borders, in extracts dated June 29, 1945. The paper is document 259 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It formed an annex to the State Department's agenda memorandum and covered territorial settlements across the continent.

The extract printed here covers Germany's northern edge. The United States is opposed, it says, to revising the Danish-German frontier, unless such a change proves necessary in connection with a possible internationalization of the Kiel Canal. Other extracts of the same paper appear elsewhere in the volume, dealing with the bigger questions, above all the German-Polish frontier. The Danish point is small, but it shows the care with which the briefing book settled even minor border questions before the leaders met.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d359:
Restitution of looted property is coordinated in a Washington cable to Pauley dated June 26, 1945. It passes on a message the Joint Chiefs had sent General Eisenhower at the President's request on June 23. The President had approved a recommendation of Pauley's about removals from land held by American forces in Germany and Austria.

Under the rule, any removal of property for restitution first needed approval from the American representative on the Reparations Commission. Such coordination was essential, the message says, because restitution touched broad reparations policy. Yet it was not to delay unduly the return of works of art to the countries they were taken from.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d459:
Revised strength figures for Bulgaria arrive in Kirk's cable from Caserta of July 3, 1945, reporting General Oxley once more. The Bulgarian Army, Oxley said, should now be read as thirteen infantry divisions, one cavalry division, one guards division at Sofia, and one armored division in process of formation. The Red Army's strength in Bulgaria he estimated at 250,000 men.

Most Soviet aircraft, the report adds, are in Bulgaria, and airfields north and south of the Balkan mountains will be taken into use. Kirk also notes a Bulgarian War Ministry bulletin giving British strength in Greece as nine motorized infantry divisions. The figures are false, he remarks, but Moscow may let them stand to justify its own buildup.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d559:
Alexander Kirk, the U.S. ambassador in Italy, reported from Caserta on June 19, 1945. His wire is document 559 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It follows talks between Allied and Yugoslav officers over Venezia Giulia, the land around Trieste.

Kirk passes on word from General Morgan at 13 Corps. Three Yugoslav envoys had gone to Belgrade to consult and were due back at noon on June 18. Talks would not restart until June 19. The point that most troubled the Yugoslavs was civil rule in the zone. They had set up committees on the Russian model, while the Allies meant to use their own military government system.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d59:
Only part of President Truman's June 14, 1945 message to Stalin is printed as document 59 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. One paragraph is left out and can be found in the published Stalin correspondence. What remains is Truman's warm closing, sent as the two leaders prepared to meet in person near Berlin.

Truman says he is confident that the friendly understanding and cooperation built during the war against the Nazis will go on to preserve peace and goodwill between their countries. He looks forward with much pleasure to meeting Stalin soon and talking over their shared problems in full. The friendly tone belongs to the last weeks before Potsdam, when open Allied friction over Europe was already growing beneath it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d659:
Ambassador Caffery sent the agreed text for notifying Moscow about Tangier from Paris on June 27, 1945. The secret wire is document 659 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The British ambassador in Moscow and the French charge would deliver it on June 30.

The message says the end of the war in Europe makes it timely to act. Spain should be called on to withdraw its troops and administration from the Tangier zone. Britain and France, with the United States, are preparing talks in Paris to concert that approach. The talks will also settle details for restoring an international regime on a provisional basis. A new Tangier convention would be negotiated later. The Soviet government, the message promises, will be kept informed of developments.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1059:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled the Secretary of State at Potsdam on July 17, 1945, about supervising the coming Greek elections. A British draft proposed that the four Allied governments share the task. Washington agrees in substance, but objects to framing the approach as an invitation to Moscow and Paris.

The cable offers substitute wording. It rests on Allied duties to Greece and the pledges made at Yalta. Greece's own government, a party to the Varkiza Agreement, has accepted supervision by the four Allies named. The draft voices earnest hope that the Soviet and French governments will agree to take part. Byrnes may settle timing and phrasing with the British at the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1159:
Winant cabled from London again on 19 July 1945, his second dispatch in two days. The pace shows how closely the embassy reported during the summit's first week. British politics were in suspense, with an election count due within the week.

Each dispatch layered fresh detail onto Washington's picture of its ally. The home office could weigh British stands at Potsdam against the mood Winant heard at home. This cable keeps that running account going. It is a small part of a large flow, but the flow itself is the story: a wartime embassy working at full stretch.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1259:
Sato cabled Togo on 28 July 1945, the day Tokyo's premier spoke to the press about the Allied terms. The Moscow envoy's reports kept arriving while Japan's leaders stalled in public. His channel was now the only live move Tokyo had left.

Sato could report only what Moscow gave him: courtesy, delay, and no firm word. Behind the delay, Soviet armies were massing in the east for their own entry into the war. The envoy sensed the trap more clearly than Tokyo did. This dispatch is his word from that day, part of the secret thread the Allies read in full.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1359:
J. Rives Childs reported again from the Tangier talks to the acting secretary of state on 26 July 1945. His first report in the volume is dated eight days earlier. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Talks about Tangier moved slowly, since several powers claimed a say in the port city's rule. A second report lets readers measure what changed across a week of negotiation. Childs wrote for a Washington audience that was watching Potsdam first and Tangier second, so his papers had to make a small city's case clearly. The pair of reports shows patient, detailed work on a question most histories pass over in a line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-159: This editorial note appears unnumbered after document 710 in the second volume of the Potsdam papers. Written by the Foreign Relations editors, it guides readers at a point where the files grow dense. Such notes cite sources, explain links, and mark missing pieces. The note keeps the reader's footing sure near the conference's close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-59:
An editorial note in volume two of the Potsdam papers draws on Stimson's diary for July 22, 1945. No official record of the conversation has been found, the editors say. Stimson, Bundy, and Lord Cherwell talked with Churchill at British headquarters for over an hour that morning.

Stimson records that Churchill read Groves' report in full at the meeting. Churchill then told him what he had noticed at the Three's session the day before. Truman, Churchill said, was evidently much fortified by something that had happened. He stood up to the Russians in a most emphatic and decisive manner, Churchill said. He told them that on certain demands they absolutely could not have their way. Now I know what happened to Truman yesterday, Churchill added. Reading the report had made Truman a changed man, and Churchill felt the same lift himself.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d759:
The British delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 27, 1945, as document 759. It arrived just as Attlee returned with a new government behind him. British texts carried the alliance's second voice. This one joined the numbered papers of the second Potsdam volume.

A British proposal lets readers triangulate the talks. Where London's draft sits between Washington's and Moscow's, the deal's center comes clear. The document also shows a new government acting fast. Attlee's team had days, not months, to shape its line. The proposal stands as proof of how quickly the British machine reset itself mid-conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d859:
Document 859 is a draft of the Economic Subcommittee's report, dated July 18, 1945. Drafts preceded the report the conference later received. This early version shows the experts' first framing of the economic questions. It was kept with the conference files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A draft report lets readers watch judgment form. Lines that later hardened appear here still soft. The document pairs with the subcommittee's finished report in this run. Between the two, the group's mind can be seen changing. Such pairs are the surest guide to how expert bodies actually work: slowly, in writing, toward a text all can sign.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d959:
Josiah DuBois, a member of the American reparations delegation, wrote this legal memorandum for Edwin Pauley, filed with the July 29, 1945 papers. The question is whether gold held by American forces at Frankfurt may be treated as war booty. That question stands even where the gold's source can be traced.

DuBois reviews the Allied pledge not to honor transfers of looted gold. He then cites the Hague rules, which let an occupier seize state property usable for war. The gold, he concludes, was plainly used on behalf of the German state. On strict law, apart from policy, it may be treated as booty.
frus-1952-54v10-d259: A 1952-1954 FRUS editorial note on joint U, s, action regarding iran. The coup against Mossadegh approached. This note provides that background. Later readers can locate it. History keeps its place secure. It is kept for readers to consult. It is kept for study by scholars.
frus-1961-63v11-d59: A 1961-1963 FRUS editorial note from the Missile Crisis volume. The background. This note provides that context. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
frus-1969-76v01-d59: A 1969-1976 FRUS memorandum from the foundations volume. The new administration's thinking. This document preserves that memo. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
gao-gaoreports-b-295959: International Outsourcing Services took its May 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297959: NCR Government Systems doubled its May 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298259: Southwest Educational Development Laboratory took its July 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The lab said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Research outfits get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298759: Symetrics Industries took its October 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298859: Squires Timber Company took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Timber deals get the same full hearing as the tech ones.
gao-gaoreports-b-299859: Alpha Genesis challenged a 2007 federal award, and GAO's ruling gives the final answer. The firm said the bid process was unfair; the call tests each claim and closes the book. For research and service firms in the government market, the verdict is another line in the fair-bidding code.
gao-gaoreports-b-310759: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Tiger Truck LLC. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-259: A thin GAO record from 2005 — docket gao-05-259 — survives mostly as a title. The metadata offers little more than the identifier. The entry marks its place in the catalog. The record was thin. The entry marks its place in the catalog.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-459: Small shops' slice of DOE contracts needed watching in 2005, and GAO's report says a sharper eye could keep the door open. The findings demand the vigilance. The report warns that the small shops deserved their share. The small shops deserved their share.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-859: The visa process needed staffing and sharing in 2005, and GAO's report says improvements in personnel and information exchange would help. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the borders deserved well-run gates. The improvements had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-259: Immigration benefit fraud needed more controls in 2006, and GAO's report says additional safeguards and a sanctions strategy could enhance DHS's control. The findings demand the tools. The report warns that the benefit pipeline should not leak. The controls had to be added.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-59: Medicare therapy payments were poorly targeted in 2005, and GAO's report says little progress had been made in matching payments to needs. The findings target the waste. The report warns that the patients deserved needs-based care. The progress had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-659: The Fed's auction computers needed securing in 2006, and GAO's report says the Federal Reserve had to address the Treasury auction systems. The findings target the vulnerabilities. The report warns that the nation's debt sales needed locked-down tech. The systems had to be secure.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-859: Homeless veterans' programs needed better follow-up in 2006, and GAO's report says improved communication could enhance the grant program. The findings demand the outreach. The report warns that the street's veterans deserved persistent help. The programs had to reach them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-159: The District's buying system was broken in 2007, and GAO's report says the procurement setup needed major reform. The findings demand the overhaul. The report warns that the capital's contracts deserved better than chaos. The city had to buy like it meant it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-259: Reserve troops' job rights needed better policing in 2007, and GAO's report says more action was required to oversee employment protections. The findings demand the enforcement. The report's cause: those who serve should not lose their jobs for it. The uniform should not cost a career.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-559: Handshake deals were hiding in the Pentagon's books in 2007 — GAO's report says open-ended contract actions were undercounted and slow to get finalized. The findings expose the paperwork limbo where billions sat. The report demands that handshake buying get real contracts, and get them fast.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-59: Medicare's medical-equipment bills were full of errors in 2007, and GAO's report says improvements were needed to curb the improper payments. The findings target the waste. The report warns that the wheelchair invoices needed a closer look. The program was paying for ghosts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-759: Tank-killing tech needed a fair trial in 2007 — GAO's report dissects how the Pentagon judged active protection systems for armored vehicles. The findings grade the evaluation game. The report asks whether the best shield won, or just the best-connected bidder.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-159: This 2007 GAO report takes a hard look at military Base Realignments and Closures: Cost Estimates Have Increased and Are Likely to Continue to Evolve. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-359: GAO published its findings on medicare Advantage: Increased Spending Relative to Medicare Fee-for-Service May Not Always Reduce Beneficiary Out-of-Pocket Costs in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-59: This 2007 GAO report grades U.S. trade deals struck under fast-track rules — the process that lets the White House cut pacts Congress then votes up or down. GAO checks whether the deal-makers heard out Congress and private firms as the law demands. The report gives Congress a scorecard on talks that shape jobs and prices at home.
goncharov-oblomov-1859:
Ivan Goncharov published Oblomov in 1859, his comic-tragic monument to Russian inertia in one Petersburg flat. Ilya Oblomov cannot rise from his sofa, and his gown became shorthand for a whole social disease. Oblomovshchina, the word the novel coined, indicted the gentry's sloth for the rest of the century.

Oblomov plans to reform his estate, answer letters, and rise by noon, and fails at all three daily. His friend Stolz, half German and all energy, drags him into society and to Olga, who loves and tests him. Olga's love nearly wakes him, but the sofa, the gown, and Agafya's quiet kitchen win him back for good. He dies, stout and still, having chosen the peace of Oblomovka, his childhood paradise of sleep and food, over life. Goncharov's pity keeps the satire human, and Oblomov remains Russia's most loved failure.
greenmantle-pg559: Buchan's Richard Hannay returns in this First World War thriller set across Germany and the Ottoman Empire. Disguised and traveling under false names, Hannay and his companions race to uncover a German scheme to ignite a Muslim holy war against the Allies. Written by a man who worked in British intelligence, the novel blends real wartime fear with the non-stop pursuit that made the Hannay books famous.
helvetius-de-lesprit-1759:
Claude Adrien Helvétius published De l'Esprit, On Mind, in Paris in 1758, and the London English translation of 1759 is the text here. The book, Englished as Essays on the Mind, and its Several Faculties, was burned by the hangman in France for its bold materialist psychology. Helvétius was forced to recant, and the scandal made his fame.

His doctrine holds that self-interest is the spring of all judgment and morals. Men call actions just or unjust as those actions help or harm them and theirs. Education and law, then, can shape virtue by shaping interest. The argument shocked its age and fed the radical thought of the next. It still bites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowisohn-solomo:
Solomon Löwisohn (1788–1821) was a Hungarian historian and poet born at Mor, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Alexander Büchler tells his brief life. He studied at the yeshivah of Prague, then worked as a corrector in a Vienna printing house. He died in his hometown at about thirty-three.

The article lists his Hebrew dialogue of 1811, his poems of 1816, and his work on the geography of the Bible. It also notes his essay on the language of the Mishnah, his translations of festival prayers, and his history lectures of 1820, of which only the first volume appeared. His most important work, the entry says, was that unfinished history. The profile preserves the record of an early Hebrew writer whose career ended before his main project could be completed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maggid-10259:
Maggid, the itinerant Jewish preacher, is portrayed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. A maggid was a storyteller-preacher, distinct from the darshan, the scholarly lecturer who usually held a rabbinic post. The full title maggid mesharim, preacher of uprightness, dates from about the sixteenth century. Jewish leadership, the article says, always had these two classes.

The entry shows why the maggid drew crowds. Early preachers built sermons on questions from the audience, as the Passover Haggadah still does. People once left Rabbi Hiyya's lecture room to hear Rabbi Abbahu preach. Abbahu soothed Hiyya by comparing them to merchants, one selling diamonds, the other trinkets in greater demand. Some preachers mixed law and lore in one talk to please every listener. Others, like Rabbi Ze'era, scorned preachers who twisted verses to suit the moment. The article gives a lively picture of popular preaching across the centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meier-moritz-he:
Moritz Hermann Eduard Meier, a German philologist of Greek law and oratory, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman. Born at Glogau, in Silesia, on January 1, 1796, he studied at Berlin, Breslau, and Berlin again, taking his doctorate in 1818; he had embraced Christianity the year before. After a start at Greifswald he became professor of ancient philology at Halle in 1825 and stayed there until his death on December 5, 1855.

With Schömann he wrote "Der Attische Process," on Athenian legal procedure, which won the Berlin Academy's prize. The entry lists his studies of Andocides, of Lycurgus, of Athenian arbitrators and public hospitality, and his edition of Demosthenes against Meidias. It also credits his editorial labor on journals and on the great Ersch and Gruber encyclopedia, whose sections he steered for decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendelsburg-leo:
Leon Mendelsburg, a Russian teacher and writer, is profiled by Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hodava in Russian Poland in 1819. He studied Talmud at Tomashov. Then he spent his working life in the government's Jewish schools. He was appointed teacher at Novograd-Volhynsk in 1850. In 1854 he moved to the rabbinical school at Jitomir. He stayed until the government closed the school in 1873. He settled at Koretz and later at Warsaw, where he died in March 1897.

Alongside the classroom he wrote, in German, for the "Allgemeine Zeitung des Judenthums." From 1850 onward he contributed papers the entry calls valuable. They treat the life of the Jews in Russia. They give intelligence from inside a world few German readers knew. His one book, "Dichtung und Wahrheit," Poetry and Truth, printed at Leipzig in 1862, sketches Russo-Jewish life for that same audience.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-moritz-10:
Moritz Meyer, a Berlin physician born on November 10, 1821, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman, published in 1906. He studied at Heidelberg, Halle, and Berlin, took his degree in 1844, and practiced in Berlin for the rest of his life. His specialty was diseases of the nerves.

Meyer treated nervous illness with electricity and, during his research, invented an instrument for testing how muscles and nerves react, known as the Meyersche Unterbrecher. His book on electricity applied to practical medicine appeared in 1854 and reached a fourth edition in 1883. He also wrote several articles on paralysis brought on by the constant use of snuff.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minor-solomon-z:
Solomon Zalkind Minor, born at Wilna in 1827, was the model crown rabbi of nineteenth-century Russia, in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman, published in 1906. His father, a known Talmudist, started him; from twelve he studied Bible and rabbinics alone. When Wilna's rabbinical seminary opened in 1849 he was among its first graduates.

He taught Talmud at the seminary from 1854 and became the governor-general's adviser on Jewish affairs, preaching in German an ideal of the rabbi as his flock's guardian and advocate.
