As rabbi of Minsk from 1860 he opened a Sabbath-school, a night-school for artisans, and a community library. Moscow called him in 1869, where a congregation had just been formed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-acan-hazz:
Moses Açan de Zaragua was a Spanish poet born in Catalonia, known for a poem on the game of chess. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He may be the Moses Açan who warned King Alfonso the Wise, at Cuenca in 1271, of a plot against him. The plotters were the infante Philip and the grandees of Castile.

His chess poem, written in Catalan, opens with an account of the creation of the world. In it he condemns gambling and singles out card playing as harmful. The poem was translated into Castilian about 1350, and the text survives in manuscript in the Escorial. The short entry preserves a minor voice in medieval Spanish Jewish letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nabatans-11259:
The Nabataeans were a Semitic people who overran the old Edomite country and built a kingdom reaching from Damascus to Hegra. George A. Barton wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article, with the editorial committee. Their capital was Petra, the Selah of the Old Testament. By 312 before Christ they already held the land against Greek kings.

The article clears them of confusion with the Nebajoth of Genesis and follows their caravan trade through Petra to Babylonia. Their coins name kings such as Aretas the Third and Aretas the Fourth, under whom Paul made his escape from Damascus. Nabataean troops aided Titus at Jerusalem. Under Trajan, Rome ended the kingdom and made its nearer part the province of Arabia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-ben-jehi:
Nathan ben Jehiel was an Italian maker of a great Hebrew dictionary. Wilhelm Bacher and H. G. Enelow wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Rome by 1035 and died in 1106. His family, the Anaw, was famed for Jewish learning. With his brothers he led Rome's rabbinic college.

Nathan traveled to Sicily and Narbonne to study with masters. His dictionary, the Aruk, was finished in February 1101. It drew on hundreds of older works and teachers. Hai Gaon, Hananeel, and Gershom stand among its chief sources. Its pages use Aramaic, Arabic, Persian, and Greek words. Latin, Slavonic, and Italian terms also appear in its entries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neuburger-max-1:
Max Neuburger was an Austrian doctor who wrote medicine's history. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Vienna on Dec. 8, 1868. He studied medicine at the university there. He took his degree in 1893.

After three years of hospital service, Neuburger specialized. He assisted Professor Benedikt in nervous diseases. His book on early brain and spine experiments won notice. It earned him a Vienna lectureship in medical history in 1897. He wrote on experimental pathology's beginnings next. A study of antitoxic therapy's prehistory followed in 1901. He gave chapters to Pagel's handbook of medical history. He also edited the Medizinische Blätter for two years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nissim-hayyim-b: Hayyim b. Elijah Nissim was a Turkish rabbi. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Schulim Ochser for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He probably lived in the later 1700s. Little else of his life is set down here. His one named work is Maẓa Ḥayyim. It holds homilies and comments on the Pentateuch. His son Samuel published it after him. Samuel added material of his own to the text. The book came out at Salonica in 1816.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orenstein-israe: Israel Orenstein was a Russian writer of tales and novels. Herman Rosenthal and Max Rosenthal wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Yampol, in Podolia, in 1831. At the age of twenty-one he went to live in Rumania. His first novel, in Hebrew, came out there in 1870. Its name means House of Jacob, or Tears of the Oppressed. He wrote more novels in the Jewish German tongue of the day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palaggi-hayyim-:
Hayyim Palaggi was a Turkish author and chief rabbi. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Smyrna in the year 1788. He died there in the year 1869. He was grandson, by his mother, of Joseph Hazan. He read with Isaac Gategno, an author of note.

Hayyim first led the court of his home town of Smyrna. In 1854 he was named its chief rabbi by the state. His last years were marred by loss of that post. He was put back in the post in due time, though. He held it till a year just before his death. The folk held him in great awe and love. A full troop of soldiers marched at his burial rite. He wrote twenty-six works that came out in print in life. More of his works were lost in a fire at home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parable-hebrew-:
A parable is a short tale that teaches a truth of faith. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Hebrew name is mashal, a word of wide use. That word can name a fable or a sharp saying too. The Greek word for it is the root of our word parable.

The Old Testament holds just five tales of this strict kind. A few more tales in it bear the marks of signs. One tale tells of a poor man and his one lamb. A rich man took that lamb to feed a guest at his house. The tale was told to King David by a prophet. It showed David his sin with Bathsheba, a man's wife. A second tale was told by a wise woman of Tekoah. She sought to make peace between David and his son.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pavia-gentilomo:
Eugenia Pavia-Gentilomo-Fortis was an Italian poet with deep Jewish ties. She was born at Milan in 1822 and died at Asolo in 1893. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Her Venice home drew writers and patriots for years.

She studied under the poet Luigi Carrer. Her first husband was a noted scholar of Hebrew. Her books include the poem La Regina di Saba. She also published Odi and Nuove Poesie. She wrote verses on Hebrew themes for Jewish journals. She translated medieval Hebrew poems into Italian as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pesel-graven-im:
Pesel is the Hebrew word for a graven image. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such images were carved in wood or hewn in stone. The Law expressly forbade their worship. The entry weighs the word across several books.

Gideon and Micah each kept a pesel with an ephod. King Josiah ground such idols into powder. He strewed the dust on the graves of their worshipers. In Judges the plural word puzzles translators. Some render it as quarries, not images. Scholars suggest boundary stones or a Jordan ford instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinczow-elijah-:
Elijah Pinczow was a Polish physician and Talmudist. He worked in Poland in the eighteenth century. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Few rabbis of his age wrote on mathematics. His books came out across forty years of print.

His Meleket Mahashebet treats arithmetic, algebra, and geometry. One part appeared at Frankfort in 1765, one at Berlin. His Ma'aneh Eliyahu discusses two Talmud tractates with responsa. He retold the Ikkarim as a teacher-pupil dialogue. He also published homilies and a responsa collection. Medicine and Torah shared his working life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poltava-12259:
Poltava is a government of Little Russia that came under Russian rule in 1764. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its present form dates from 1802. The census of 1897 counted 111,417 Jews there. They lived among a total of more than two million people.

The capital, also called Poltava, had a small and mostly Hasidic group at first. Growth came after a great fair moved there in 1852. A school for Jewish apprentices opened in 1861. The foes of Hasidism later built a synagogue of their own. A government rabbi served the town for twenty-three years. He helped set up schools and other bodies there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-priestly-code-1:
Priestly Code is a name made by modern scholars for one part of the Pentateuch. Emil G. Hirsch and George A. Barton wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. That part deals most with rites and rules. It treats sacrifice and cleansing above all. Its laws once formed a book of their own.

That lost book held just enough story to frame its laws. Some laws still keep their story form today. The law of circumcision is one such case. The law of the Passover is another. The article lists what the code holds, part by part. It then asks when and how the code was made.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-quemadero-quema: Quemadero was a place of execution built at Seville in Spain. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first inquisitors raised it in the year 1481. Four large statues of prophets adorned the grim place. Its own builder was a follower of Judaism in secret. He was one of the first to die by its fires. The place stood until the year 1809. Its stones were then used for walls against the French.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ramsgate-12559:
Ramsgate is a seaside town on the Kent coast of England. Joseph Jacobs and Isidore Harris wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its Jewish importance comes from Sir Moses Montefiore. In 1830 he bought the East Cliff estate there.

The article says Montefiore soon built a synagogue on the estate. Its first stone was laid in 1831. He served as its president and worshipped there often. When Lady Judith died in 1862, she was buried in its grounds. A white domed tomb rose over her grave. Seven years later he founded a college in her name. The entry ties one town to a famous man's faith and gifts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenstein-samu:
Samuel Siegmund Rosenstein was a German physician born at Berlin on February 20, 1832. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The son and grandson of rabbis, he took his medical degree in 1854.

Rosenstein taught medicine first at Gröningen, from 1866, and then at Leyden. He still held the Leyden chair when this entry was written. His chief book treats the diseases of the kidneys, in print from 1863. It reached a fourth edition in 1894, a sign of steady use. Edinburgh gave him an honorary law degree in 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saba-12959:
Saba is a Talmudic word from a root meaning to be white, or old. Crawford Howell Toy and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The short article sorts out the word's several uses in rabbinic texts.

Plainly, saba names an old man, and sabeta an old woman. A saying holds an old woman in the house a treasure, an old man ruin. The phrase that old man was long taken to mean the prophet Elijah. The tosafists, and Hai Gaon before them, rejected that reading. Saba also served as an honorific title for senior sages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samaritans-hebr:
The Samaritans are a small people living at Nablus, the ancient Shechem. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, A. Cowley, Joseph Jacobs, and Henry Minor Huxley wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. They call themselves Bene Yisrael, children of Israel.

Their separate history opens when Assyria took Samaria in 722 B.C. The city's people were deported and foreign colonists settled in their place. Lions troubled the newcomers, who blamed ignorance of the land's god. An Israelite priest sent to Bethel taught them his rites there. The result was a mixed religion, part Israelite and part idolatrous.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-san-antonio-131:
Cyrus Adler and Henry Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on San Antonio. The Spaniards founded the Texas city in 1718. It grew into the largest city in the state. Jews first settled there in 1854. That year they founded their cemetery. The article traces the community's growth from those beginnings.

The Reform congregation Beth-El was organized on May 31, 1874. A new synagogue rose on the old Travis Park site in 1903. An Orthodox congregation followed in 1890. Benevolent societies and a B'nai B'rith lodge served the town. The article also recalls Jewish soldiers and doctors in Texas history. Moses Albert Levi served as surgeon-general in Sam Houston's army. He was present at the taking of the Alamo in 1835.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scherschewski-j:
Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Judah Jüdel ben Benjamin Scherschewski. He was a Lithuanian Talmudist and Hebraist. Scherschewski was born in 1804. He died at Kovno on September 20, 1866. He studied under Jacob Meïr Yalovker. For years he worked in a Wilna business house. In his spare hours he read rabbinic works and haskalah writings.

In 1852 Scherschewski became teacher of Talmud at the Wilna rabbinical seminary. He held that post until his death. His Kur la-Zahab treats hard sayings of the Talmuds. Its first part comments on 109 haggadic passages. Its second part adds an essay on the old sages' beliefs. It then comments on 138 more passages. He also wrote a sermon and hymn for Alexander the Second's coronation. In his last years he wrote often for Ha-Karmel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scythians-13359:
Joseph Jacobs and Ira Maurice Price wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Scythians. They were a nomadic people north of the Black Sea. Their land stretched east of the Carpathian Mountains. Herodotus tells how they swept down over Media. They reached the Mediterranean shore, even Egypt's threshold. That invasion fell between 628 and 610 B.C.

Egypt's king bought the Scythians off, and they went home. As foragers and pillagers, they left no government behind them. A Palestinian city bore the name Scythopolis, earlier Beth-shean. No one knows if these barbarians gave it that name. Many think Jeremiah pictured their ravages. Ezekiel's northern hordes may also reflect them. Some link the Bible's Ashkenaz with Scythia. Paul names the Scythian as the far edge of mankind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sextus-julius-a:
Julius Africanus was a Byzantine chronographer of the early third century. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He won note for clear thinking on hard Bible questions. Writers of his age called him a Libyan philosopher.

His Greek works show Latin learning, pointing to Latin North African roots. He joined an imperial campaign in 195 and knew Abgar of Edessa well. Edessa's archives fed much of his writing. He also knew Syriac and conditions among Babylonian Jews. The entry presents a Christian scholar whose travels and languages shaped his Bible work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemini-azeret-:
Shemini Azeret is the eighth day of the festival of Sukkot. Kaufmann Kohler and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the day. Its name appears in Leviticus, Numbers, Nehemiah, and Chronicles. The word azeret means a day of assembly, scholars say.

Deuteronomy never mentions this eighth day at all. It appears only in priestly parts of the Bible. Because Passover's seventh day shares the same name, azeret came to mean closing festival. Rabbis noted Sukkot's closing feast might have fallen fifty days later. That would match the pattern set by Passover's close. God spared the people another hard journey, they said. The entry unpacks a one-day festival with a surprisingly tangled history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silberstein-mic:
Michael Silberstein was a German rabbi born at Witzenhausen in 1834. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He trained at Breslau's Jewish seminary and Berlin University. He took his doctorate in 1860 after ordination.

Silberstein served rabbinates at Lyck, Buttenhausen, and Mühringen in turn. From 1884 he officiated at Wiesbaden in Germany. He helped draft a new law for Württemberg's Jewish communities in 1869. In 1882 he spoke at the poet Auerbach's funeral. His writings include sermons and a life of Moses Mendelssohn. He also treated the social question through Mosaic legislation. A Gabriel Riesser study and a religion textbook followed. The entry lists a busy pulpit scholar of liberal Germany.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simson-martin-e:
Martin Eduard von Simson was a German jurist and statesman born in 1810. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied law at Königsberg, Berlin, Bonn, and Paris. By 1836 he was professor of Roman law at Königsberg. He also served as a judge there.

In 1848 Simson sat in the National Congress at Frankfort. He became its president that December. He led the group that offered the German crown to Frederick William IV. Later he presided over the first German Reichstag. In 1879 he became first president of the German Supreme Court. He was ennobled in 1888 and retired in 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-eno:
Solomon ben Enoch al-Kustantini was a Spanish exegete of the fourteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Grätz thought he belonged to the Al-Kustantini family of Saragossa. Members of that family took part in the fight over Maimonides. Solomon wrote on the Pentateuch in that charged setting.

His commentary is called Megalleh Amukkot, revealer of deep things. It survives in manuscript in the Vatican Library today. Samuel Zarza of Valencia quotes it in his own commentary. Solomon firmly believed in astrology as a real force. He tried to prove from Bible and Talmud one claim. The stars, he held, greatly shape the fate of man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spielmann-mario:
Marion H Spielmann was an English author and art critic born in 1858. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in London on May 22 of that year. He was educated at University College School and University College. He began as art critic on the Pall Mall Gazette in 1883.

He wrote there on G F Watts and Henriette Ronner. In 1891 he helped found the paper Black and White. From 1898 to 1905 he edited the Magazine of Art. His books include a History of Punch from 1895. He also wrote on Millais, on Ruskin, and on British sculpture. He served as sole English juror at Brussels in 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theodore-of-mop:
Theodore of Mopsuestia was a Christian bishop and famed Bible interpreter. Crawford Howell Toy and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born and schooled at Antioch, he died around 429. He taught both Nestorius and Theodoret. His school favored plain historical reading over allegory.

At twenty he published a commentary on the Psalms. It stayed his most valued work for exegesis. As bishop he fought Arian and other heresies. After his death, a church council branded his books heretical. The charge said he read the Psalms in a Jewish fashion. Modern scholars instead praise his grammar and history. The article calls him centuries ahead of his time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-totbrief-14459:
A Tötbrief was a royal edict that canceled Christian debts to Jews. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Kings, emperors, and popes all issued such decrees in Germany and France. A decree might kill only the interest owed. Others wiped out principal and interest together.

Louis VII issued the first known Tötbrief in 1146. It freed all Crusaders from debts to Jews. Philip Augustus later freed Christians for a fifth paid to himself. Louis VIII voided debts five years old in 1223. Fourteenth-century Germany saw cancellations grow common. Emperors freed towns, abbeys, and nobles from Jewish claims. Under King Wenzel the practice reached vast proportions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uceda-samuel-be:
Samuel ben Israel de Uceda was a Palestinian commentator and preacher from Safed. Wilhelm Bacher and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there early in the sixteenth century. His family name came from Uceda in Spain. He studied Cabala under Isaac Luria and Hayyim Vital.

He served as rabbi and preacher at Safed, then Constantinople. His Iggeret Shemu'el comments on the Book of Ruth. It appeared in 1557 with Rashi's notes alongside. Lehem Dim'ah treats Lamentations in the same format. His chief work, Midrash Shemu'el, covers Pirke Abot in detail. It draws on many commentaries then still in manuscript. Most of those have since reached print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-veil-14659:
A veil is a cloth cover worn over the face. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In early times a veil marked modesty in married women. Brides wore veils when meeting strangers. The custom still held in the East when this article was written.

The entry gathers Bible cases of veil use. Rebekah veiled herself when she first met Isaac. The Mishnah describes a veiled bride carried in the wedding march. Moses veiled his face after Sinai, since his skin shone brightly. Tamar used a veil as a disguise to mislead Judah. Each case shows a different use for the same cloth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-walden-aaron-be:
Aaron ben Isaiah Nathan Walden was a Polish Talmudist and editor. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Walden was born at Warsaw about 1835. He was a devoted follower of Hasidism. His fame rests on a biographical dictionary.

That work, Shem ha Gedolim he Hadash, appeared in 1864. It follows Azulai's famous model. One part lists authors and rabbis by name. The other lists book titles in order. Many entries tell of Hasidic rabbis and their miracles. His son later added an appendix of missed names. Walden also issued a five volume Psalms with rich commentary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weights-and-mea:
Weights and measures in the Bible form an old Hebrew system. Emil G. Hirsch, Immanuel Benzinger, Joseph Jacobs, and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Scripture gives the links between units clearly. Their exact modern sizes stay less certain. Rabbinic clues, like barley grains, are too loose.

The system matches the Babylonian one almost exactly. Scholars therefore derive the Hebrew standard from Babylon. Egypt's system left smaller marks here and there. Length began with the human body. Finger, hand, span, and pace were the first units. The cubit, of two spans, became the fixed standard. The entry works through length, weight, and volume in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wellhausen-juli:
Julius Wellhausen was a German Bible critic and Semitist. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hameln on May 17, 1844. He studied theology and Semitics at Göttingen. He taught there, then at Greifswald. His views on the Bible cost him his theology chair in 1882.

Wellhausen then taught Semitics at Halle and Marburg. In 1892 he returned to Göttingen. His early works treat Samuel's text and tribal Israel. His fame rests on Pentateuch analysis. He systematized the theory of its late sources. That theory dates the Priestly Code after the exile. His name now anchors modern Bible criticism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wissotzky-kalon:
Kalonymos Zeeb Wolf Wissotzky (1824-1904) was a Russian tea merchant and giver to good causes. Herman Rosenthal and Abraham Lubarsky wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Zhagory, he studied for a time at the Volozhin school. In 1858 he settled in Moscow and entered the tea trade.

Wealth did not pull him away from his town's Jewish life. He set up a Sabbath school and readings for Jewish soldiers near Moscow. He also gave Passover meals to those men. His gifts grew with his means over the years. He gave a large sum to the Alliance in Paris as a long-term fund. He backed early Zionist work with time and cash. He paid for much of the Bet ha-Sefer school in Jaffa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yannai-15059:
Yannai was the first hymn poet to use rime and name signs. Gotthard Deutsch and H. Brody wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked most likely in Palestine in the early 600s. Men spoke of the hymns of Yannai as a known set.

He is said to have made hymn sets for the whole year. Most of his work is lost to us now. Some of it may live on with no name to mark it. Three scraps show his style and craft to readers. One is a hymn set for the Great Sabbath. One is a work for the last day of Passover. One is a close piece for a Sabbath before the Ninth of Ab. His verse is less dark than that of Jose ben Jose.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zamosz-joseph-b:
Joseph ben Jacob Isaac Zamosz was a Polish rabbi of the 1700s. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as rabbi of the town of Zamosz. His chief work bears the name Mishnat Hakamim in Hebrew.

That work sorts the laws of the faith by their root. It shows which laws come from the Torah text itself. It shows which laws were added by the scribes of old. The work stands in two parts with clear aims. One part sets out the words of the old sages in plain form. One part gives fine points of law in case form. A set of notes on a work of Maimonides ends the book. He names a lost work of his on the feast laws there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zenobia-septimi:
Zenobia Septimia was empress of Palmyra and a foe of Rome. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She ruled as regent from 267 to 273 of this era. She ruled for her young son, who bore an empire rank.

She seems to have been a friend to the Jews then. Some tales claim she was of Jewish stock by birth. Those tales lack firm proof, the entry notes with care. Her tie to Jews stands in a Talmud note as well. In a brief span she spread her sway in the East. Her rule ran over all of Egypt and Syria in time. Rome's chief feared she would break faith with Rome. In 272 he made war on her realm and won it. He led her in gold chains through Rome in pomp.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zimmer-nathan-l:
Nathan Löb David Zimmer was an English scholar famed for deep piety and learning. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Fürth, Bavaria, in March 1831, he died in London on January 10, 1895. He came to England about 1850 and entered business.

Business came second to study for Zimmer, above all the hidden commentaries of the Cabala. His grasp of gematria, the reading of words by letter values, was profound. He also loved working out dates and calendars from the stars. Zimmer helped found the London Federation of Synagogues and wrote often for the Jewish press. Some saw him as the original of Karlkammer in Zangwill's Children of the Ghetto.
lady-hester-or-ursula-s-narrative-pg4659:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Lady Hester is told by Ursula, a member of the family. She writes so that future reports of their history will be correct. The old days at Trevorsham already seem remote to her.

The contents promise a peerage case, a farm, and a white doe's warning. Hunting and duck shooting bring outdoor scenes. A legacy from Trevor shapes later events. Yonge blends family chronicle with quiet suspense. This Project Gutenberg copy matches the other edition of the same novel in the library. Yonge sets private family honor against public legal claims. The peerage question gives old griefs a fresh, sharp edge.
lavater-de-spectris-latin-1659:
Ludwig Lavater, a Zurich pastor, wrote his book on specters in the sixteenth century. This Latin edition of 1659 covers specters, lemures, and great and unusual noises, the full range of things that go bump in a Reformed night. Lavater gives Swiss Protestant demonology of apparitions its learned form.

He sorts apparitions into kinds and tests each against Scripture. Some he allows as souls or angels, and others he assigns to demons or fraud. Strange noises receive the same patient treatment. The book took ghosts seriously at a high scholarly level. Protestant Switzerland's care with the spirit world speaks here, thorough, biblical, and wary of Rome's purgatory alike.
linnaeus-systema-naturae-vol2-1759:
Volume 2 of Linnaeus's Systema Naturae, tenth edition, appeared in 1759. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands in Latin. Volume 1 had covered animals; Volume 2 completes the system with the plant and mineral kingdoms, Vegetabilia and Mineralia.

Plants are sorted by Linnaeus's sexual system, counting stamens and pistils to place each kind. The mineral kingdom follows, classed by his scheme of earths, salts, and stones. Later botany replaced his plant system with natural families, but his two-part names endured. The volume completes the 1758 and 1759 baseline from which modern naming of living things is reckoned.
nightingale-notes-on-hospitals-1859:
Notes on Hospitals, from 1859, made Florence Nightingale a founder of hospital design. The volume joins two papers she read at Liverpool on ward construction. Her Royal Commission evidence and her articles from the Builder stand alongside them. Together they argue that buildings themselves can heal or kill.

Bad air, crowding, and poor drainage, she shows, drive hospital death rates up. Wide wards, windows, and space between beds drive them down. Her evidence rests on numbers gathered across many hospitals. The book began evidence based thinking about hospital architecture. Builders and doctors still cite its rules. It shows statistics turned into brick and air.
onomatologia-curiosa-artificiosa-et-magi: An unknown compiler published this German lexicon in 1759. Its title promises a natural magic lexicon in alphabetical order. The record lists over fifteen hundred columns of entries. Subjects include natural science, mathematics, and household arts. The hosted sample preserves garbled scan text of the title page. Readers can confirm the title and scope from that page. Clear body text cannot be read in this sample.
openalex-w1917539659:
Chittaranjan Kole, Manoj Prasad, and many co-authors wrote this review. It appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science in August 2015. Climate change now cuts farm yields across the world, they note. Rising food prices signal drastic edible yield loss ahead. Plant scientists must breed crops that withstand warming.

Genomics-assisted breeding uses DNA data to speed crop improvement. The review surveys progress and prospects in that field. It covers tools that link genes to stress tolerance traits. Heat, drought, and flood resilience are central concerns. The authors chart how genomics can guide faster breeding. Their aim is crops ready for a harsher climate.
openalex-w1966542159:
María Falcone Ferreyra, Sebastián Rius, and Paula Casati wrote this review. It appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2012. All three authors worked in Rosario, Argentina. Flavonoids are plant compounds with many metabolic roles. They color flowers and shield plants from stress.

Genes switch flavonoid production on and off in plants. Three families of control factors guide that process, they review. Knowing the pathways lets growers and breeders adjust them. Uses in farming and biotechnology follow from that control. The review maps synthesis, function, and applied potential. It serves plant scientists and crop improvers alike.
openalex-w2095012959:
Arilda Schmidt Godoy reviewed the history and promise of qualitative research in the social sciences. Her article appeared in a Brazilian business journal in 1995. Social science long favoured counting and measurement. A different approach grew slowly alongside it. It studies meanings, settings and lived experience.

Godoy surveys the main authors behind that approach. She traces the works that shaped the method. Qualitative study suits questions that numbers miss. It can reveal how people understand their own worlds. The article presents it as a fruitful research path. It also notes the method's growing acceptance. Students of administration still read it as an entry point.
openalex-w2346290259:
Massimo Iorizzo, Shelby Ellison, Douglas Senalik, and colleagues published this genome study in Nature Genetics in 2016. They deliver a high-quality, chromosome-scale assembly of the carrot genome. Carrot belongs to a major plant branch, the asterids, whose other lineage had almost no sequenced genomes for comparison.

The team used a doubled-haploid orange carrot, chosen for its uniform DNA. Their analysis uncovered the mechanism controlling carotenoid buildup, the pigment that makes roots orange and supplies vitamin A precursors. They also resequenced thirty-five relatives spanning the carrot genus's diversity. Comparing genomes traced asterid evolution and the histories of several gene families. The resource should speed discovery and breeding in carrot, lettuce, sunflower, and kin.
openalex-w2588882259:
Ronald P. de Vries, Robert W. Riley, and Ad Wiebenga lead a very large team on this 2017 study in Genome Biology. It compares the genomes of fungi in the genus Aspergillus. These fungi matter hugely to people: some serve industry, others cause disease or spoil food with poisons. Eight Aspergillus genomes had been studied before, raising questions about how species specialize.

The team sequenced ten new, highly diverse Aspergillus species and compared them in depth. They examined metabolism, stress response, biomass breakdown, and signaling across the genus. The comparison revealed both shared groundwork and sharp differences between species. Highlights include signs of possible sex in supposedly asexual species, and acid-production genes marking the black aspergilli. Lab experiments backed up several genomic findings. A family tree built from the genomes clarifies how the new species fit into the genus.
openalex-w2794003659:
Marcelo Valério reviewed José Contreras's book on teacher autonomy in this 2002 review, written in Portuguese. The book, Autonomia de professores, is the Brazilian edition of a Spanish work of nearly three hundred pages. Contreras, of the University of Barcelona, treats teacher autonomy as a quality of education itself. It is not merely a professional perk for teachers.

Autonomy, he argues, means awareness of teaching, of doing and being a teacher, and of education's meaning in society. Knowledge for teaching cannot split theory from practice; both must meet inside real human contexts. The review traces the book's response to decades of devaluing teachers through technical rationality. Contreras answers with ideas like the democratic school and the reflective teacher. He also examines teacher professionalism as everyday resistance to lost status. Valério's review maps a book still central to debates on teachers' work.
openalex-w2968902559:
Michael Selvaraj, Alejandro Vergara, Henry Ruiz, and colleagues published this study in Plant Methods in 2019. It builds an artificial intelligence system that spots banana diseases and pests from photographs. Banana is a staple food in many developing countries, and its production is hit by many diseases and pests.

The team gathered large sets of expert-checked symptom images from disease hotspots in Africa and southern India. They retrained three deep learning model designs on these images, building six models covering eighteen classes of damage by plant part. Two designs, ResNet50 and InceptionV2, performed better than a lighter mobile design. The system aims to give farmers fast, on-the-spot diagnosis.
openalex-w2980977859:
Kuldeep Dhama, Shyma Latheef, Maryam Dadar, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences. It surveys biomarkers for diseases and disorders linked to stress. A biomarker is any measurable trait that signals a body process, a disease state, or a response to treatment.

A perfect biomarker would be specific to one disease, safe and easy to measure, and quick to give steady results across groups. Beyond diagnosis, biomarkers can forecast how a disease will progress and whether a therapy is working. The authors review stress markers that show when a person is outside healthy balance. Their survey weighs the diagnostic, forecasting, and treatment value of these markers for stress-related illness.
openalex-w4200090259:
Julia Joswig, Christian Wirth, Meredith Schuman, and colleagues mapped how plant traits vary across the globe, in Nature Ecology and Evolution in 2021. Traits such as tree height, leaf size, and seed size describe how plants live and grow. Biologists long suspected that climate and soil together shape these traits. Examples had piled up for decades without one framework to hold them.

As their title states, the authors find that climate and soil factors explain a two-dimensional spectrum of trait variation. One axis follows water and temperature, the other soil richness and leaf economics. Such a map helps predict how plant communities may shift as climates change. It also links local leaf traits to the working of whole ecosystems.
openalex-w7204232059: Deepfakes poison the information well, and this paper proposes a defense. The authors present ETHOS-SE, a socio-technical framework for fighting AI-generated disinformation: part detection tech, part social design. They address the gap between lab advances and real-world trust. A forward-looking study of defending truth in the synthetic age.
openalex-w7204461359: Government agencies need plans, not just reactions. This article studies the upsides of strategic planning in Brazil's indirect public administration, the state-run bodies that manage public interests. Based on descriptive research and literature review, the authors argue that structured planning serves the public mission better. A management study for readers who believe bureaucracy can be steered.
openalex-w7204463159: The Amazon holds a dazzling share of the world's orchids, and this study takes their census. The authors synthesize current knowledge of the orchid family in Amazonas state: species, endemics, hybrids, pollination, and conservation, using data current to mid-2026. A botanical overview as rich as its subject, and a baseline for protecting it.
openalex-w7204757659: Bones and teeth build themselves from calcium phosphate, and labs want to copy the trick. This review covers biomineralization-inspired routes to functional bioceramics. The authors surveyed how body-fluid chemistry guides the growth. A biomaterials review of nature's building code.
openalex-w7205005059: Radishes are simple, but growing them well takes science. This agronomy study tested how different levels of shade affect radish growth in the soil and climate of western Amazonia. Conducted at the Federal University of Acre, the experiment measured which shade conditions produced the best crop. A small, concrete piece of agricultural research with direct value for farmers working under the Amazon sun.
openalex-w7205009059: Future science teachers learn their craft partly in real classrooms through Brazil's PIBID program. This study asks students in 7th and 8th grade what they thought of those trainee teachers and how well theory met practice in their science lessons. The authors measure the impact on learning and on the trainees' growth. A ground-level view of teacher training where the judges are the teenagers.
peregrine-s-progress-pg7059: Jeffery Farnol's hero Peregrine progresses through Regency England — high roads, old inns, duels at dawn, and ladies in distress — in the author's inimitable romantic style. Dashing, colorful, and utterly Farnol from first page to last. A swashbuckling delight for all lovers of the historical romance.
phrenological-development-of-robert-burn: Phrenological Development of Robert Burns, 1859. The poet's skull. It is preserved here. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
phrenology-and-other-poems-1859: Phrenology, and Other Poems, 1859. The phrenological verse. This book preserves that poetry. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it.
plos-pbio-0020259:
Earl F. Glynn, Paul C. Megee, Hong-Guo Yu, and their team mapped a chromosome glue in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. Cohesin is a protein complex that holds sister chromosomes together after copying, until the cell is ready to split them. The team charted where cohesin sits across the yeast genome.

A full map shows cohesin is not spread evenly. It pools at certain regions, including near chromosome centers. That pattern hints at how the glue is loaded and where it works hardest. Faulty chromosome splitting leads to cancer and birth defects, so the rules of the glue matter broadly. Yeast gives the cleanest map, and its core rules hold in human cells.
plos-pone-0000059:
R. Henrik Nilsson, Martin Ryberg, Erik Kristiansson, and co-authors audited the trustworthiness of public DNA databases in a 2006 paper. Biologists deposit identified DNA sequences in shared databases and later researchers trust those labels. A wrong label quietly poisons every study that reuses the sequence. The team checked the labels from a fungal perspective.

Fungi are a hard test case, since many species look alike and names shift often. Measuring how reliable fungal sequence labels were gave the whole field a warning and a benchmark. Database hygiene sounds dull, but modern biology runs on shared sequences, and this study asked whether the foundation was sound.
plos-pone-0000159:
Kevin T. Williams, Steven P. Young, Alison Negus, and colleagues published this immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It reports that C4b binding protein, part of the complement system, binds to CD154 on immune cells. That binding blocks CD40-driven death of cholangiocytes, the cells lining the bile ducts.

The authors call it a novel link between complement and epithelial cell survival. In plain terms, a blood protein best known for tagging invaders also protects the body's own duct cells from immune-triggered death. The finding matters for liver and bile duct diseases where those cells are lost.
plos-pone-0000259:
Isabella Mutschler, Andreas Schulze-Bonhage, Volkmar Glauche, and colleagues published this brain imaging paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The insular cortex, buried deep in the brain, helps link sensation to action. The authors report a rapid sound-action association effect there: the region responds quickly when a sound is tied to a movement the listener must make.

Fast linking of sounds to actions matters for speech, music, and everyday reactions. The study times and locates that link in the human insula using brain imaging. It adds the insula to the map of regions that bind hearing to doing, a bond at the heart of skilled behavior.
plos-pone-0000359:
Natalay Kouprina, Vladimir N. Noskov, Adam Pavlicek, and colleagues published this sperm protein evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. SPANX genes make proteins found in sperm, and the SPANX-N branch is newer in evolution. The authors study the evolutionary diversification of SPANX-N gene structure and expression across primates.

Sperm proteins evolve fast, often under pressure from sexual selection and conflict. Tracing how SPANX-N copies multiplied and diverged shows that speed in action. The work also bears on fertility research, since sperm-specific proteins are candidate targets for contraception and infertility diagnosis.
plos-pone-0000459:
Albrecht von Brunn and colleagues mapped how the SARS coronavirus's proteins interact with each other, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. SARS, a severe respiratory disease, emerged in 2002 and was contained within two years. The team analyzed intraviral protein-protein interactions across the virus's ORFeome, the full set of its protein-coding regions.

An interaction map shows which viral proteins must work together, exposing joints where a drug might pry the machine apart. With SARS gone from circulation, such maps keep the knowledge ready should a similar coronavirus return. The approach, mapping a whole virus at once, has since become standard for emerging pathogens.
plos-pone-0000559:
Christina L. Kress and colleagues tested plant compounds against a mouse form of leukemia, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The compounds are triterpenoids, a large family of plant chemicals. In mice bred to develop chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small B cell lymphoma, the compounds showed anti-tumor action on their own, with no partner drug.

Action from a single agent in a true-to-life mouse model is a real early milestone. This leukemia is the most common adult form and is often slow but not curable, so new chemical families are welcome. The study moves triterpenoids from folk remedy chemistry toward tested cancer leads.
plos-pone-0000659:
Sandor E. Karpathy, Xiang Qin, Jason Gioia and co-authors published the genome sequence of a mouth bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fusobacterium nucleatum is a prominent member of the oral microbiota and a common cause of human infection. The species splits into five subspecies. Their subject, subspecies polymorphum, strain ATCC 10953, had been well characterized in the lab.

The title calls this subspecies genetically tractable, meaning its genes can be manipulated for experiments. A full genome sequence plus tractability makes a strong research platform. The sequence lets scientists hunt for the genes behind its place in dental plaque and its role in infections beyond the mouth.
plos-pone-0000759:
Bruce S. Lieberman and Adrian L. Melott re-examined claims of a rhythm in the history of life, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Earlier work had reported a 62 million year periodicity in biodiversity across the Phanerozoic, the era of visible animal life. Related claims covered cycles in origination and extinction as well. Such a cycle, if real, would demand an extraordinary cause.

The authors re-tested the evidence and report the signal is robust against variations in how the data are handled. Robustness is not proof of a cause, and the paper considers the case rather than closing it. A regular pulse in extinction and recovery would reshape how evolution's history is read.
plos-pone-0000859:
Ciriaco Ligios, Giovanna Maria Cancedda, Ilan Margalith and co-authors found sick prion protein stored in the kidneys of sheep ill with scrapie. Prions are misshapen proteins that cause fatal brain diseases in humans and in farm animals. They had been found in tissues outside the brain and lymph system before. Prion infectivity had also been found in the blood of deer and sheep.

That blood link led the team to the kidney, the organ that filters blood. They report prion deposits both in kidney lining cells and in the tissue between them. Kidney spread counts for two reasons. It may aid tests, since kidneys and urine are easy to reach. It also counts for safety, in transplants and in the food chain.
plos-pone-0000959:
Michal Grzmil, Danny Whiting, John Maule and colleagues followed a cancer gene through zebrafish development, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene, INT6, was found as a site where a mouse mammary tumor virus lands and drives tumors. Its levels are altered in human cancers, but its exact role in tumor growth stayed unclear, and no animal model existed to study it.

Working in zebrafish, the team report that INT6 and the MEK signaling pathway converge during development. A shared path between a cancer gene and a major growth signal is a strong lead. The fish model also gives future studies a living system for testing that lead.
plos-pone-0001059:
Mahdi Jalili, Suzie Lavoie, Patricia Deppen and colleagues mapped faulty brain connections in schizophrenia using EEG, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The dysconnection hypothesis blames schizophrenia on abnormal links between brain areas. Scans had shown widespread structural changes suggesting exactly that.

What was missing was a functional map to sit beside the structural one. Using state space analysis of EEG recordings, the team reveal a dysconnection topography, a pattern of where the working links falter. EEG is cheap and fast compared with scanners, so a functional map built on it could reach clinics. The work ties a theory of schizophrenia to measurable signals.
plos-pone-0001159:
Fresh produce has been tied to repeated outbreaks of E. coli O157:H7, a dangerous food-poisoning bacterium. Michael Cooley and co-authors tracked the bacterium in a major California produce region in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Between 1995 and 2006, 22 produce outbreaks were documented in the United States, nearly half traced to California lettuce or spinach.

The authors measured how often the bacterium occurs in the region and followed its movement through the environment. Pinning down where it persists, in water, soil, or wildlife, is key to keeping it off crops. Their data inform farm practices aimed at safer vegetables.
plos-pone-0001259:
Government agencies want to reduce animal testing in toxicology, replacing mammal assays with tests in simple organisms. Windy Boyd, Sandra McBride, and Jonathan Freedman evaluated such an assay in the worm C. elegans, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The worm is attractive for its short life cycle and low cost.

The authors measured how genetic mutations and chemical exposures affect the worm's feeding, using a novel high-throughput screening assay. Feeding is a sensitive, measurable behavior that chemicals can disturb. Their evaluation checks whether feeding screens could serve as an early warning system for toxicity.
plos-pone-0001359:
Angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels, has been described as a component of inflammatory bowel disease. Levels of the vessel growth factor VEGF are increased in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis mucosa. Gaëlle Cane and colleagues asked whether a gut bacterium can drive that growth, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their subject was a diffusely adhering Escherichia coli strain associated with Crohn's disease.

The authors report up-regulation of intestinal VEGF by this E. coli. A bacterium provoking vessel growth in the gut wall would tie infection-like processes to the inflammation of Crohn's. Their result gives that hypothesis a mechanism.
plos-pone-0001459:
Simone Sandkühler and Joydeep Bhattacharya wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on insight, the flash when a hard problem clicks. Such flashes have a clear shape: a block, then a swift reshaping of the problem, then a deep grasp. The pair recorded brain waves as people solved problems with and without that flash.

Their wave data tie insight to distinct brain patterns at the moment of the break. Those marks help split true insight from slow grind work. The study grounds a famed but vague event in hard signals. It may guide ways to teach and to set tasks that help insight occur.
plos-pone-0001559:
Charles Warden, Seong-Ho Kim, and Soojin Yi wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on hidden RNA roles inside protein coding zones. Codes that sit inside a gene's protein span were thought to serve that protein alone. Fresh computer work hints some spans also fold into working RNAs. The team tested that claim in yeast proteins.

They found that spans flagged as dual use change at a slower rate over time. Slow change is a mark of a real job held by selection. That backs the claim that some coding spans do double duty. It adds a layer to how gene codes should be read.
plos-pone-0001659:
Jiang Zhu, Fuhong He, Jing Wang, and their co-authors built a math model of the transcriptome in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The transcriptome is the full set of RNA messages a cell makes. New multiplex sequencing tools could now collect millions of short transcript tags in a single run, far more than older methods, at much lower cost.

With that flood of tag counts, researchers need sound ways to infer the true levels of each message. The authors model transcript levels from sampling data and test how well the model recovers known patterns. The full text gives the model's assumptions, the math, and the checks against real data. Better models of tag sampling help every study that counts RNA to judge gene activity.
plos-pone-0001759:
Gino Boily, Erin L. Seifert, Lisa Bevilacqua, and their co-authors studied mice lacking a lifespan-linked gene in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The yeast sir2 gene and its counterparts in flies and worms govern lifespan and the response to caloric restriction. SirT1 is the mammalian version.

The team studied mice carrying two null copies of SirT1 and mapped how they handle energy metabolism and caloric restriction. The full text gives the metabolic measurements and the restriction response. Sirtuins are the targets of much-hyped longevity research and drug programs. Careful mouse studies like this one set the factual floor for what these genes actually do to energy balance.
plos-pone-0001859:
Peter Dudek and Didier Picard mapped estrogen receptor signaling crosstalk in breast cancer cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Estrogen receptor alpha is a transcription factor switched on by ligands. A wide variety of other extracellular signals can activate it in the absence of estrogen. The impact of these alternate modes of activation on gene patterns had not been charted.

Their genome study maps the signaling crosstalk of estrogen receptor alpha in breast cancer cells: which gene programs each route yields. The full text gives the gene patterns and the shared ground. Hormone therapy resistance in breast cancer often uses these alternate routes, so charting them helps design later treatments.
plos-pone-0001959:
David Dupret and co-authors tested whether new neurons in the adult brain are needed for one kind of memory, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The dentate gyrus, part of the hippocampus, is one of the few brain zones where new neurons are born all through adult life. That growth had been proposed as a way the brain stores spatial memory, but proof of cause was thin.

The team blocked or cut adult neurogenesis and tested spatial relational memory, the memory for how places relate. As the title states, that memory requires the new growth. A causal link here shapes how scientists think about learning, aging, and brain repair.
plos-pone-0002059:
Magali Irla and co-authors restored a missing immune protein in mice by zapping genes into the thymus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Gene therapy needs ways to deliver DNA that are both efficient and safe, and viral and non-viral carriers still have open problems on both counts. The team report a new one-pole electroporation system for non-viral delivery.

They used it in the living thymus, the organ where T cells mature, to restore ZAP-70, a protein that T cells need to signal. Restoring a protein inside the organ itself is a step toward fixing immune defects at their source.
plos-pone-0002159:
Abraham Hodgson, Abudulai Adams Forgor, Daniel Chandramohan, and co-authors tested an infant vaccine in northern Ghana, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Adding meningitis vaccines to routine baby shots could cut the toll of meningococcal meningitis in Africa's meningitis belt. The vaccine under study combined protection against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, hepatitis B, Hib, and meningococcal groups A and C.

In this phase II trial, infants received the combined shot. The team could then check safety, plus the strength and staying power of the immune response. They also tested immune memory. A single shot that guards against many diseases at once eases the strain on rural clinics.
plos-pone-0002259:
Josette Raymond, Jean-Michel Thiberge, Nicolas Kalach, and co-authors traced how a stomach bacterium spreads inside families, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Helicobacter pylori infects about half the world and can cause ulcers and stomach cancer. Its spread across continents had been traced, but how it passes between people in a household was not clearly described.

The team used macro-arrays, tools that read many bacterial genes at once, to compare strains within three families. Matching strains show the routes infection takes between parents and children. Knowing the route helps decide whom to test and treat when one family member falls ill.
plos-pone-0002359:
Jegannath Korukottu and co-authors solved the 3D structure of a scorpion toxin with a newer magnetic method, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Solid-state NMR spectroscopy can give structural information on proteins that resist the standard routes of X-ray crystallography and solution NMR. Its resolution, though, was long in question.

The team determined the high-resolution 3D structure of kaliotoxin, a small toxin from scorpion venom that blocks potassium channels. Their structure reaches a resolution comparable to the established methods. Proving the method on a real toxin opens membrane proteins and fibers, long out of reach, to structural study.
plos-pone-0002459:
Saeed and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Uzma Saeed, Lalitha Durgadoss, R. Khader Valli, among others. Its subject is knockdown of Cytosolic Glutaredoxin 1 Leads to Loss of Mitochondrial Membrane Potential: Implication in Neurodegenerative Diseases. Mitochondrial dysfunction including that caused by oxidative stress has been implicated in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002559:
Kuenz joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Bettina Kuenz, Andreas Lutterotti, Rainer Ehling, among others. Its subject is cerebrospinal Fluid B Cells Correlate with Early Brain Inflammation in Multiple Sclerosis. There is accumulating evidence from immunological, pathological and therapeutic studies that B cells are key components in the pathophysiology of multiple sclerosis (MS).

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002659:
Pierre Daubersies and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was genetic immunisation by liver stage antigen 3 protects chimpanzees against malaria despite low immune responses. The catalog record names Pierre Daubersies first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The true interest of genetic immunisation might have been hastily underestimated based on overall immunogenicity data in humans and lack of parallelism with other. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002759:
Daniela Hartl and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was impairment of adolescent hippocampal plasticity in a mouse model for alzheimer's disease precedes disease phenotype. Authorship is credited in the record to Daniela Hartl and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The amyloid precursor protein (APP) was assumed to be an important neuron-morphoregulatory protein and plays a central role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002859:
Scott Glaberman and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was characterization of a nonclassical class i MHC gene in a reptile, the galápagos marine iguana ( amblyrhynchus cristatus ). The full author list in the catalog record begins with Scott Glaberman, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Squamates are a diverse order of vertebrates, representing more than 7,000 species. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002959:
Boye Nielsen, Mikala Egeblad, Fritz Rank and co-authors tracked the enzyme MMP13 in mouse breast tumors in 2008. MMP13, also called collagenase 3, remodels the matrix around cells. In human breast cancer it appears in support cells at the earliest invasive stages, which suggested it helps tumors progress.

In mice, a viral gene drove mammary tumors while the team watched where MMP13 was induced. Despite its early presence, it did not influence tumor progression in this model, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, the contrast is a caution against assuming a marker is also a driver.
plos-pone-0003059:
Sridhara Chakravarthy, Tara Keck, Martijn Roelandse and co-authors built a tool for expressing several transgenes in single neurons in 2008. Mosaic mice that glow green in scattered neurons, like Golgi staining, have been very useful for studying neuron structure and function. Probing the molecular events behind structural plasticity needed more control.

Their system uses Cre dependence, so multiple added genes switch on only in chosen isolated neurons of the adult forebrain. Published in PLOS ONE, single-cell control lets researchers test gene combinations in one neuron while neighbors stay normal, a clean comparison. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003159:
Guilian Xu, Celeste Karch, Ning Li and colleagues study a helper protein in Alzheimer's related amyloid build-up in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Receptor-associated protein, or RAP, works in the endoplasmic reticulum to help several membrane receptor proteins mature. Those receptors include LRP and SorLA/LR11, both tied to amyloid processing.

Using APP/PS1 transgenic mice, the team test whether RAP plays a central role in modulating amyloid-beta deposition, as the title states. Readers see a support protein move to the centre of a disease question. The work may point to fresh ways to slow amyloid build-up.
plos-pone-0003259:
Jos A. Hageman, Margriet M. W. B. Hendriks, Johan A. Westerhuis and colleagues introduce a data modelling idea in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. One expanding area in functional genomics is metabolomics, measuring the metabolome of an organism. Data from such studies are very diverse in nature, based on the design of each study. In the past, such spread was captured in complex statistical models.

The authors present simplivariate models, with ideas and first examples. Readers get a plea for simpler models that match how metabolite data are really made. Clearer models are easier to test, explain, and trust in biology labs.
plos-pone-0003359:
Kristin M. Watts and David A. Hunstad dissect a chaperone protein in pathogenic E. coli in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. SurA is a periplasmic peptidyl-prolyl isomerase and chaperone of Escherichia coli and other Gram-negative bacteria. In contrast to other such enzymes, SurA appears to have a distinct role. It chaperones newly made porins destined for insertion into the outer membrane.

The authors identify the parts of SurA required for outer membrane biogenesis in uropathogenic Escherichia coli. Readers learn which parts of a helper protein are needed for building the bacterial surface. Outer membrane assembly is a drug target because Gram-negative bacteria depend on it.
plos-pone-0003459:
Albert Nienhaus and co-authors surveyed latex-allergic health workers in Germany for this 2008 study. Many nurses and doctors react to natural rubber latex gloves. Germany had pushed powder-free gloves to cut that exposure. The team asked how affected workers were doing after the change.

A total of 196 workers with reported latex allergy answered their survey. Questions covered work ability and quality of life. The answers show whether the glove rules truly helped those already harmed. Such follow-up tells regulators if a workplace fix reaches real lives. Follow-up surveys like this one test whether safety rules work in practice.
plos-pone-0003559:
Raphaël Scharfmann and co-authors traced the origins of insulin cells in this 2008 paper. Islets of Langerhans are tiny organs that control blood sugar. Beta cells inside them make insulin, alongside other hormone cell types. Most knowledge of islet formation came from rodent development.

Within single human islets, beta cells arose from multiple progenitors. One islet is thus a mix of several founding lines. That mixed origin changes how scientists picture islet growth. It also matters for growing replacement beta cells for diabetes therapy. Human islets differ from rodent ones, so direct human data carry extra weight.
plos-pone-0003659:
Ben Cooper, Eberhard Fuchs, and Gabriele Flügge published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Long-lasting stress is known to reshape the branches and contact points of neurons. The team asked whether it also changes M6a, a protein that sits on the surface of nerve fibers.

They found that chronic stress regulates how much M6a the brain produces. The change adds a surface protein to the list of things stress alters in neurons. That list matters for grasping how strain over weeks can impair the transfer of signals between brain cells and affect mood.
plos-pone-0003759:
Robert Grützmann, Bela Molnar, Christian Pilarsky, and colleagues published this cancer screening study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Colorectal cancer is a leading cause of cancer death, yet early detection raises survival above ninety percent. Fewer than half of at-risk Americans were screened regularly at the time. A blood test could change that.

The team built an assay that detects methylated Septin 9 DNA in peripheral blood. The marker flagged colorectal cancer with useful sensitivity in their tests. A simple blood draw that catches this cancer early could save many lives.
plos-pone-0003859:
Emi Kinameri, Takashi Inoue, Jun Aruga, and colleagues published this brain development study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Building a working central nervous system requires tight control of progenitor growth, cell cycle exit, and differentiation. The Notch-Hes program is one conserved part of that control.

The team mapped where the Prdm family of transcription factors is expressed in the developing mouse brain. They also studied how Prdm proteins interact with the Notch-Hes pathway during neurogenesis. The patterns show two gene systems cooperating to shape the growing nervous system. Maps like this guide the hunt for the signals that time each step.
plos-pone-0003959:
Juan Rodríguez-Vita, Eva Sánchez-Galán, Beatriz Santamaría, and co-authors studied statin effects on vessel wall cells in 2008. Statin drugs lower cholesterol and clearly help in cardiovascular disease. The growth factor TGF-beta may also protect against artery hardening. It balances inflammation and vessel wall growth in that setting.

Their PLOS ONE article reports statins need the TGF-beta and Smad path to work. Through it, statins govern how smooth muscle cells in vessels behave. That dependence reveals a hidden part of how statins protect arteries. It may guide pairing statins with other vessel drugs. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004059:
Alessandro de Mello Varani, Rangel Celso Souza, Helder I. Nakaya, and co-authors traced virus relics in a plant pathogen in 2008. Xylella fastidiosa is a bacterium that causes costly plant diseases. Its sequenced genomes carry many prophage-like elements. Those virus remnants make up as much as 15 percent of the genome.

Their PLOS ONE article asks where those prophage regions came from. It also weighs how they shaped differences between strains. Imported virus DNA can bring new traits to a pathogen. Tracing its origins helps explain how plant diseases diversify. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004159:
Louise Wolf and colleagues published this developmental study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Transcription factors are proteins that switch sets of genes on and off to build a specific cell type. Pax6 is one such factor, and it is essential for building the eye, including the lens.

Working in the mouse lens, the team mapped the gene networks that depend on Pax6. They identified which genes Pax6 controls directly or indirectly as the lens forms. The resulting network map helps explain how a single factor can organise the growth of a whole structure. The lens is the clear structure that focuses light in the eye.
plos-pone-0004259:
Mandy Lam and colleagues published this yeast cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Attaching ubiquitin tags to proteins is essential for many steps of protein traffic inside cells. The team set out to clarify the role of Ubp2, a yeast enzyme that removes those tags.

They had established that Ubp2 interacts with Rsp5, an enzyme that adds the tags. Here they report that this interaction is required for sorting transporters and receptors in the multivesicular body pathway, the route that delivers proteins for destruction. A tag remover and a tag adder must cooperate to keep the sorting line moving.
plos-pone-0004359:
Jiayang Qin and colleagues published this fermentation study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Demand for lactic acid is rising because it is the monomer for polylactic acid, a greener plastic. Pure L-lactic acid is a must for making good polymer, and producing it cheaply matters.

The team isolated a new thermophilic strain, Bacillus sp. 2-6, that produces polymer-grade L-lactic acid by fermentation without sterilisation. Skipping that step cuts energy and cost. A heat-loving bacterium that tolerates unsterile conditions makes green plastic cheaper to brew. Heat-loving microbes also shrug off many contaminants that spoil normal brews.
plos-pone-0004459:
A bacterial cleanup system that rescues stuck protein-making machines also shapes growth, show Chunzhong Yang and John Glover in PLOS ONE in 2009. When a ribosome stalls on a broken message, a molecule called tmRNA steps in with its partner protein, SmpB. Together they restart the process, end it cleanly, and free the ribosome for new work.

The team studied this tagging system in Streptomyces coelicolor, a soil bacterium famed for making antibiotics. They found the system plays important roles in how the bacterium grows and develops through its life cycle. That is more than housekeeping: development in this species is tied to the making of useful drugs. The work links a basic rescue tool to the timing of a complex bacterial life.
plos-pone-0004559:
Three ways of silencing a chosen gene are compared head to head by Gwang Lee, Leah Santat, Mi Sook Chang, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. RNA interference, called RNAi, lets researchers turn a gene down and watch what changes. The platforms include small interfering RNA, short hairpin RNA, and antisense oligonucleotides, each with its own strengths.

The team used different versions of each system to silence the same target genes in signaling molecules. Comparing them on equal terms shows which is strongest, cleanest, and most dependable. Gene silencing is a daily tool in biology and a hoped-for class of medicines. A fair comparison helps labs choose the right tool instead of learning by failed experiments.
plos-pone-0004659:
Biomedical scientists' views on ethics advice services are surveyed by Jennifer McCormick, Angie Boyce, and Mildred Cho in PLOS ONE in 2009. Research ethics consultation programs are being established to address the ethical, societal, and policy considerations of biomedical research. Many are modeled after clinical ethics consultation services, which began in hospitals to help with hard cases at the bedside.

Whether bench scientists want or would use such a service is an open question. The authors measured scientists' perceptions of the ethical and social implications of their work and of consultation itself. If researchers see ethics help as useful rather than as policing, such programs can be built to fit. The study grounds that design in the users' own views.
plos-pone-0004759:
Elizabeth Stillwell and colleagues showed that adding normal stem cells to mouse embryos broadly corrects a muscle disease model, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a severe muscle wasting disease with no cure. It stems from a fault in the dystrophin gene, and mdx mice copy many of its features.

The team injected normal embryonic stem cells into mdx embryos at an early stage. The grown mice showed broad correction of disease traits. Early cell mixing thus helped muscles body wide. The work informs debate on stem cell therapy timing and reach. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory.
plos-pone-0004859:
Dietmar Zinner, Michael Arnold, and Christian Roos asked whether the new primate genus Rungwecebus is actually a baboon, in PLOS ONE in 2009. In 2005 a new primate species from Tanzania, the kipunji, was described as a mangabey. Molecular studies based on papionins including a limited baboon sample suggested different placement, prompting broader genetic testing with improved geographic sampling of baboon diversity.

Evidence favors baboon affinity over a separate genus. Taxonomy affects conservation priorities and funding. Highland mangabey groups need protection regardless of name. Genetics clarifies evolutionary relationships. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004959:
False memories can feel completely real. Earlier work cut them with magnetic stimulation of the left temporal lobe. That stimulation was applied after learning. Paulo Boggio and colleagues tested a different approach in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used direct electrical stimulation of the temporal lobe cortex. They applied it during learning, during recall, or both.

Volunteers took a false memory task under the stimulation. False memories dropped across the stimulation phases. The work points to the temporal lobe as a practical target. Stimulating it may improve the accuracy of what people remember. That prospect matters wherever memory testimony carries weight.
plos-pone-0005059:
Adenovirus vectors can deliver vaccines and genes. Two obstacles shadow their use. One is safety. The other is pre-existing immunity that neutralizes the carrier. Eric Weaver and colleagues compared three designs in PLOS ONE in 2009. They tested replication-competent vectors, first-generation vectors, and helper-dependent ones.

Helper-dependent vectors were proposed as safer alternatives. The head-to-head comparison weighs safety against immune punch. It shows which design balances the two best. The work guides the choice of viral carrier. Future vaccines and gene therapies depend on such choices. A systematic comparison beats guesswork. It also reveals what each design asks of the patient's immune system.
plos-pone-0005159:
Brain blood vessels must widen on demand. A receptor called M5 helps them respond to acetylcholine. Mice lacking that receptor suffer chronically narrowed cerebral vessels. Naohito Kitamura and colleagues tested a treatment in PLOS ONE in 2009. The treatment was estrogen. The condition modeled is cerebrovascular insufficiency, too little blood flow to the brain.

Estrogen showed beneficial effects in the mouse model. It eased the vessel dysfunction caused by the missing receptor. The hormone protected the brain's blood supply. The finding hints at why estrogen matters for vessel health. It may also inform care after menopause, when estrogen falls. A mouse model cannot settle human questions. It can show where to look.
plos-pone-0005259:
A missing enzyme called G6PD can make some malaria drugs dangerous for the patient. Data on how common that deficiency is in Latin American malaria zones were scarce. Santana and colleagues surveyed men near Manaus in the Brazilian Amazon, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The cross-sectional survey measured deficiency in men living in one community in the endemic area. Local prevalence numbers guide which malaria drugs can be given safely there. The work fills a safety gap for treatment programs in the Amazon region. Safe drug choice in that region turns on facts like these, since the wrong drug can harm a man who lacks this enzyme and not help his malaria.
plos-pone-0005359:
Reading lights up a region called the left inferior frontal gyrus, a known hub for word recognition. When that region joins the reading process was unclear. Cornelissen and colleagues timed its activation with magnetoencephalography in PLOS ONE in 2009.

MEG tracks brain activity with fine timing, so it can catch fast steps. The region activated within the first two hundred milliseconds of reading. Such an early start means frontal areas shape word recognition almost from the first glance, not as a late add-on. Fast brain steps are hard to catch with slow scans, so a time-true method like this one is the right tool when the claim rests on the first blink of a word.
plos-pone-0005459:
Hsin-Chou Yang and colleagues hunted genes for early high blood pressure in Taiwan, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. High blood pressure that starts young is thought to owe more to genes than the kind that starts late in life. Finding those genes could aid prevention.

Their search scanned the genomes of people with early disease in two stages. The scan flagged regions of DNA linked to the condition in Han Chinese families. Each flagged region gives follow-up studies a place to look for the exact gene changes that raise blood pressure early.
plos-pone-0005559:
Silvia Sirchia and co-authors studied a gene-silencing strand in breast cancer cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Female cells switch off one of their two X chromosomes early in development. A strand called XIST runs that switch-off.

Workers had linked faults in the process to breast cancer, above all through BRCA1, a gene that raises cancer risk when faulty. The team examined how XIST behaves in breast cancer cells. Odd behaviour of XIST could disturb the balance of X genes and play a part in how these cancers grow.
plos-pone-0005659:
Fayna Díaz-San Segundo and co-authors studied immune suppression during foot-and-mouth disease in pigs in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The virus is among the most contagious animal viruses known and ruins herds across whole regions. How the immune system answers it was still partly unclear.

The team found that a calming immune signal, IL-10, rises early and suppresses the pigs' defences during acute infection. That suppression may help the virus spread fast before immunity recovers. Blocking the signal is one idea for better vaccines or treatments. A calming signal that helps the virus may also harm the host later if it lingers too long.
plos-pone-0005759:
Graciela Navarro Mora and co-authors asked in 2009 whether a rat model of epilepsy needs a long seizure bout to set the disease in motion. Pilocarpine triggers seizures in rats that mimic human temporal lobe epilepsy. Many reports held that at least an hour of status epilepticus, a nonstop seizure state, was required.
