The team tested whether lasting epilepsy follows without that full hour of crisis. If shorter bouts suffice, the damage model of the disease changes. Their question matters because most human cases are not watched from the first minute. The model shapes how new epilepsy drugs get screened.
plos-pone-0005859:
Aida Muslimović and co-authors modeled in 2009 exactly how a cancer drug snaps DNA strands. Etoposide treats several cancers by trapping topoisomerase II, an enzyme that cuts and reseals DNA to untangle it. Trapped mid-cut, the enzyme leaves linked double-strand breaks.

The team's numerical analysis counts and characterizes those breaks. Precise counts help predict both the drug's killing power and its side effects, including later leukemias linked to this drug class. Modeling offers a cheaper lens than endless cell experiments. It also helps compare new drugs in the same family before animal testing.
plos-pone-0005959:
Stem cells from the brain may calm an immune attack instead of just replacing lost cells. Stefano Pluchino, Lucia Zanotti, Elena Brambilla and colleagues tested that idea in 2009 in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. Their PLOS ONE paper studies neural stem and precursor cells injected into the body of a sick animal.

The injected cells ease the disease, and the team traces much of that gain to a calming effect on dendritic cells, the immune system's scouts. With the scouts restrained, the attack on the brain softens. The work supports a cell therapy that works by retraining the immune system, not only by patching damage after it is done.
plos-pone-0006059:
Stopping breastfeeding early can cut HIV spread to a baby, but it can also raise other risks. Louise Kuhn, Grace Aldrovandi, Moses Sinkala and colleagues re-examined that trade in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper revisits a trial of early weaning for HIV-free survival of children born to infected mothers, this time splitting results by how sick the mother was.

Their first analysis found no overall benefit, and early weaning was poorly accepted in practice. The split view asks whether benefit hid inside one group while harm sat in another. Feeding guidance for mothers with HIV must weigh both viruses and hunger, and this finer reading helps set that guidance fairly.
plos-pone-0006159:
Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, and its drivers are still being named. Yuan Lu, Sarra Ryan, David Elliott and colleagues found a crowded suspect region in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper reports amplification and overexpression of two microRNAs, miR-30b and miR-30d, and of the gene KHDRBS3, all at one stretch of chromosome 8.

A region copied extra times in tumors usually holds a gene the tumor profits from. Three candidates in one stretch now need sorting, which the paper begins. Identifying the critical genes of this cancer is the stated path to better treatment, and this locus gives that search a precise address.
plos-pone-0006259:
A mother's diet in pregnancy can tune her child's appetite for life. Hui Chen, David Simar, and Margaret Morris studied brain appetite circuits in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on maternal obesity. Early nutrition shapes hypothalamic neurons, including cells making neuropeptide Y, a strong hunger signal, and cells that suppress appetite.

Offspring of obese mothers carried programmed changes in those circuits. The later diet after birth interacted with the early programming. Together the two stages set the child's drive to eat. The work helps explain how obesity risk passes between generations without gene changes alone.
plos-pone-0006359:
The adult brain keeps adding new neurons in the smell centre, and experience decides which survive. Serena Bovetti and colleagues enriched the odour environment of mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The olfactory bulb constantly integrates new inhibitory interneurons of two types, whose survival depends on experience.

Odour enrichment changed expression of GAD67 and growth and change molecules in the newborn cells. New neurons thus tune their chemistry to match their inputs. The finding shows adult neurogenesis responding to everyday sensory life. It may inform rehabilitation approaches that use sensory training. Rich smell worlds may thus be a real tool for brain care, not just a treat.
plos-pone-0006459:
Alan Bilsland and colleagues explored a network route to quieting cancer cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Telomerase is an enzyme that maintains telomeres, the caps on chromosomes, and lets cells keep dividing. It is a promising cancer target, yet few small-molecule blockers of it exist. In cancer cells, switching the hTERT gene back on drives telomerase production.

The team studied how blocking an enzyme called GSK3 affects that gene. Their title describes dynamic suppression of telomerase through network effects. Instead of hitting telomerase head-on, they shifted the web around it. Web-level thinking may open drug paths that single-target work has missed.
plos-pone-0006559:
George Jiang, Meng Shi, Solomon Conteh, and colleagues tested malaria vaccines in monkeys in PLOS ONE in 2009. Using newer vaccine platforms that worked against malaria in rodent models, they tested five immunization regimens. The challenge parasite was Plasmodium knowlesi in rhesus monkeys. Sterile protection, complete prevention of infection, was the goal.

Comparing heterologous regimens, which mix different vaccine types, shows which combinations protect best. Primate tests are a critical gateway before human trials. Malaria vaccines have historically struggled to give sterile protection. Each regimen comparison narrows the search for one that works.
plos-pone-0006659:
Sergey Nikolaev, Christian Iseli, Andrew Sharp, and colleagues targeted a DNA region to find genomic variation in PLOS ONE in 2009. Detection of rare polymorphisms and causative mutations of genetic diseases in a targeted genomic area has become a major goal. It informs understanding of genomic and phenotypic variation. The team selected a nine megabase DNA region and applied high throughput sequencing.

Deep sequencing of one region finds variants that genome-wide scans miss. Rare variants may explain diseases that common-variant studies cannot. Their approach balances cost and depth before whole genomes were routine. It is a snapshot of genomics strategy in transition.
plos-pone-0006759:
Steven A. L. W. Vanhoutvin and colleagues measured gene changes in the human colon after butyrate exposure in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber in the colon. Fermentation yields short-chain fatty acids, mainly acetate, propionate, and butyrate. Butyrate influences many processes in the gut lining. Its mechanism of action was mostly unknown.

The study determined which genes butyrate switches on or off. Samples came from human colonic mucosa, the colon's inner lining. A transcriptional map shows the breadth of butyrate's reach. It may explain links between fiber intake and colon health. It also gives candidate pathways for butyrate's role in preventing disease.
plos-pone-0006859:
Dangeruta Kersulyte and her team re-read a stretch of DNA in the stomach germ Helicobacter pylori in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some genes show up in just some strains of a germ. Those strain-bound genes can sway how the germ acts and evolves. The first two full reads of this germ's DNA showed one stretch crammed with such genes. It was dubbed a plasticity zone.

The team showed those zones are in fact a new kind of jumping DNA. Jumping DNA can hop in and out of genomes. Hops explain how strain-bound genes spread and mix. That mix fuels the germ's knack for life in man's stomach. It also blurs bids to guess a strain's acts from one DNA read.
plos-pone-0006959:
Anish Das and Vivian Bellofatto studied a gene-making enzyme in a parasite in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their organism was Trypanosoma brucei, which causes sleeping sickness. The enzyme was RNA polymerase II, which copies genes into RNA. Its largest part carries a tail domain, the CTD, built from repeating units in most species.

The parasite's version of that tail is non-canonical, meaning it breaks the usual pattern. The pair tested whether this odd tail is still essential. It proved required for productive RNA synthesis. Their work shows a core gene expression machine can be reshaped in parasites.
plos-pone-0007059:
Colleen Snyder, Emelyn Shroff, Jing Liu, and colleagues traced cell death from nitric oxide in PLOS ONE in 2009. Nitric oxide can switch on the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis, the cell's self-kill program. How that pathway gets triggered was not known. The team followed the signal step by step inside exposed cells.

They found nitric oxide works by regulating the anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family. Two killer members, BAX and BAK, became activated. Cytochrome c then escaped from the mitochondria. The chain explains how a simple gas orders a cell to die, a process relevant to inflammation and tissue injury.
plos-pone-0007159:
Anuj Kumar Sharma, Amjad Ali, Rajan Gogna, and colleagues worked with the guardian protein p53 in PLOS ONE in 2009. The start region of p53 is loose and disordered, without a fixed shape. It carries the parts that switch genes on and drive cell death. It also holds an auto-inhibitory element that restrains the protein.

The team used the amino-terminal region on its own. It stabilized p53 that heat had damaged, and restored its normal wild form. A fragment rescuing the full protein is a neat result. It hints at ways to rescue faulty p53 in tumors, a long-sought goal.
plos-pone-0007259:
Eloïse Raoust, Viviane Balloy, Ignacio Garcia-Verdugo, and colleagues studied lung defenses against bacteria in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Human lungs inhale thousands of liters of air daily, carrying many airborne pathogens. Innate immunity is essential to defend the lungs against that constant exposure from the environment.

Recognition of microbial patterns triggers much of that defense. The authors test two Pseudomonas aeruginosa components, LPS and flagellin. They report that either one is sufficient to activate TLR-dependent signaling. They study both alveolar macrophages and airway epithelial cells in mice during lung infection.
plos-pone-0007359:
Sunando Roy, Jennie Lavine, Francesca Chiaromonte, and colleagues compared immune responses to one versus two lentiviruses in 2009. Feline and human immunodeficiency viruses are lentiviruses. They cause progressive immune decline and death in infected cats and humans, and preventing immune collapse remains a central research goal for both diseases.

The authors use multivariate statistical analyses of host responses. They compare single and dual lentiviral infections. They demonstrate unique immune response patterns for each case. Distinguishing those patterns helps researchers understand why some infections progress faster, especially when two viruses share one host.
plos-pone-0007459:
Anna Bachmann and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 based on malaria parasites taken from a patient whose spleen had been removed. Malaria parasites usually dodge the spleen by sticking infected red blood cells to vessel walls. That sticking, called sequestration, uses parasite proteins from large multi-copy gene families. The team asked what happens when no spleen is present.

In this patient, the parasites showed no sequestration. The gene families behind the sticking proteins were also silent. Without a spleen to evade, the parasite had dropped its hiding strategy. The case shows how flexibly the parasite tailors its survival tactics to the host's body. It also hints at how much the spleen shapes malaria's course.
plos-pone-0007559:
Veronika Pozharskaya and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on lung fibrosis, a disease in which lung tissue scars and stiffens. Part of the scarring involves epithelial cells changing into mesenchyme-like cells, a switch called epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The team studied a regulator named Twist and its role in driving that switch in the lung. Twist is better known from embryonic development.

In fibrotic lungs, Twist helps push epithelial cells across the transition. Those converted cells add to the scar-making population. Pinning the transformation on a named regulator gives researchers a target. Slowing Twist might slow the scarring that steals breath. The study connects a developmental switch to an adult disease of aging lungs. It also adds to growing evidence that fibrosis replays embryo programs in the wrong place.
plos-pone-0007659:
Ingibjörg Jonsdottir and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 testing proposed blood markers of chronic stress. Psychosocial stress is a growing cause of mental ill-health and sick leave in many countries. Valid markers would help doctors diagnose and follow it. A recent study had suggested candidates: the immune signal MCP-1 and certain growth factors. The team measured those candidates in people under prolonged psychosocial stress.

The candidates did not hold up as markers. Levels failed to separate the stressed group as a useful test must. A negative result like this steers the field's search elsewhere. It also guards clinics against adopting a test that does not work. Stress medicine needs markers badly, which makes rigorous rejection valuable. The study clears the board of two plausible but failing options.
plos-pone-0007759:
Nicholas Boulais and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines Merkel cells, touch sensors found in rat skin. These cells sit beside nerve endings and form complexes tied to fine touch. They help detect light pressure and texture.

The cells carry channels that let calcium enter when the membrane moves. The authors tested two kinds of response. They found the cells act as both mechanoreceptors and osmoreceptors. That means they sense physical touch and shifts in water balance. The dual role deepens the picture of how skin reads the world.
plos-pone-0007859:
Tudor Badea and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It introduces two new mouse lines for tracing the shape of single neurons. To map a neuron's branches, scientists label just a few cells brightly. The tool they use is a tamoxifen-controlled switch, CreER, with matching DNA markers.

The new lines let researchers turn labeling on at chosen times. Sparse labeling makes one cell stand out from its neighbors. That clarity is essential for drawing accurate wiring diagrams of the brain. The lines are a resource for labs studying neuronal morphology in development and disease.
plos-pone-0007959:
Jean-Marie Launay and colleagues traced a lasting mark left by smoking in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied 115 men: men who smoked, men who never had, and men who had quit. The focus was an enzyme that breaks down serotonin, a signal chemical tied to blood vessel health.

Smokers carried an epigenetic change, a lasting chemical tag, on the system that runs that enzyme, and former smokers kept much of it. That staying power may explain why vessel harm lingers long after the last cigarette. The work gives a clear reason to quit early, before the mark sets deep.
plos-pone-0008059:
Josep Lluis and colleagues found a way to make liver cancer cells fear low oxygen in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tumors often thrive in low oxygen, using a survival chain through the proteins cSrc and NF-kB. The team raised levels of an enzyme that builds a membrane fat called GD3.

With more of that fat, the survival chain faltered and the cells gave in to oxygen shortage. Tumors in animals grew less as a result. The work names a fresh weak point in a cancer that sorely needs new lines of attack.
plos-pone-0008159:
Valerie Abadie and colleagues showed that a first meeting with an antigen shapes all later answers in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Antigens are the marks the immune system learns to fight. The cells that first present those marks, antigen-presenting cells, carry the news to the wider system.

The manner of that first meeting stamped a lasting quality on the response, strong in some arms of immunity and weak in others. Vaccine makers chase exactly that control: the right first meeting can yield broad, durable defense. The study shows the stamp is set early and by the presenter.
plos-pone-0008259:
Brent J. Sinclair and colleagues filmed ice forming inside insects in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Some insects survive freezing, while others die from it. The biochemistry of freeze tolerance is becoming well known. But the actual process of ice formation inside the body was mostly speculation. The team used synchrotron X-rays to watch it directly.

They imaged intact insects in real time as freezing occurred. Both lethal and non-lethal freezing were observed. Seeing where ice starts and spreads explains how damage happens. It also shows how tolerant species control ice. The method opens a window on a hidden process.
plos-pone-0008359:
Isabella Pallotta and her team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about how platelets are made in bone marrow. Platelets are the small bits in blood that seal cuts. They are cast off by large marrow cells named megakaryocytes. How those cells grow, change form, and shed platelets is not well known. Signs point to a rich web of cell touch, the stuff round the cells, and push and pull from the flesh.

The team set out the bone zone that hugs bone cells as a model for this birth of platelets. That zone is the home ground where the large cells grow up. A good model of that home can show how platelets form and slip into the blood. The point counts for care of bleed and clot ills.
plos-pone-0008459:
Zahra Hasan and co-authors measure immune signals in tuberculosis in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Signals called chemokines draw immune cells to infection sites. Among them are CCL2, CCL3, and CXCL8. Other signals, such as interferon gamma, help fight the germ. Yet it was unclear if these signals mark how severe the disease is. The team focus on CCL2 responses to the tuberculosis germ.

They find CCL2 responses track with disease severity. Higher or lower levels line up with worse or milder cases. Such a marker could help grade illness without invasive tests. It may also point to paths that drive lung damage.
plos-pone-0008559:
Gary Lupyan and co-authors argue language shape reflects social shape in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Languages differ greatly in syntax and morphology. They also differ in the social settings where they are learned and used. A common view held grammars to be unrelated to those settings. The authors challenge that view with a statistical analysis across many languages. They compare grammatical complexity with social factors such as population size.

They find language structure is partly determined by social structure. Languages spoken by large, dispersed groups tend toward simpler morphology. Smaller, tighter communities sustain more complex forms. The result links how societies are built to how their languages are built.
plos-pone-0008659:
Kristy Brumfield and co-authors characterize a sterol gene in an alga in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The predominant sterol in membranes of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is ergosterol. Ergosterol is commonly found in fungi but rarely in higher plants. Higher plants and fungi synthesize sterols by different pathways. The alga sits between those traditions evolutionarily. The team study its ERG3 ortholog, a gene involved in ergosterol biosynthesis. Orthologs are matching genes in different species.

Their functional characterization confirms the gene's role in making ergosterol. That confirms the alga uses a fungal-like sterol path. Chlamydomonas is a major model for photosynthesis and biofuel research. Knowing its membrane chemistry helps engineer strains for fuel production.
plos-pone-0008759:
Lisa Aziz-Zadeh, Tong Sheng, and Anahita Gheytanchi mapped the brain areas behind speech melody. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prosody is the tune of speech: pitch, rhythm, and tone. It carries both grammar and feeling between speakers. Much of social life depends on hearing that tune well. The brain zones for making and hearing it might overlap.

Scans showed shared premotor regions for perceiving and producing prosody. Activity there tracked with empathy scores and with prosody skill. Shared machinery would explain why good listeners often speak expressively. The map links speech melody to social understanding.
plos-pone-0008859:
Jason Holland, Eloisi Caldas-Lopes, Vadim Divilov, and colleagues built a radioactive tracer to watch a cancer drug work in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trastuzumab is an antibody drug for HER2-positive breast cancer. Labeling it with zirconium-89 lets scanners track it in the body. A second drug, an Hsp90 inhibitor, can lower HER2 levels. Clinicians need a way to measure that lowering without biopsies.

Scans with the tracer measured HER2 changes after Hsp90 treatment. The imaging readout matched the drug's pharmacodynamic effect. Noninvasive measurement could guide dosing in future patients. The tracer turns a hidden drug effect into a visible number.
plos-pone-0008959:
Syed Gilani and co-authors searched for a blood warning sign in a scarring lung disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis stiffens the lungs for reasons doctors do not fully know. Many patients show signs that their immune system is switched on. T cells that fight for years can lose a helper protein called CD28 from their surface.

The team measured CD28 loss on CD4 T cells in patients' blood. Patients whose cells had shed more CD28 tended to fare worse. The marker could help doctors spot early who needs closer watching or trials. It also points at worn-out T cells as part of the disease itself.
plos-pone-0009059:
Pawandeep Dhami and co-authors zoomed in on the control landscape of a master blood gene, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, SCL or TAL1, is essential for making blood cells. Its activity is governed by many control elements scattered around it. Those elements must switch it on in stem cells and off elsewhere.

The team scanned a long stretch of DNA with tiling microarrays. New control features kept appearing beyond the known ones. The regulatory landscape proved denser and more layered than thought. Understanding it matters because TAL1 faults can drive leukaemia.
plos-pone-0009159:
Guillaume Osterstock and co-authors pinned down how the hunger hormone talks to growth neurons, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ghrelin is a hormone from the stomach that rises before meals. It targets the arcuate nucleus, a control centre deep in the brain. From there, neurons releasing GHRH trigger growth hormone secretion.

Neighbouring NPY neurons were long thought to relay ghrelin's message onward. The team showed ghrelin stimulates the GHRH neurons directly instead. A direct line like this simplifies the circuit behind growth hormone pulses. It also bears on how hunger signals and growth signals intertwine in the brain.
plos-pone-0009259:
Siddheshwar Utge and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Depression and broken sleep often arrive together. Both are tied to the circadian system, the body's daily clock. The authors suspected that some clock genes raise the risk of depression with disturbed sleep, including early waking.

They systematically tested circadian genes in a population-based sample of people. One gene, TIMELESS, was associated with depression and sleep disturbance. A systematic screen like this weighs each clock gene on the same terms. The finding gives sleep and mood researchers a concrete gene to examine more closely.
plos-pone-0009359:
Sahar Houshdaran and co-authors published this ovarian cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Epithelial ovarian cancer is a major killer of women around the world. It comes in several subtypes, each with its own behavior and molecular marks. Chemical DNA tags, called methylation, are part of that identity.

The team profiled methylation across tumors and cell lines of this cancer. Comparing the two shows which marks are stable features of the disease. It also warns where lab cell lines drift away from real tumors. Such profiles can guide the search for markers that detect this quiet cancer earlier.
plos-pone-0009459:
Yong Zhao and colleagues examined a protein variant and a cancer linked virus in PLOS ONE in 2010. Epstein Barr virus can change human B cells, a type of immune cell, so they grow without normal limits. A protein called IRF-7 helps cells fight viruses. One short form of it, IRF-7C, is made when the main message is cut and rejoined in a new way.

The team found that this short form does two things at once. It helps the virus driven change in some ways and holds it back in others. That double role helps explain how the virus tips cells toward cancer. It also shows a point where the process might be stopped.
plos-pone-0009559:
Ralph Stelzer, Lars Chittka, and Marc Carlton followed bumblebees in British cities in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bumblebees are normally seen in spring and summer in northern Europe. Yet the buff tailed bumblebee, Bombus terrestris, had been spotted in mild recent winters in southern England. The team asked what flowers feed these winter bees. They also measured how fast the bees could gather food.

Winter bees in towns reached high foraging rates, matching summer levels. City gardens and parks offer flowers even in the cold months. Warmer winters and urban planting together may be rewriting the bee's year. The study shows what cities can plant to keep these pollinators fed.
plos-pone-0009659:
Henning Lauterbach and co-authors tested a vaccine given after infection in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Modified Vaccinia Ankara is a weakened virus used as a safe vaccine strain. It is a relative of the smallpox vaccine. The question was whether it can still help after a lethal infection has begun. The team immunized mice after exposure and studied which immune responses the rescue required.

Post exposure vaccination could protect mice that would otherwise die. The study identifies which arms of immunity that protection needs. Such knowledge guides design of vaccines meant for use after an attack or outbreak. It sets the bar that any emergency vaccine must clear.
plos-pone-0009859:
Some tuberculosis patients test negative on the standard smear test yet still carry the disease. J. Lucian Davis and colleagues checked whether doctors can spot those cases by signs and scans. Their study in Uganda appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The patients were HIV-infected inpatients, a group where smear-negative TB is common and deadly. The team tested clinical and radiographic factors, symptoms and chest images, against true diagnoses. Those factors did not diagnose the disease accurately. The cross-sectional study argues for better lab tests in such wards. Missing these cases delays care and spreads infection.
plos-pone-0009959:
A chance mutation in a lab mouse created a model for a group of human diseases. Paul Odgren and colleagues described the scruffy mutant and its cause. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The name comes from the mouse's untidy fur and ears.

The mutation is called Disheveled Hair and Ear, or Dhe for short. It arose spontaneously in the Lmna gene. Lmna faults cause human laminopathies, diseases of the cell nucleus's frame. A ready mouse model lets researchers test ideas for those rare diseases. Spontaneous means the mutation arose on its own.
plos-pone-0010059:
Michael Rosenberg tackled a quiet flaw in research statistics in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Meta-analysis combines results from many studies into one overall effect size. A common formula turns a chi-square test result into a correlation value for that purpose. Rosenberg showed the formula hides an assumption that can fail in real cases.

When that assumption fails, the converted effect size can come out too large. He offered a corrected, more general formula to use instead. Better conversions mean combined study results, often used to guide policy and medicine, rest on sounder math.
plos-pone-0010159:
The authors were Silvia Volpe, Sylvia Thelen, Thomas Pertel, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study filmed immune cells on the move. Monocytic cells migrate toward chemical attractants with a fast, amoeba-like crawl. To move, a cell must polarize, building a clear front and back. Which signals control that step was still disputed.

The team tested an enzyme family called PI 3-kinase, long suspected in migration. Their title reports the result: polarization happened independently of that enzyme's activity. The finding redirects the search for the true steering signals inside migrating immune cells.
plos-pone-0010259:
Sébastien Viel, Marianne Vaugoyeau, and Christine Assaiante studied posture without gravity in 2010. People control balance and movement using stable reference frames, mental anchors for body position. The team asked how losing gravitational information changes which frame the body chooses. They analyzed forearm stabilization during a sit-to-stand movement in microgravity, achieved on parabolic flights.

Their title gives the direction of the finding: posture falls back to the egocentric frame, anchored on the body itself. Their PLOS ONE results help explain how astronauts adapt movement in space. The flights gave brief windows of weightlessness for each test run.
plos-pone-0010359:
Hye Young Shin and co-workers examined a calcium channel's role in making neurons, for PLOS ONE in 2010. Young neural cells take in calcium mainly through store-operated channels. Calcium signals help steer how these cells grow and specialize. One channel type, called TRPC5, had an unclear part in that process. The team studied progenitor cells marked by a surface tag called A2B5.

They found TRPC5 helps drive those progenitors to become neurons. Blocking or boosting the channel changed how the cells matured. That gives researchers a handle for guiding stem-like cells in the lab. Controlled neuron production matters for disease models and repair ideas. A single channel, it turns out, can act as a switch for cell fate.
plos-pone-0010459:
Marzia Massignani and colleagues improved how glowing probes reach the inside of living cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. Microscopes let scientists watch events inside cells in real space and time. Probes that glow make chosen structures visible. Many probes, though, get trapped in pockets and never reach the open cell interior. The team worked on delivery vehicles that release their cargo properly inside.

Better delivery means clearer images and fewer false readings. It also lowers the dose needed, keeping cells healthier during imaging. Their method effectively placed probes in the cytosol, the cell's main fluid. Imaging tools shape what questions biology can ask. This study sharpens one of its most basic tools.
plos-pone-0010559:
Mai Tuyet Vuong and colleagues tested whether two kidney diseases share genetic risk and found no support for overlap in PLOS ONE in 2010. The two diseases, IgA nephropathy and lupus nephritis, both inflame the kidney's filters. Genetics matters in each. The group had earlier tied one disease to variants in a growth factor gene, TGFB1. Similar autoimmune ties suggested the risks might be shared.

Their data did not support a shared genetic basis between the two. A clear negative result prevents wasted hunting along a false trail. It also sharpens each disease's separate genetic story. Kidney inflammation has many forms that look alike under a microscope. Genetics can split what appearance joins. This study performs one such split, honestly reported.
plos-pone-0010659:
Juliet Moncaster and colleagues linked eye and brain changes in Down syndrome, in PLOS ONE in 2010. People with Down syndrome carry an extra copy of the APP gene. That gene makes the amyloid protein that builds up in Alzheimer's disease, which many develop early.

The team found amyloid buildup in the lens of the eye that mirrored buildup in the brain. The lens can be examined quickly and without surgery. If eye changes track brain changes, a lens check could flag Alzheimer's risk early. Early warning matters most in a group where dementia is common but hard to diagnose.
plos-pone-0010759:
Sayera Banu and colleagues surveyed tuberculosis inside Dhaka Central Jail in Bangladesh, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prisons pack people closely, and TB thrives in such air. Little was known about TB rates or drug resistance in Bangladeshi prisons, though the jail is the largest in the country.

Health teams actively screened inmates rather than waiting for volunteers. Lung TB proved common, and some cases resisted standard drugs. Crowding and prior treatment raised the risk further. Inmates cycle back to the community, so prison TB is public TB. The authors call for routine screening and full treatment inside the walls.
plos-pone-0010859:
Nadav Bar and Rivka Dikstein published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. PTEN is a tumor suppressor that brakes a growth pathway centered on AKT, a protein that helps cells survive and divide. PTEN is lost in many cancers. The authors examined miR-22, a small regulatory RNA, and found it acts inside this very pathway.

They show miR-22 directly lowers PTEN levels by binding its gene message. In a twist, AKT itself raises miR-22, so the pathway contains a self-reinforcing loop: more AKT activity means less of its own brake. Live imaging showed miR-22 also speeds AKT's response when growth signals arrive. Bar and Dikstein reveal a small RNA that can tilt cells toward growth, a mechanism worth watching in cancer biology.
plos-pone-0010959:
Dong-Dong Wu, Wei Jin, Xiao-Dan Hao and co-authors published this human evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human skeletons changed fast after modern people spread out of Africa, possibly under natural selection. The authors focused on BMP3, a gene that restrains bone building and lowers bone density, making it a plausible target of that change.

They resequenced the gene in people from four widely separated populations and looked for the statistical fingerprints of positive selection. The gene carried an excess of protein-changing variants and unusually low diversity, and in Europeans its common forms showed the long, uniform stretches typical of a recent selective sweep. Wu and colleagues argue that bone biology was actively reshaped in recent human history, with different patterns in different populations.
plos-pone-0011059:
Syed Faizan Ali, Samia Ayub, Nauman Fazal Manzoor and co-authors published this health survey in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cervical cancer is a leading killer of women in developing countries, though it is preventable by screening and vaccination. The authors tested whether the front-line health workers of Karachi, medical interns and nursing staff in major hospitals, actually know the disease they are meant to fight.

Four hundred staff across three tertiary hospitals answered an interview-based questionnaire. Almost everyone recognized cervical cancer as a disease, but only about a quarter knew some of its basic facts, and knowledge of prevention was patchier still. Ali and colleagues document an uncomfortable gap: the people tasked with counseling women lack the facts themselves. Their survey makes the case for targeted education inside hospitals, not just public campaigns.
plos-pone-0011159:
Prescott, Hall, Acuna-Retamar and colleagues studied hantaviruses in PLOS ONE in 2010. New World hantaviruses cause severe lung disease in people. The team used lab cells that lack the usual first line antiviral signal to see what backup alarms the viruses still trigger.

Even without that main signal, the cells turned on a related backup signal, interferon lambda. That shows the sensing system has layers that can cover for each other. Finding a backup path reveals a possible weak point in the virus. It also deepens basic knowledge of how cells first detect invading viruses.
plos-pone-0011259:
Vieira, Atzingen, Oliveira and colleagues hunted invasion tools of a fever germ in PLOS ONE in 2010. The germ causes leptospirosis, a tropical disease spread through water touched by animal urine. In lab tests, the team found new surface proteins that grab plasminogen, a blood protein the germ can exploit.

By binding that protein, the germ may borrow its cutting power to push through tissues. Naming new binding proteins reveals tricks the germ uses to invade. Each such protein is a possible target for drugs or vaccines. Blocking the grab could slow the germ's spread inside the body.
plos-pone-0011359:
Anthony Oliva and colleagues argued in 2010 for a new way to study mouse behavior in the lab. Lab mice are usually tested in bare cages with simple tasks, far from the rich settings where mouse behavior evolved. The authors proposed borrowing the approach of field biology, which watches what animals actually do across a full day in a fuller setting.

Under their plan, labs would record natural behaviors such as foraging, social contact, and exploration in enriched spaces, then link them to brain activity. Richer behavior gives brain research a firmer base, since a circuit can only be understood against the actions it truly serves. The paper is a call to redesign experiments. It asks neuroscience to measure real behavior first, instead of forcing mice into tasks with little link to their lives.
plos-pone-0011459:
Konrad Noben-Trauth and co-authors mapped a hearing loss trait in mice in 2010 to learn how progressive deafness is inherited. The trait, called Snhl1, causes sensorineural hearing loss that worsens over time, much like common age-related hearing loss in people. The team used the LXS set of recombinant inbred mouse strains, whose shuffled genomes let researchers corner the regions behind a trait.

By relating hearing measures across the strains to their genomes, they narrowed where the responsible genes sit and described how the loss unfolds. Mouse mapping of this kind lays groundwork for finding the human genes that decide who keeps their hearing into old age. It also gives hearing research a defined model in which protective treatments can be tested before anyone thinks of human trials.
plos-pone-0011559:
Deborah Pajalunga and co-authors asked in 2010 what locks mature muscle cells out of copying their DNA forever. Finished muscle fibers are terminally differentiated: they have left the cell cycle for good, which protects against muscle tumors but also limits repair. The team tested whether the block is merely an absence of go signals, or an active, built-in hindrance inside the mature cell.

DNA replication proved to be intrinsically hindered in terminally differentiated myotubes, stalling even when the machinery for copying was supplied. The door is not just locked; the doorway is bricked up. Such a deep safeguard explains why muscle cancers are rare despite muscle's size and longevity. It also tells regenerative medicine the truth about its challenge: coaxing mature muscle to divide means dismantling a safeguard evolution installed on purpose.
plos-pone-0011659:
Laurence Weiss and colleagues followed HIV patients who paused their drug treatment, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lasting immune activation is a central driver of HIV disease progression. Regulatory T cells, which calm immune responses, could help by reducing that activation, or harm by weakening the attack on the virus itself.

The team measured regulatory T cells and activation markers in patients interrupting therapy. Their analysis weighs how the two move together as treatment stops and virus returns. The findings inform the risky question of treatment breaks, helping clinicians judge whether the immune system's brakes are friend or foe.
plos-pone-0011759:
Tamara Clark and co-authors followed young children in Kampala, Uganda, for four years, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Combination drug therapies had become the recommended treatment for uncomplicated malaria. The team used a longitudinal design to measure how often malaria struck and to compare three combination regimens in an urban setting.

Children aged one to ten were enrolled from randomly selected households and tracked over time. The long watch records both the burden of repeated infection and whether the drugs keep working in real life. Such evidence guides malaria treatment policy where children face bout after bout.
plos-pone-0011859:
Ping Li and colleagues reported in 2010 on a gene that is switched on too strongly in chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The gene makes ROR1, a receptor-like protein found on the leukemia cells. The team suspected the transcription factor Stat3, which is constantly active in this leukemia and can bind control regions near genes.

Their work shows Stat3 turning on the ROR1 gene in these cancer cells. That gives the leukemia a chain of command worth interrupting: a signal protein that will not switch off keeps a surface receptor plentiful. Surface proteins are reachable by drugs and antibodies, so explaining where ROR1 comes from helps point treatment research at both the receptor and the switch behind it.
plos-pone-0011959:
Catherine Hobaiter and Richard Byrne reported in 2010 a striking case of imitation among wild chimpanzees. Whether chimps truly learn movements by imitation in nature, rather than by trial and error, has been doubted despite rich evidence for chimp tool traditions. A natural event offered a rare test.

A disabled chimpanzee had developed an unusual movement procedure to overcome its handicap. Able-bodied companions then adopted the same procedure. Copying a technique from an individual who invented it under pressure is strong evidence for social learning of motor skills in the wild. The case widens what chimpanzee culture can include: not just tools, but workarounds for the body itself.
plos-pone-0012059:
Claire Marionnet and co-workers compared in 2010 how the two main skin cell types answer ordinary daily sunlight. Most lab sun studies use harsh midday simulators, a worst case rarely matching daily life. The team used a non-extreme daily ultraviolet spectrum on reconstructed skin, a lab-grown skin model.

Keratinocytes, the surface cells, and fibroblasts, the deeper support cells, mounted different oxidative stress responses to the same daily dose. Layered skin evidently divides the labor of sun defense. Realistic dosing matters for sunscreen and skin aging claims, since a defense that holds at noon in the desert may be the wrong one to measure for a walk to work.
plos-pone-0012159:
Nasser Al-Daghri, Omar Al-Attas, Majed Alokail, and co-authors surveyed metabolic health among adult Arabs in PLOS ONE in 2010. Metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risks including belly fat, high blood sugar, and poor blood fats, had been found very common in Saudi Arabia ten years earlier, with no follow-up since. Their team examined a random sample of nearly three thousand adults.

They found the full syndrome had grown less common, yet unhealthy blood fats remained stubbornly widespread. Splitting the trend that way matters: the overall picture improved while one risk stayed stuck. Health planners can aim at the stubborn piece, cholesterol and fat handling, rather than celebrating or panicking over the whole.
plos-pone-0012259:
Judith Glynn, Saad Alghamdi, Kim Mallard, and co-authors tracked tuberculosis strain families in northern Malawi across twenty years, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Whether some strains spread faster or hit harder than others is a live question, yet almost nobody had watched one population's strain mix change over decades. Their population-based study could also test how HIV, which exploded in that period, reshaped the tuberculosis picture.

Following the same community's strains for twenty years turns snapshots into a movie. Shifts in the mix can show whether the epidemic favors certain families and whether HIV opened the door to them. Tuberculosis control programs need that intelligence to know if the enemy itself is changing.
plos-pone-0012359:
Virginie Rhein, Maria Giese, Ginette Baysang and colleagues examined ginkgo leaf extract in brain cells harmed by amyloid, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Alzheimer's disease shows early failure of mitochondria, the cell parts that make energy. The team had shown that amyloid beta, the protein that builds up in Alzheimer's, weakens that energy making in human brain cells.

Adding a standard ginkgo extract improved the cells' energy output and rescued much of the amyloid-caused failure. The work does not prove ginkgo helps patients, but it pins down one clear effect in cells: support for failing mitochondria. That gives future trials a concrete target to test rather than a vague hope.
plos-pone-0012459:
Valeriy Poroyko, James White, Mei Wang and colleagues compared gut microbe activity in piglets fed by mother or by formula, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. How first foods shape the microbes of the newborn gut, and what those microbes do, is poorly understood yet vital for infant health. Piglets serve as a close stand-in for human babies in gut studies.

The team read which genes gut microbes switched on under each diet. Microbial activity differed clearly between milk-fed and formula-fed piglets. The contrast gives formula makers concrete microbial targets and deepens knowledge of how early diet programs the gut for later health.
plos-pone-0012559:
Yiqiang Zhang, Tao-Sheng Li, Shuo-Tsan Lee and colleagues showed adult heart muscle cells can rewind and divide, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mammalian cardiomyocytes were long classed as terminally differentiated, unable to proliferate after birth, which is why heart attacks scar instead of heal. Simpler animals like zebrafish regrow heart muscle freely, raising envy and questions.

The team induced mammalian cardiomyocytes to dedifferentiate — step back toward an immature state — and then proliferate. If the trick can be made safe in a damaged human heart, regeneration might replace scarring. The study is a proof that the supposed lock on heart cell division can be picked.
plos-pone-0012659:
Le Saout, Villard, Cabasse and co-authors studied what happens when the body runs short of T cells. In that state, called lymphopenia, naive T cells grow and turn into cells that look like memory cells, even without meeting a real germ. This growth can break tolerance and turn T cells against the body itself.

Their 2010 paper shows the signal IL-2 helps CD4 T cells drive that breakdown for CD8 memory-like cells. The finding matters for patients whose T cells are wiped out by illness or treatment, then regrow in risky ways.
plos-pone-0012759:
Brown and Sorhannus set a molecular timescale for a vast group of algae and their relatives. Stramenopiles include diatoms and brown algae as well as water moulds, and they fill oceans and fresh waters. Their deep family history was murky in 2010, with few firm dates for when the main branches split.

Their 2010 gene-based clock suggests the split dates are far younger than fossil-based guesses implied. If the fossils were read too old, the group's rise must be retold. A corrected timescale reshapes ideas about when these organisms began shaping ocean chemistry.
plos-pone-0012859:
Krall, Canales, Kairath and co-authors made kidney filter cells overproduce a calcium channel in mice and caused kidney disease. Faults in the TRPC6 channel gene run in families with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, a scarring kidney disease of children and adults. Their 2010 study put extra copies of the normal or mutant channel into mouse podocytes, the filter cells.

Either version, at high enough levels, was enough to produce glomerular disease. That means dosage itself can be harmful, not only broken channels. The finding widens how doctors should read TRPC6 test results.
plos-pone-0316959:
Dubey and colleagues, in a 2026 study, use zebrafish to ask how losing a motor protein changes the way animals respond to anesthetic drugs. The protein, called kif5Aa, helps move mitochondria, the cell's power sources, along nerve cells. One anesthetic, propofol, is known to bind to this protein's motor part.

Larvae without the protein were more sensitive to propofol and to etomidate, and most strongly to etomidate. They were less sensitive to a different sedative, dexmedetomidine, and showed no change with ketamine. In nerve cells, each drug also moved mitochondria in its own pattern, and some effects vanished when the protein was missing. The work shows that anesthetics do not act in one shared way. Each drug touches the cell's transport machinery in a distinct manner, which may help explain their varied effects on the brain.
plos-pone-0338359:
Lauren Suchman and seven colleagues interview women about contraceptive side effects in Ethiopia and Kenya. Their 2026 qualitative study involved eighty-three women in Nairobi, Kisumu, Addis Ababa, and the Amhara region. Side effects are a leading reason women stop contraception worldwide. Good counselling should help them anticipate and manage those effects. The women described what support they actually received, and what they wished for.

Counselling quality in their accounts was patchy. Many wanted fuller discussion of side effects at the first visit and at follow-ups. Once side effects began, most women simply endured them. They managed on their own, often with shop-bought remedies, rather than returning to a provider. The gap between clinic promises and lived experience is the core finding. Services that counsel honestly and stay available could keep more women protected on their own terms.
plos-pone-0340559:
Anjum John and co-authors piloted a survey study of HPV vaccine knowledge among school families in Kerala, India. India carries the world's heaviest cervical cancer burden, yet vaccine awareness and uptake stay low. Their 2026 pilot ran in one school with students aged eleven to fifteen, their parents, and their teachers.

The questionnaire, offered in English and Malayalam, was tested for clarity and smooth administration during school hours. Seventy-five students joined the pilot round. The team deliberately ran no hypothesis tests: the point was to find weak questions and fix procedures first. John and colleagues present the refined instrument as ready for a larger analytical study of vaccine attitudes.
plos-pone-0343859:
Agani Afaya and seven colleagues explore what it means to lose fertility to gynecological cancer in Ghana, in this 2026 qualitative study. Fourteen women treated for cervical, ovarian, uterine, or endometrial cancer at a referral hospital described their experiences in interviews conducted in English, Twi, or Ewe. In a society where motherhood anchors identity, marriage, and standing, treatment that ends fertility strikes far beyond the body.

Three themes intertwined: psychological and emotional turmoil, social challenges, and hard-won coping. Younger, single, and childless women felt fertility loss most sharply as a threat to womanhood and relationships. Women still in treatment dwelled on symptoms, while survivors dwelled on the children they would not have. Stigma, strained partnerships, money worries, and interrupted schooling piled on. Prayer, family support, and staying with treatment sustained hope. The authors call for care that includes fertility counseling and psychosocial support.
plos-pone-0345859:
Maurizio Catino, Alberto Aziani, and Sara Rocchi analyze marriages between clans of the 'Ndrangheta, Italy's powerful mafia network, as a tool of power. Court records document hundreds of alliances sealed by marriages among more than six hundred clans. Their 2026 study maps this marriage web and tests how a clan's position in it relates to strength and to the network's survival.

Powerful clans sat at the web's center, but ties between weaker clans were the load-bearing ones: removing them in simulation broke the web fastest. Status alone did not dictate who gave or received brides. Clans with a balanced flow of brides held the most central spots. Marriage, the authors show, is organizational engineering, not mere tradition.
plos-pone-0346059:
Theofanis Angelis and colleagues tuned a U-Net learning model to outline the surface skin layer in scans of sun damaged pre cancerous skin spots. Hand outlining is slow and varies by reader. Many settings were tried: image sizes, batch sizes, and training lengths, scored against expert outlines with overlap measures.

A small image size with tiny batches and short training won, reaching strong overlap scores. Bigger images and longer training cost more time without real gains and sometimes overfit. A lean, well tuned model can standardise skin layer measures for lesion studies, freeing experts for judgement calls rather than tracing.
plos-pone-0347759:
Irina Ekimova and colleagues undertook a worldwide revision of the flabellin sea slugs, a beautiful but taxonomically tangled family of shell-less marine snails. Earlier studies had split the group's eighty-four known species into twenty-nine genera across seven families, yet the family tree kept shifting between analyses. The team retested which genera are truly natural groups and which body features mark the higher branches.

They folded in overlooked species and material from poorly studied regions, combining family-tree analysis with anatomy. Sea slug classification swings between lumpers and splitters because hidden species look identical and body traits mislead. A tested, stable framework matters beyond naming: these slugs are indicators of ocean health, and nobody can track a species that science cannot reliably define.
plos-pone-0347859:
Yanping Guo and colleagues estimated soil salt in the farmland topsoil of an oasis in Xinjiang, China, using the rainbow of light reflected from the ground. Salt ruins arid farmland, and measuring it field by field is slow. Hyperspectral sensors capture far more detail than the eye, but the data are noisy and tangled. The 2026 study combined several mathematical reshaping techniques with four learning algorithms in every pairing.

One transformed view of the spectrum correlated most strongly with measured salt, and a deep forest algorithm modelled best overall. Their champion combination explained most variation in training and a fair share in held-out tests. The framework gives arid-region managers a faster salinity watch.
plos-pone-0348059:
Zhangjie Yang and co-workers finger a DNA repair enzyme as a driver of bladder cancer growth. Inflammation and this cancer feed each other, but the enzyme's part was unexplored. Their 2026 study tests what happens in bladder cancer cells when the enzyme acts, tracking cell growth, spread, and the signals switched on inside.

Cells with the enzyme active multiplied faster, formed more colonies, and moved and invaded more boldly. The enzyme switched on a master inflammation pathway inside the cells. Blocking that pathway logic makes the enzyme a candidate drug target. The work adds a repair protein to the list of unlikely cancer promoters and gives drug hunters a fresh handle on bladder tumors.
plos-pone-0348359:
Xiang Huang and colleagues proposed a smarter caching method for cloud, edge, and end device systems in 2026. Caches near users speed services, but terminal data is private and changes constantly, so cache plans go stale and unbalanced.

Their method learns from device data without gathering it raw, updates step by step as data changes, and weighs each node's real capacity. Popular data is then placed on edge and end nodes in ranked order. The design aims at higher hit rates and fairer loads without leaking private information. Simulations in the paper test whether the gains hold in shifting conditions.
plos-pone-0348759:
Abdulkarim M Meraya and colleagues surveyed one hundred and ten people living with sickle cell disease in Saudi Arabia's Jazan region, where the inherited blood condition is common. A questionnaire probed physical health, pain, social life, mental strain, and money worries, giving a rounded picture of what the disease costs beyond hospital walls.

Fewer than four in ten respondents held a job, and more than half carried heavy out-of-pocket costs, with transport to care the single largest expense. Heavier spending tracked with worse physical health. Most patients used the standard protective drug hydroxyurea, while newer treatments barely featured. The authors say the region's burden is as much economic and emotional as medical, and they call for support that reaches wallets and daily life, not only clinics.
plos-pone-0348959:
Jade Jansen and seven colleagues test two vaccine boosters for a surprising second talent, in this 2026 PLOS ONE laboratory study. The additives, one a bacterial fat fragment and the other a nanoparticle built from soapbark extract, are meant to strengthen HIV vaccines. A worry was that waking the immune system might also wake dormant HIV in people on treatment.

In cell tests the stronger additive provoked immune cells to release signals that switched dormant virus on. More importantly, in samples from treated patients it shrank the pool of virus that could be reactivated. Boosters that both rouse immunity and drain the hiding places of HIV could serve a future cure strategy.
plos-pone-0349259:
Ticomporn Luangwattanawilai and colleagues tested three new 3D-printed bone graft materials in rats, aiming to beat a common flaw: the standard printed graft dissolves so slowly that it blocks new bone. The new scaffolds are printed by binder jetting and made from calcium phosphate forms that the body can absorb. Each was placed into a hole drilled in a rat's skull and compared with older grafts.

Scans and tissue checks showed that two of the new materials, the monetite and brushite versions, grew more new bone and stirred more bone-cell activity than the controls. They also left far less leftover graft behind. The team presents them as strong candidates for repairing bone defects in patients, pending the longer testing that human use demands.
plos-pone-0349359:
EDITORIAL FLAG: this entry is an Expression of Concern from the PLOS One Editors, not a research article. It warns readers about a previously published study of cell signalling networks in lung cancer, and it advises that the study be read with caution. After publication, editors found questions about the paper's peer review and about many of its figures.

Several blot images showed apparent splice marks, and panels across figures looked strikingly alike, in places even rotated. The authors supplied underlying data and explanations that settled some concerns, but the original films behind one key figure are gone, leaving that worry unresolved. The peer review questions were never cleared. The editors therefore left the concern standing while publishing the supporting files for readers to judge.
plos-pone-0349559:
Eustes Kigongo and colleagues lay out a plan to study abuse of older people in Lira district, a rural area of northern Uganda. About nineteen thousand residents there are over sixty, and reports suggest many face mistreatment by caregivers or the public. Yet little is known about what forms the abuse takes or how elders cope with it. The protocol was written before fieldwork began in twenty twenty-five.

Around three hundred and thirty elders chosen at random will answer a questionnaire built around a standard elder abuse screening test, and some will give longer interviews about their experiences. Numbers will show how common each form of abuse is, while interviews explain coping strategies in elders' own words. No findings are reported yet; the value lies in the design.
plos-pone-0349759:
Bruno Alves-Maciel and colleagues estimated how many high school students in each United States state identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual, split by sex, age, and race. Many states run youth risk surveys, but some never ask about sexual identity. Learning models were trained on states with answers, separately for each sex, then applied to states with gaps for 2021.

Models beat a simpler comparison method at matching known state values. Estimates ranged from about five to thirty percent across groups and states. Filled in states landed in the same range. Health planners can use such estimates to size services and track gaps for sexual minority youth where direct survey data are missing.
plos-pone-0349859:
Xiaowei Chen, Azlan Abdul Aziz, and Zainuddin Ibrahim tested whether brain waves can predict how interactive art shifts feelings. Earlier work often used brain scans or mood forms alone. Their data joined brain recordings before and after art contact with standard mood scores, split into five wave bands from slow to fast.

A transformer model, a newer learning design, beat older rivals at forecasting mood change, though accuracy stayed modest. Slow delta waves linked most with recovery of calm mood. Faster beta and gamma shifts tracked rises in positive feelings, while negative feelings fell clearly after contact. Joining brain and self report, the authors argue, gives a fuller picture of art and emotion.
plos-pone-0350659:
Rachael Jefferson and six colleagues teach sun safety inside the school curriculum in Australia. Their 2026 study ran at one independent girls' secondary school. Australia suffers some of the world's highest youth melanoma rates. Teenagers often chase tans and feel invulnerable. Students aged thirteen to fifteen attended workshops woven into their health and physical education classes. Surveys measured knowledge, tanning attitudes, and protective habits before, right after, and months later.

Knowledge jumped significantly after the workshops. Five months on, it remained above where it started. Students also reported using sunscreen and protective behaviours more often. The glamour of tanning faded: fewer agreed a suntan looks good. Gains appeared across ethnic groups alike. One school limits how far the findings stretch, as the authors admit. Still, embedding sun safety in ordinary lessons, rather than one-off campaigns, demonstrably held teenagers' attention and changed reported habits.
plos-pone-0350859:
Babies who grow poorly in the womb face higher odds of fatty liver and metabolic disease later. Kalonda Alpha Mutamba and colleagues tested puerarin, a plant compound from kudzu root, in rat pups born small after protein-poor pregnancies, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Pups received the compound during their first three weeks of life. Liver scans using two MRI methods, blood fat profiles, and a fat-burning gene's activity were tracked at three ages up to twelve weeks. Growth-restricted pups showed liver changes from the earliest check. The authors examine whether early puerarin softens those changes, a first step toward protecting children whose growth was limited before birth.
plos-pone-0351059:
Qiying Chen and colleagues compared two weekly and daily style diabetes drugs for cost and health value in China. Both drugs help control blood sugar in type two diabetes. A model followed a virtual cohort for twenty five years, using British long term risk equations and head to head trial data, with Chinese costs and quality of life weights.

Semaglutide cost more overall and gained a bit more quality adjusted life than dulaglutide. Extra cost per added quality year landed near twice yearly income per person, inside the range Chinese guidance counts as acceptable. Checks on uncertain inputs left the verdict steady. Payers can defend the pricier drug on value grounds, though budgets will still feel the higher spend.
plos-pone-0351159:
Kecheng Su and colleagues extend a gold rush inspired search method to problems where two goals pull in opposite ways. Drone route planning is their test case: the shortest route may pass close to hazards. Their version keeps a store of good trade off routes and uses guide points to keep choices spread across the trade off curve.

Across eighteen standard test problems the method beat seven rival methods on closeness to ideal answers, spread, and quality. The team then pitted the top four methods on drone routes that balance length against threat. Their method again came out ahead. Better trade off search could help planners pick routes that fit each missions risk limits.
plos-pone-0351659:
Nigeria offered free vaccination against human papillomavirus to girls aged nine to fourteen in 2023, but rumors about fertility and population control slowed uptake in places. Abdulmujeeb Opeyemi Muhammad-Olodo and Laura Asher held group discussions with caregivers in Kwara State for this 2026 PLOS One study.

Forty-one caregivers joined, most of them women, split between those who accepted the shot and a small group who refused. Trust proved layered: faith in government programs, in health workers, and in community voices all mattered. Hearing the discussions in the local Yoruba language let fears surface plainly. The authors use the themes to suggest how campaigns can answer doubts.
plos-pone-0351759:
Neel Godbole and colleagues describe a plan to audit wellbeing programs for American medical students. Medical students report far more stress, anxiety, and depression than the general public. Schools have answered with support programs of many shapes. Yet no one has mapped how those programs are built, staffed, and used. This protocol mixes a scan of program websites and documents with interviews and focus groups.

The end product will be a framework any school can apply to its own program. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. Its premise is simple. A program that exists on paper but stays unknown or mismatched to student needs is not yet a working program. Wellbeing support deserves the same audit culture as teaching.
plos-pone-0351859:
Benjamin Blau and three colleagues examine this 2026 PLOS One economics paper on whether a landmark 1984 American drug law changed how much pharmaceutical firms innovate. The Hatch-Waxman Act tried to balance patent protection for new drugs against cheaper generic competition, and a 2003 amendment adjusted the deal again. The authors compared drug industry research spending with other industries before and after each change.

Pharmaceutical research and development rose markedly relative to other industries after the 1984 act took effect. The 2003 amendment showed no such boost and, if anything, was linked to reduced innovation. The authors conclude that drug innovation responds strongly to policy choices that change the expected rewards for developing new medicines.
plos-pone-0351959:
Ziyang Li attacks a quiet flaw in how computers group unlabelled data. The 2026 study concerns deep clustering, where a neural network sorts records into groups nobody has named. Standard methods grade confidence with softmax probabilities. Those numbers are relative, squeezed against rival groups, so ambiguous items get forced into high confidence. Even a recent calibrated framework inherits the problem. Li swaps the calibration head for a different yardstick: prediction error, an absolute measure of how well each sample fits its cluster.

A frozen teacher-student pair supplies the measuring stick. Fit no longer depends on how bad alternatives look. Visualisations showed cleaner boundaries and tighter clusters. Benchmark experiments put the framework at the front of the field, including on a deliberately challenging dataset. Clustering runs under much of data science, from cell typing to customer sorting. A method that knows when it does not know makes all of them safer.
plos-pone-0352159:
Yu-Tsung Lin and colleagues asked whether a simple blood protein measured before surgery predicts who lives longest after a spine procedure. The operation, vertebroplasty, injects cement into a crushed vertebra, most often in older adults with weak bones. Albumin, the protein in question, doubles as a rough gauge of nutrition, and low levels had forecast poor results after other operations.

Among a hundred forty-five patients followed for roughly two to three years, those with low albumin before surgery died at clearly higher rates than those with normal levels. The link held after accounting for age, weight, smoking, and other illnesses. The authors read the result as a nutrition warning: frail, underfed patients face steeper odds, and spotting them early could guide feeding support and closer follow-up.
plos-pone-0352259:
Md Uddin and eight colleagues profile a mangrove fruit and the foods made from it. Their 2026 study examines Sonneratia apetala, a mangrove tree whose fruit coastal communities traditionally eat. The team extracted pectin and vitamin C from the fruit. They profiled its amino acids and antioxidant strength. Jam, jelly, and pickle made from the fruit went through the same battery. Fungal screening checked whether any of it was safe to store and sell.

The raw fruit proved rich in essential amino acids, led by histidine. Processing destroyed much of that bounty, though histidine survived stubbornly. Extracted pectin and vitamin C both came out at high purity. Root extract showed striking antioxidant power in laboratory assays, tracking its phenol content. Best of all, no fungal growth appeared in any sample. An underused mangrove fruit, properly processed, looks like a safe and genuinely nutritious local resource.
plos-pone-0352359:
Yutong Liu asked who benefits from open government data, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Cities publish open data to spur innovation, but access may favor places and firms already well connected. Liu studied how open data relates to entry into innovation networks that link cities.

The findings test whether open data widens the circle or mainly helps the already connected pull further ahead. That question matters for fairness in regional growth: data policy sold as openness should be checked for who actually gains. City leaders can use such evidence to pair data release with outreach, so smaller cities and new firms can join networks instead of watching them from outside.
plos-pone-0352459:
Muhammad Mozumder and seven colleagues validate a four-question mental health screener in Bangla. Their 2026 study responds to Bangladesh's shortage of mental health professionals. The PHQ-4 asks two questions about depression and two about anxiety. It takes under a minute to complete. Three hundred fifty-seven adults from one urban and two rural communities took part. Trained mental health professionals collected the data. The Bangla version's structure and reliability were then put through formal psychometric tests.

The results were about as clean as validation studies get. The expected two-factor structure fitted excellently. The scale worked the same across sex, age, and mental health state. Internal consistency was high. Scores correlated strongly with two longer established questionnaires and with rated mental health. For community health workers screening door to door, a validated one-minute tool in the local language is a practical breakthrough toward earlier help.
plos-pone-0352659:
Xu Zhu and four colleagues check whether a simple ratio from routine blood tests can forecast survival in cardiogenic shock, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. In this emergency the heart suddenly cannot pump enough blood, and many patients die within a year. The team pulled records for nearly twelve hundred intensive care patients from a large American database and divided a kidney-related measure, blood urea nitrogen, by the blood protein albumin.

Patients with higher ratios died more often in hospital and within a year, in a steady staircase across low, medium, and high groups. Adding the ratio improved existing risk scores slightly. A cheap, instant marker like this could help doctors triage the sickest hearts faster.
plos-pone-0352759:
Sunyoung Choi and five colleagues compare what faces show with what people say they feel. Their 2026 study recruited one hundred forty-eight healthy Korean adults. Participants watched video clips designed to stir joy, anxiety, sadness, or neutral calm. Cameras recorded their spontaneous facial expressions throughout. Software scored the expressions automatically. Afterwards, participants rated their own emotions on several scales.

The clips worked. Both self-reports and facial patterns reflected the intended emotions. Yet the two channels did not always move together. Women displayed stronger positive facial expressions than men during the joyful clips. Self-reported experience did not mirror that gap in the same way. Such mismatches matter for emotion research. A study trusting only questionnaires, or only faces, would draw different conclusions about the same viewers. Measuring both is the safer design this work demonstrates.
plos-pone-0352859:
Muhammad Jawad Ullah and five colleagues published this 2026 food safety study of Salmonella in shop-sold beef in Peshawar, Pakistan. From two hundred and fifty samples bought in city, village, and fringe markets, they cultured the bacteria, confirmed them by gene test, checked drug resistance, and profiled genetic variety.

Three in five samples carried Salmonella, with rural markets worst. Resistance to a common antibiotic was nearly universal, yet the strains were genetically diverse, pointing to many separate entry points along the supply chain. Ullah frames shop beef as a serious reservoir needing surveillance.
plos-pone-0353059:
Xinju Zhan and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One benchmark study testing fifteen leading language models on China's national nurse licensing examination across three years. Nearly ten thousand real exam questions were used, and models were only tested on exams released after the model itself, keeping the contest fair. Both Chinese and international models took part.

Performance climbed steeply: top accuracy rose from under half in 2022 to nearly four-fifths by 2025. Chinese-made models consistently beat international rivals, though the gap narrowed. Models handled knowledge questions better than applied clinical skills questions, and nearly half of the top models' remaining errors were failures of clinical judgment, like choosing the wrong nursing priority. The authors say passing an exam is not the same as thinking like a nurse.
plos-pone-0353159:
Maryam Kazemipoor, Shima Habibzadeh, and Fatemeh Keshmiri investigate unprofessional behaviour among dental students in Iran, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. One hundred and forty students at one medical university were rated by their clinical teachers, by nurses, and by themselves, using a multi-source feedback method. Interviews then explored why students said these behaviours happen.

Lapses clustered around responsibility and respect for others. Junior students and male students were rated worst. Students blamed personal pressures such as profit focus, but also pointed to poor role models and weak training structures above them. The authors recommend feedback systems like theirs, paired with early responsibility training and better examples from senior clinicians.
plos-pone-0353259:
Ling Sun led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of Shuangyu Granule, a traditional Chinese medicine used against influenza. Advanced instruments catalogued its ingredients in the dish and which of them reached the blood, while network analysis and single-cell data from flu patients predicted which immune genes the mixture might touch.

Key ingredients then calmed inflammatory gene activity and cut several inflammatory signals in cell tests. Sun suggests the granule cools excessive flu inflammation through many ingredients acting on many targets, a pattern typical of herbal formulas.
plos-pone-0353359:
Jang and colleagues linked blood pressure levels to hidden heart artery disease in a 2026 study. More than seven thousand adults without symptoms or known heart disease had heart scans during health checkups in Korea. Pressure was grouped from normal through two stages of hypertension under current American guidance.

Scans sorted arteries into normal, mildly narrowed, and seriously narrowed. Comparing groups shows how even modest pressure rises track with silent plaque before any symptoms appear. Such evidence matters because treatment thresholds are debated: if raised pressure already matches visible artery damage, earlier treatment gains support. The checkup setting also shows scanning can reveal risk that office numbers alone understate.
plos-pone-0353559:
Reuben S. Maghembe published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE testing whether gene-activity signatures that distinguish bacterial from viral infection survive the move to new patient data. Doctors need that distinction to use antibiotics wisely, but signatures often fail outside their discovery dataset. Maghembe fixed five whole-blood response modules in one public cohort, then applied them unchanged to two external cohorts, including one measured on a different technology, and stress-tested the results.

All five modules pointed the expected way in both cohorts. Four passed strict statistical correction comfortably, while the fifth stayed directionally right but borderline. Thousands of robustness checks, changing reference groups, case definitions, and deleting genes one or two at a time, almost never flipped a result. One alternative scoring method shifted support between two modules but changed no directions. These host-response modules, the author concludes, travel unusually well, a precondition for a clinical test.
plos-pone-0353759:
Louise de Palaminy led a team of six authors on this 2026 study of medieval Islamic gold coins and the trans-Saharan trade. Fatimid dinars were the era's global currency, supposedly struck from West African gold, but proof of origin was thin. The team combined trace element and three-isotope analysis on eleven coins.

Two distinct metal stocks appeared. Copper and iron signatures fit weathered West African ores, yet lead signatures pointed somewhere else, raising questions about where gold was processed and whether old metal was reused. The chemical detective work reopens a classic trade mystery.
plos-pone-0353859:
Divya Gumudavelly and seven colleagues interview HIV clinic staff in central Uganda about the mental health care they improvise for their patients, in this 2026 qualitative study. Mental illness is common among people living with HIV, and policy pushes integration, yet Uganda has almost no formal mental health infrastructure inside HIV services. Sixteen providers at two clinics described their routines, obstacles, and workarounds in semi-structured interviews.

Without formal integrated services, providers reported tension with their institutions and sometimes with patients. They bridged the gaps through adaptive habits the authors sum up as just trying to make it work. Those hidden efforts keep patients cared for but take a toll on the providers themselves. The authors argue integration plans should recognize, resource, and protect this invisible labor instead of assuming new protocols alone will do the job.
plos-pone-0354159:
Hanif Abdul Rahman and Hein Minn Tun use in 2026 computer learning methods to forecast how warming past set climate limits could raise disease worldwide. They modelled outcomes at three levels of warming above early industrial times. A first stage searched for curved patterns and sharp thresholds, and a second stage tried to explain the pathways behind them.

Even at the lowest level studied, deaths and years lost to heat rose by roughly two thirds from a recent baseline. At higher warming the rises grew much steeper, and heart disease burden climbed too. People in low resource places bore the heaviest load in the forecasts, the authors report.
plos-pone-0354259:
