Zhao and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a review comparing cholesterol drugs in people with diabetes. Diabetes sharply raises the risk of clogged arteries and heart death, and the menu of lipid drugs keeps growing: statins, fibrates, absorption blockers, and newer injectable and oral classes. Which works best and safest for diabetic patients, head to head, is unsettled.

The planned network review will search the major trial databases with no language limits, keeping only randomized trials that compare these drugs alone or in combination. Two reviewers will screen and judge quality separately. Main outcomes are heart events; secondary outcomes include blood fat levels, heart biomarkers, risk scores, and side effects. Certainty will be graded with a network-specific framework, and results published for peer review. As a protocol, the paper promises a method, not an answer; the ranking of drugs awaits the review itself.
plos-pone-0354359: Naik and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on making a magnesium alloy resist rust. The alloy, AZ91, is light and prized for vehicles, but it corrodes easily. The team paired a severe shaping treatment called ECAP with heat treatments. The title reports that the pairing improved corrosion performance more than either alone. Lighter car parts save fuel only if they last.
plos-pone-0354459: Ansar and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on catching copied work that crosses languages. A student might translate a Persian text into English to hide copying. The team's deep learning system aims to spot such cross-language plagiarism between English and Persian. Tools like this help schools and journals guard honest work as translation software grows stronger.
plos-pone-0354959:
Koki Takeda and five colleagues published this 2026 safety study of a chemotherapy drug and a rare eye swelling. Scanning Japan's national side-effect database across two decades, including hundreds of thousands of reports. They checked whether paclitaxel and its albumin-bound form were reported with macular edema, fluid swelling at the center of the retina, more often than expected.

Both forms showed strong reporting signals, the albumin-bound one much stronger. Diabetes and certain glaucoma eye drops also flagged higher reporting. Takeda advises closer eye monitoring for patients on this chemotherapy with those extra risks.
plos-pone-0355059:
Chidera Ejike and colleagues set out in 2026 a review plan on studies that use photovoice to explore how green spaces affect community health. Photovoice lets people photograph and discuss their own surroundings, giving views that standard research often misses, especially in dry regions. The review will gather projects where taking photos was a core method with human participants.

Searches will cover databases and grey sources with no language limit, reaching back to when the method was first described. Screening and extraction will be done in duplicate, and trust in key findings will be rated with standard tools. Community actions that grew from projects are a central interest.
plos-pone-0355159:
Maha Atout and colleagues survey in 2026 what mothers in Jordan do at home when a young child has a fever related seizure. Mothers who attended clinics and wards at two public hospitals in the north answered a structured questionnaire. Most children were under six, and mothers were usually first on the scene.

More than two thirds acted in broadly proper ways, such as placing the child safely and watching how long the episode lasted. Many still panicked, and some used harmful steps such as chest massage. Better knowledge and a more positive outlook linked strongly to safer action, leading the authors to urge focused teaching by health staff.
plos-pone-0355259:
RETRACTED: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 retraction notice, withdrawing an earlier rat study that had claimed a food preservative compound eased early brain injury after bleeding around the brain. Readers should not rely on that study's findings. Concerns centred on several figures and on how the animals were treated.

Editors found a control image that appeared reused, a protein band size that raised doubt about identity, and overlapping panels that undermined related counts. Pain relief, humane endpoints, and approval details had not been reported, and anaesthetic and fluid choices raised welfare worries. Original data were missing, so the concerns could not be cleared.
plos-pone-0355359:
Qingmin Kong and co-authors studied how power plant production workers in China reinvent themselves as salespeople under electricity market reform. Selling used to be foreign to generation companies; reform made it a frontline job. Their 2026 dual-case study of two new-energy firms mixed grounded interviews with a supporting survey.

Beyond the expected blend of selling skill and service skill, a third capability stood out: digital capability, working with data platforms and online customers. Each capability stacked in two layers, foundation first, innovation second, with the first required before the second grows. Three growth paths appeared, led by analytics, by relationships, or by a third route. Kong and colleagues model the transition for other reforming utilities.
plos-pone-0355559:
Po-Yueh Chen and co-authors linked weather records with flu-like illness counts across Taiwan over five recent years. Flu timing follows weather in cooler climates, but the pattern is murkier in subtropical places. Their 2026 study used public health and weather data covering thousands of county-weeks in seventeen counties and cities.

Humidity showed the clearest pattern: more humid weeks came with fewer flu-like illness reports. Air pressure showed a weaker link in the same direction. Temperature and rainfall showed no reliable overall link. Patterns varied sharply by region, with humidity mattering most in the north. Chen and colleagues argue Taiwan's flu planning should treat weather effects as regional, not national.
plos-pone-0355659:
Retraction notice. The PLOS One editors formally withdrew a published study claiming antiviral effects for KIOM-C, a herbal medicine, across several viruses. This 2026 notice is the second retraction involving the same medicine and research group. It records why the journal concluded the antiviral findings could not stand.

Panels in the paper appear to match panels in another article while claiming to show different experiments. The statistics section named a test suited to two-group comparisons, yet many experiments used more groups and variables. The notice also records an undisclosed patent interest: the corresponding author was an inventor on a patent tied to the tested medicine. Readers should not rely on the retracted claims.
plos-pone-0355859:
Turgut Batuhan Baturalp and Selim Bozkurt built a simpler artificial left ventricle for testing heart devices and conditions. Bench circulation rigs often need complex controls, while animal work raises ethical concerns. Their 2026 study first compared actuation options with a structured decision method, then built the winner.

The chosen design squeezes a latex chamber with pneumatic artificial muscles, which contract when filled with air. The prototype beat at several resting and raised heart rates, healthy and diseased settings alike. It pushed flows above two litres per minute. Its tip twisted and shortened much like a real ventricle wall. The authors call it a promising early testbed for cardiac research.
plos-pone-0355959:
Xu Zhixin and co-authors built a fibre-optic listening system that can watch several points inside high-voltage switchgear at once. Loose metal particles inside gas-insulated gear spark partial discharges that precede failure. Standard sensors hear only one point at a time. Their 2026 method sweeps the light frequency to give each sensor its own channel on a single decoding box.

Bench tests on real switchgear fitted with four sensing units followed. The system picked up discharge signals and identified which cavity held the defect. Sensitivity matched conventional single-point interferometric sensors, the design's starting benchmark. Xu and colleagues present frequency-division fibre sensing as a practical route to distributed condition monitoring in modern power equipment.
plos-pone-0356059:
Jasper Mol and co-authors built a pipeline that fishes bacteria out of mixed communities by the sugars on their surfaces. Those sugars steer immune responses, but standard gene surveys cannot see them. Their 2026 method uses human immune sensor proteins as probes, sorting matching bacteria before gene sequencing identifies them.

Tests on a mock community recovered known interacting strains even at low abundance. Applied to stool samples from healthy donors, the pipeline named specific bacteria that bind each of two sensors. Follow-up cultures confirmed the matches. Mol and colleagues describe the platform as modular: other sensors and patient samples can be swapped in to map which microbes the immune system can actually taste.
plos-pone-0356359: An and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a protein that helps liver cancer hide from the immune system. The protein, FABP5, is the focus of their lab work. They report that it shapes a suppressive setting around the tumor through a chain involving NF-kB and PD-L1, both known immune switches. Blocking such chains is a major aim in modern cancer drug design.
plos-pone-0356759:
Haiwei Du, Runsen Lai, and Jianhua Zhu reconstructed a deadly kind of mountain disaster: the debris flow that races down steep gullies. A catchment in China's North Tianshan range served as their case. Their 2026 study combined field surveys and laboratory soil tests. It also used a validated flood simulation program. The program replayed a 2024 event and then tested how worse storms would behave.

The replay matched the real flood's depth and footprint closely. The recipe for disaster combined three things. Shattered rock supplied debris, steep slopes sped it up, and short intense rain pulled the trigger. Under a once-a-century storm, the simulated flow ran several meters deep at highway speeds. The danger zone swelled over downstream settlements. Such zonation gives engineers defensible lines for barriers and building bans.
plos-pone-0357159:
Yuri Fukai, Amane Fujiwara, and Kohei Matsuno test whether algae sleeping in Arctic seafloor mud can seed the autumn blooms now appearing on the Chukchi shelf. Stronger winds over open water stir sediments upward, and a recent field study suggested buried diatoms ride along. The team incubated natural water communities two ways, adding nutrients alone or nutrients plus microalgae-bearing sediment, and watched growth, species, and light use.

Both treatments bloomed, with diatoms leading. Sediment sped the start by adding ready cells, while growth rates and light efficiency stayed similar. Nutrient-only tanks favored open-water autumn species, while sediment tanks filled with species typical of the seafloor. Fukai and colleagues say resuspension shapes not just bloom timing but which community the Arctic gets.
plos-pone-0357259:
Ling Zong and Kexin Zhou published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on older adults in China who live with several chronic diseases at once. The study asks what family and social support do to their mental health. Using a nationally representative 2020 survey, they modeled how multimorbidity relates to mental health, and whether family or wider social support changes that link.

More diseases went with poorer mental health. Both supports were themselves linked to better mental health, but only family support changed the disease link, surprisingly: the mental health penalty of multimorbidity grew steeper where family support was higher. That effect weakened with age and vanished past eighty, while family support's direct benefit followed a U-shape across age groups. Close family involvement, they warn, is not automatically protective, and programs should work with families carefully rather than simply urging more of it.
plos-pone-0357459:
Siliang Guo, Yan Qu, and Youjia Liu published a 2026 economics study in PLOS ONE on whether education keeps Chinese families from sliding back into poverty. China has ended absolute poverty, but keeping families out is a different challenge. Using four waves of a national family panel survey from 2014 to 2020, the authors measured each household's stock of educational human capital and modeled relapse risk with several statistical approaches.

More education clearly lowered the chance of falling back into poverty. The protection ran through three channels: family members finding non-farm jobs, higher household income, and better family health. Households that themselves invested more in education got extra benefit, while heavy health spending diluted the effect. The protective impact grew stronger for families at highest relapse risk, and was larger in eastern and urban areas than elsewhere. The authors argue education budgets are anti-poverty insurance, especially where relapse risk concentrates.
plos-pone-0357759:
Ankit and coauthors published a 2026 materials paper in PLOS ONE on copper-graphite composites, blends prized for carrying current and resisting wear, made by pressing and baking metal powders. Three settings govern the result: how much graphite goes in, how hot the baking runs, and how long it lasts. Instead of trial and error, the team used response surface methodology to model how those settings jointly determine density and hardness.

A fitted quadratic model matched the measured values closely, with negligible error, and formal analysis confirmed which settings mattered. The best combination used a modest graphite share, a high sintering temperature, and a mid-length hold, giving the densest and hardest material in their tests. The model lets manufacturers dial in target density or hardness on paper first, cutting wasted runs, and gives powder metallurgy shops a template for other blends.
plos-pone-0357959:
Francisca Édla Santos Leite Gurgel and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE from Fortaleza, Brazil, on teaching pregnant women with diabetes how to care for themselves. Standard hospital handouts can be hard going for women with limited reading skills. So the team wrote the guidance as a cordel, a traditional Brazilian booklet of rhymed verse, working with health researchers and cordel poets, and tested it at two public maternity hospitals.

Hospitalized pregnant women rated every item of the booklet as fully valid, and forty expert judges nearly matched them, giving top or near-top clarity and relevance scores. Experts strongly agreed on the content overall, though they ranked individual items in quite different orders. The cordel, they say, is a culturally rooted format that makes discharge guidance easier to grasp and remember, and this early validation invites wider testing of whether it changes self-care.
plos-pone-0358259: Tang and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study that mines public data on stool fats and gene activity. Their combined computer analysis hints that the COX-2 pathway may be linked with one fat molecule, named CE(20:4). The link sits along the path from benign colon growths to cancer. A candidate link from free data can guide lab work on early colon cancer signs.
plos-pone-0358359:
Zongtao Li led a team of seven authors linking a common molecule to kidney damage in diabetes, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Lactate, known for the burn of hard exercise, may also signal renal trouble in diabetic kidney disease. The team combined animal experiments, clinical cohorts, and bioinformatics in one exploratory analysis.

Li's work ties higher serum lactate to worse kidney function across those sources. A cheap blood measure that warns early of failing kidneys would be valuable, since current markers lag behind damage. Triangulating across animals, patients, and gene data strengthens a claim that any one source could not carry. The analysis is exploratory by design, marking lactate as a lead worth testing in larger, focused studies.
plos-pone-0358459:
Braulio Tapia and colleagues studied in 2026 how fish communities differ from place to place on the rocky reefs of the Juan Fernández Archipelago. The islands, far off the coast of Chile in the southeastern Pacific, sit inside a marine protected area. The team examined demersal fish, those living near the reef floor, and asked how their groupings vary across the protected waters.

Understanding that spatial variety, called heterogeneity, is practical knowledge for conservation. A protected area drawn without it may guard plenty of water but miss the spots where particular communities thrive. The authors link their findings to the archipelago's conservation plans, showing where protection is well placed and where management may need adjusting.
plos-pone-0358659:
Muhammad Ali Ibrahim Kazi leads a team of eight studying heart outcomes in people who live with both inflammatory bowel disease and type 2 diabetes, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The pairing is dangerous, since gut inflammation and blood sugar problems feed each other's damage to blood vessels. The authors asked whether modern diabetes drugs in the GLP-1 family are linked to fewer heart events in this high risk group.

Using a large international health records network, they matched over sixteen thousand treated patients with similar untreated ones. Treated patients showed lower rates across the board: heart attack, heart failure, stroke, dangerous rhythms, and blood clots in veins and lungs. The authors caution that records based comparisons show association, not proof of cause, and that the study cannot separate the two drug types it pooled together.
plos-pone-0358759: Cui and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on hearing machine faults through noise. Bearings in spinning machines wear out, and their fault signals hide in loud, shifting conditions. The team's Wavelet-Mamba network mixes wave-based signal cleaning with a modern sequence model. Catching a failing bearing early can prevent a breakdown that stops a whole line.
plos-pone-0358959:
Rustam Akhmedov and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on exercise and women's health. It is an eight-week intervention study of indoor cycling, commonly called spinning. Outcomes cover body image, how the women see their own bodies, and anthropometric measurements, standard measures like weight and waist size.

Tracking body image alongside body measurements matters because the two do not always move together. A program can shrink a waist while leaving self-image untouched, or lift confidence before bodies change. Fitness practitioners designing women's cycling programs are the readers for evidence that joins the physical and the psychological.
plos-pone-0359559:
Joanna L'Heureux and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on the oral microbiome, the community of microbes living in the mouth. The authors look for signatures of ageing and of cognitive function in that community. Their cohorts come from distinct geographical regions, letting place enter the comparison.

Mouth microbes are easy to sample, so a signature tied to cognition would be a convenient window on brain health. Geography matters because diet and environment shape the microbiome strongly. Researchers of ageing and dementia screening are the readers for signatures that hold across places rather than reflecting one town's habits.
plos-pone-0359659: Shah, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on why muscles waste away. Using a tool called decoupleR, Shah compared the activity of transcription factors, the switches that turn genes on and off. Three causes of wasting were set side by side: space flight, old age, and lack of use. Seeing where the three match or split can point to shared targets for drugs or training plans.
plos-pone-0359859:
John Yinger published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies world-record envelopes in racing events: the outer limits that link how fast athletes can go and how far. The focus is the speed-distance trade-off, the way top speed falls as race distance grows.

An envelope here means the boundary formed by world records across distances, from sprints to marathons. Fitting that boundary shows the underlying rule connecting speed and endurance in human performance. Sports scientists use such limits to judge how close current athletes are to what bodies can do, and to spot records that break the pattern.
plos-pone-0359959:
Quang Toai Ton, Thanh Hien Vu, Thanh Nguyen Vu, and Tuong Le published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents HSCM-Lane, a computer vision system for lane segmentation, marking exactly which pixels in a road image belong to lane lines. The system is built on a ResNet encoder-decoder design.

Added to that base is context modeling that uses shifted windows at several levels, a way for the network to consider both fine line detail and the wider road scene. Lane marking detection is a core skill for driver assistance and self-driving cars. Engineers comparing segmentation architectures can judge whether this context modeling earns its extra complexity on road images.
plos-pone-0360059:
Ankit Singh, Varun Dutt, and Akash Rao studied in 2026 how mental effort and brain stimulation together shape the way people make decisions from experience. Their experiments vary cognitive load, how much a person's working memory is burdened, and apply prefrontal neuromodulation, gentle stimulation of the brain region behind the forehead that handles planning. They watch how these factors change exploration, risk taking, and the search for information.

Experience based decisions, learned by trying options and seeing outcomes, differ from choices made from written descriptions. Knowing how a loaded or stimulated brain explores helps explain everyday choices under pressure. The work speaks to psychology, to economics, and to the design of training for people whose risky decisions carry real costs.

Hidaka's team at RIKEN and Kyoto built a platform that profiles protein phosphorylation inside single cells. Marked proteins are scarce, so one-cell-at-a-time reads have lagged behind bulk assays. Their system labels one cell's proteins with dye and fishes out phosphorylated targets with motif antibodies. A custom light-sheet scope then counts single molecules after tiny gel separation.

The team applied the platform to casein kinase 2 substrates in HeLa cells. Adding a phosphatase blocker piled up phosphorylated substrates as foreseen. True one-cell runs exposed uneven patterns across weight regions. That cell-to-cell spread in signaling vanished inside bulk means, the authors note.

Amagawa and co-workers in Japan sorted older diabetes outpatients into four muscle-health categories and compared body-composition markers across them. The categories run from normal through presarcopenia and dynapenia to full sarcopenia. Nearly seven hundred patients aged sixty-five or older took part. Grip strength and a muscle mass index anchored the classification.

As category worsened, patients were older, with more water held outside cells and more glycation products accumulated. Phase angle, grip strength, and walking speed all declined step by step. The water ratio linked independently to both grip strength and muscle mass. The authors suggest these bedside measures track muscle decline in diabetic elders.
pmc-13242459:
Ahmad Toubasi and Thuraya Al-Sayegh reviewed clinical trials to count how often immune checkpoint inhibitors cause neurological side effects. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in the Journal of Neurology in 2026. These cancer drugs free the immune system to attack tumors, but case reports have described nerve and brain problems in some patients. The authors pooled trials of previously untreated patients who received only these drugs.

Across 31 trials covering close to nine thousand patients, neurological side effects proved very rare, on the order of one case in five thousand. Using two checkpoint drugs together did not raise the rate compared with using one. Rates also looked similar across cancer types, including lung cancer and liver cancer. The authors still call for patient-level data to learn which individuals face the most risk.

The target pollutant, 4-nitrophenol, pours out of factories and harms human health, so a catalyst that neutralizes it while also fighting germs would be doubly useful.

It also stopped two problem bacteria, Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae, leaving clear zones around test samples. In catalytic trials it sped the conversion of 4-nitrophenol into a far less harmful aminophenol. Microscopy confirmed the hybrid structure, and charge readings suggested good stability in water. Affan presents the material as a plant-based route to treating polluted water.

A small mixed group of testers in Rwanda ran the system under normal and abnormal medical conditions, and the authors judge the results highly efficient and secure. The real barrier they attack is access: modelers in low-resource settings often cannot afford the software stack. Web delivery, they argue, turns an expensive local tool into shared infrastructure.

Kazuhiro Kurihara and co-authors tested whether wearable sensors plus machine learning can tell bipolar disorder from health. Their study appeared in PCN Reports in 2026. Twenty-three patients in a stable phase and forty-three controls wore wrist trackers for two weeks of sleep recording. A separate wearable measured core body temperature for three days, letting the team estimate each person's nightly temperature low point and how it aligned with sleep.

A base model fed only temperature and sleep features separated the groups moderately well. Adding basic background variables lifted its discrimination to a strong level in cross-validation. Sleep length and wake time, and their offset from the temperature low, carried the most weight in explaining the model's calls. The authors are upfront about the small sample and call the result preliminary. Body temperature rhythm, they suggest, is an underused signal in psychiatry that wearables can now capture cheaply.

Toon Janssen and colleagues summed up a decade of European research on why parents hesitate over childhood vaccines. Their systematic review appeared in Human Vaccines and Immunotherapeutics in 2026. They gathered forty-nine studies from 2015 to 2024 across the WHO European Region, excluding flu and HPV shots. The findings were sorted through the WHO's 3C lens of confidence, complacency, and convenience.

Trust in health workers emerged as the strongest lever on the confidence side. Working the other way were fear of side effects, practical barriers, and the belief that the diseases are no longer dangerous. Who hesitates, and why, shifted with each country's culture and health system. The authors therefore reject one-size campaigns. Their prescription is tailored national strategies that strengthen the parent-doctor bond and strip out practical obstacles.
pmc-13245759:
Mogensen, Guarrasi, and Behndig asked whether artificial intelligence can pick which brain-fluid shunt patients will walk better, in this 2026 PLOS One study. Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus causes gait trouble, memory problems, and incontinence, and a shunt draining excess fluid helps many patients, but not all, and surgery carries risk. The team applied three advanced approaches to preoperative MRI scans from one hundred forty-nine shunted patients.

Three quarters of the patients had responded. Even so, every model performed poorly: none reached the accuracy level considered clinically useful, with a texture-feature radiomics model doing least badly. The authors conclude structural MRI alone, however cleverly analyzed, cannot reliably forecast shunt response, and call for multimodal inputs and large multi-center datasets before AI earns a place in this decision.

Li, Wang, and Zhang review how estrogen and inflammation feed each other in adenomyosis, in this 2026 Seminars in Immunopathology article. In adenomyosis, tissue like the womb's lining grows into the uterine muscle, causing enlargement, heavy periods, pelvic pain, and infertility. Local estrogen excess and chronic inflammation are both established players, but how they interact has been less clear than either role alone.

The review assembles the molecular evidence into a vicious cycle: estrogen promotes inflammation, inflammation boosts local estrogen production. Together they drive lesion growth, with named signaling pathways carrying each step. It then surveys targeted drugs that interrupt the loop, from hormone suppressors to anti-inflammatory strategies, and the clinical evidence behind them. The authors aim the synthesis at designing better treatments for a common, hard disease.
pmc-13246759:
Molinari, Lusi, and Bianconi review why aggressive brain tumors survive treatment, in this 2026 Communications Biology article. High-grade gliomas usually return after radiation and the drug temozolomide. The authors focus on glioma stem cells, a stubborn subpopulation that does not merely repair DNA damage faster, but rewires its whole damage-response system to endure it.

The review weaves together checkpoint signaling, tolerance of replication stress, choices among repair pathways, chromatin and RNA regulation, translation control, metabolism, and signals from the tumor's surroundings. Framing these as one flexible network, which the authors call DNA damage response plasticity, explains tumor persistence. It also reveals weak points where future drugs might break the network rather than a single repair step.

McMillan and a large consortium of developmental psychologists sum up ten years of the ManyBabies project, in this 2026 brief report. Some celebrated infant findings replicated well across labs, and others did not. The authors argue that simply enlarging samples cannot fix weaknesses built into study designs themselves. They distill three lessons aimed at a developmental science that is more reliable and more inclusive of the world's babies, not just those near wealthy universities.

Fu and team make, in 2026, cellulose fibers with spider-silk-like toughness by copying the helical nanostructure of cherry bark. Magic lingered. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
thoreau-plea-for-captain-john-brown-1859:
Henry David Thoreau gave A Plea for Captain John Brown as a speech in 1859, then in print. The thunderous defense of John Brown followed the raid on Harpers Ferry that same fall in Virginia. Many call it the most radical abolitionist address of the era in the North at the time.

Thoreau hails Brown as a man of principle, not a madman, in the first public defense. He scorns editors and churchmen who damned Brown while they tolerated slavery's daily violence in the South. Brown's gallows, he argues, will make the cross itself seem less sacred to coming generations of Americans. The plea dared a Concord audience to rank conscience above law, order, and union in 1859. It helped turn Brown from felon to martyr in the Northern mind before the war.
tob-0159:
Rudolf Steiner published The Philosophy of Freedom in 1894, before his fame as founder of Anthroposophy. The book asks how a person can act freely in a world science describes as ruled by causes. Steiner answers through the act of thinking itself.

When thought grasps its own nature, he argues, a person can choose deeds from insight rather than habit or command. Moral imagination then shapes free action. The work is his most rigorous piece of philosophy, argued step by step. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Later Steiner schools still build on its account of freedom.
tob-4059:
Volume two of Isis Unveiled, devoted to theology, completes the 1877 work that brought Theosophy to the world. Blavatsky traces Christianity, Buddhism, and the mystery faiths back to one old wisdom tradition. Churches, she charges, buried that inheritance under dogma, priestcraft, and literal readings of symbols.

Learned and fierce, the volume quotes scripture and the church fathers against their custodians, a method guaranteed to make enemies, as it did. Read together with volume one's attack on science, the theology half shows Blavatsky's full strategy: reclaim a universal ancient religion from both the laboratory's materialism and the pulpit's orthodoxy. Few debuts in occult literature arrived louder.
tob-4159:
Beatrice M. Hinkle's translation of Jung's Psychology of the Unconscious, the 1916 English edition, launched analytical psychology in America. In Hinkle's rendering, Jung's break with Freud unfolds across a long interpretation of one patient's fantasies. Libido appears as creative life force, and myths and symbols as the unconscious speaking in its native tongue.

Dreams, fairy tales, hero myths, and religions are read as one great text of the psyche's transformations. Hinkle, a practicing analyst, faced the task of inventing English terms for Jung's new vocabulary. Readers comparing this duplicate record with its twin nearby will find the same landmark text; its influence justifies the repetition.
tob-4259:
Henrik Ibsen wrote Peer Gynt as a dramatic poem in 1867, and William and Charles Archer's translation carried it to English readers in the edition of 1876. Peer, a boastful Norwegian farmer's son, talks his way out of every duty life sets him. Trolls crown him; the Button-Moulder waits to melt him down.

Solveig, who loves him, waits in the hut through all his wandering years. The play swings between satire, fairy tale, and sharp judgment on a self that never commits. The Archers' verse keeps Ibsen's music and bite. Verified from the 1919 edition, Peer Gynt stands the most Norwegian of plays, and the most universal.
turgenev-house-of-gentlefolk-1859:
A House of Gentlefolk, Turgenev's novel of 1859, is given here in Constance Garnett's English. Fyodor Lavretsky returns to Russia after years abroad and a broken marriage. At the Kalitin house he meets Liza, a grave, devout girl, and falls in love with her.

News that Lavretsky's wife has died seems to clear their path at last. Then the wife herself appears, alive, and hope closes for both lovers. Liza withdraws to a convent, and Lavretsky accepts a life of quiet work. Turgenev writes the tale in his most lyrical manner. It became his most loved novel in Russia, an elegy for the gentry world that raised him.
un-ga-res-2159: Who speaks for China at the United Nations? Resolution 2159, adopted on 29 November 1966, deals with the rule for deciding, not the claim itself. A 1950 vote had said such fights should be judged by the Charter's aims and the facts of each case. A 1961 vote then classed any change in China's seat as an important question, needing a two-thirds majority. The 1966 text states, in full, that the 1961 ruling remains valid.
un-ga-res-a-69-59:
Keep your word: that is the blunt core of Resolution A/69/59, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. States care deeply, it says, that rights and duties from the pacts they sign are honored in full. Keeping faith with the Charter, and with arms and spread-control deals, is cast as a must for peace and calm at home and abroad.

A state that breaks its deals, the text warns, does more than harm itself. It puts at risk all states that lean on the curbs and pledges in those deals for their own safety. The trust that pacts are kept is treated as a shared shield, worth guarding for its own sake.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 2159 (XXI) was adopted on 29 November 1966. It concerned the representation of China in the United Nations. It recalled the Assembly's 1961 ruling, made under Article 18 of the Charter. Under that ruling, any proposal to change China's representation counts as an important question, needing a two-thirds vote. It also recalled the 1965 vote affirming that ruling. The resolution then states, in one line, that the 1961 decision remains valid.

Resolution 69/59 of the General Assembly is about compliance with non-proliferation, arms limitation, and disarmament agreements. The Assembly stresses that such agreements work only if they are fully complied with and enforced. It stresses that non-compliance endangers states that rely on the agreements' limits. It urges all states to meet their obligations in full. It calls on those out of compliance to decide to return to it. It asks member states to help build capacity. It asks them to hold violators accountable in line with the Charter.
un-sc-res-1359:
A draft framework for Western Sahara's future reached the parties in 2001. On 29 June 2001 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 30 November 2001. The Secretary-General's envoy had drawn up the draft Framework Agreement. The Council backed his plan to invite the parties to direct or proximity talks. They could debate the draft and suggest exact changes. Nothing would be agreed until everything was agreed.

The Polisario Front's own proposals would also be weighed during the talks. The Council restated the goal of a free and fair referendum. It also recalled the safety rules for United Nations staff. The extension kept the mission alive while a new political track opened. That track later gave way to the 2003 peace plan.
un-sc-res-1459: Readers meet Resolution 1459 here as a Security Council record, catalogued with a date of 2002. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1559:
Lebanon stood at the center of this decision on 2 September 2004. The Security Council backed the full sovereignty and independence of Lebanon. It noted with concern that foreign forces still remained on Lebanese soil. It also pointed to armed militias that blocked the government from ruling all its own land. A presidential election was near, and the Council wanted it free of outside pressure.

The resolution calls on all remaining foreign forces to withdraw from Lebanon. It demands the disbanding and disarmament of every militia, Lebanese or not. It supports a free and fair presidential vote under Lebanese rules alone. The Secretary-General had thirty days to report on compliance.
un-sc-res-1659:
Afghanistan's post-Bonn framework was endorsed by the Security Council on 15 February 2006. The Afghanistan Compact had been launched in London on 31 January 2006. Afghanistan's foreign minister wrote to the Secretary-General on 6 February with the news. The Council said security, governance, and development gains reinforce each other, and that the fight against terror and narcotics threats went on.

The Council endorsed the Compact and its annexes as the framework for partnership between Kabul and the international community. Both sides were called to carry out its promises in full. The United Nations was confirmed in its central, impartial role, including joint steering of the effort. A joint board to steer and track the work was welcomed. The Council noted the interim national growth strategy and NATO's continuing lead of the security force. It also flagged the danger of opium growing and trafficking to the whole project.
un-sc-res-1759: Resolution 1759 dates to 2007 in the Council's sequence, and the collection keeps its official text through English Wikisource. A resolution's preamble is its argument; its operative paragraphs are its orders. This entry contains both, in the order voted, making it a complete primary source for whatever question the members were deciding.
un-sc-res-1859:
The Council spoke on Iraq through Resolution 1859, adopted on 22 December 2008. Iraq had gained ground on security, politics, and the economy. It still needed outside support to advance further. Money from oil and gas sales flowed into the Development Fund for Iraq under international watch.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends those fund arrangements until 31 December 2009. The advisory board that watches the fund keeps its task for the same span. Legal shields on Iraqi oil and fund assets also stay in place. A review is due at Iraq's request or by 15 June 2009. The Council will also review every Iraq resolution since 1990, aiming to restore the country's old standing.
un-sc-res-2059:
Syria's observer mission received its last short lifeline in Resolution 2059, adopted in July 2012. UN observers had entered Syria to watch a ceasefire that never held. With fighting spreading, the Council renewed their mandate for a final thirty days.

The text ties any further extension to a real drop in violence and an end to heavy weapons use in towns. Those conditions were not met, and the mission soon closed. The resolution is a small document with a bleak weight: it records the moment a monitoring effort admitted the war had outgrown it.
un-sc-res-259:
Arab civilians under Israeli occupation were the concern of a Security Council decision of 27 September 1968. Resolution 237 (1967) had called on Israel to protect the welfare and safety of people in the areas taken in the June 1967 war. The Secretary-General had reported on his efforts. Israel kept setting conditions for receiving his special representative, and the Council deplored the delay.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to send a special representative urgently to the Arab territories held by Israel since 5 June 1967. The envoy would report on how resolution 237 (1967) was being applied. Israel was asked to receive the representative, cooperate with him, and ease his work. All concerned were urged to give the Secretary-General full cooperation in the effort. The text kept the welfare of the occupied population on the Council's agenda while access for its envoy remained blocked.
un-sc-res-359: The United Nations Security Council issued Resolution 359 as one of its formal decisions, and the catalog carries it under the year 1974. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them.
un-sc-res-459:
Lebanon's interim force was renewed amid strain on 19 December 1979. The Secretary-General's report on UNIFIL lay before the Council. Cease-fire breaches went on, the force faced attacks, and blocks stood in the way of its full deployment. Lebanon asked for the renewal, and its government was working to restore its authority in the south.

The Council restated the aims of resolutions 425 (1978) and 450 (1979). It backed the Secretary-General's work to firm up the cease-fire and called on all parties to stop acts that clashed with UNIFIL's aims. The force and its commander won high praise for their performance. Lebanon's plan to protect its archaeological and cultural sites was noted with support. The Council then renewed UNIFIL's mandate for six months, to 19 June 1980. Member states were urged to use their sway so the force could deploy in full.
un-sc-res-59:
The killing of the United Nations mediator in Palestine was taken up on 19 October 1948. Count Folke Bernadotte and observer Colonel André Sérot had been assassinated on 17 September 1948. The Acting Mediator reported on the murders and on the troubles facing truce supervision. Israel's provisional government had sent no account of its investigation into the killings.

The Council noted that silence with concern. It ordered Israel's government to report soon on the progress of the inquiry. The report had to state what steps had been taken over official negligence or other factors in the crime. Both sides were reminded that their duties under resolutions 54 and 56 (1948) stood in full. The Council ruled that observers and truce staff must get ready access to airfields, ports, truce lines, and key points. Their aircraft and transport needed safe conduct, and both sides had to aid inquiries into truce breaches.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Fresh plans for Western Sahara stirred the file in the summer of 2001. A draft deal would give the land wide self-rule for a time. The final call on its fate would come later, by vote. James Baker, the chief's envoy, drove the talks. Resolution 1359 passed with no dissent on 29 June 2001.

MINURSO, the UN team in the land, stayed to 30 November 2001. The Council backed Baker's bid to get all sides in one room. The Polisario Front's own plans would still get a fair look. One rule was stressed: no part was agreed till all was agreed. The text also pressed a grim point. Both sides had to free all those held since the war began. The fate of the missing had to be faced.

Rough diamonds get a world certification scheme, and the Council backs it on 28 January 2003. Illegal diamond sales from war zones had funded armed conflicts in several countries. Governments, the diamond industry, and civic groups had built the Kimberley Process together, and it was adopted at Interlaken in November 2002.

The scheme is strongly supported as a real blow against trade in conflict diamonds, and the industry's voluntary self-regulation alongside it is welcomed. The widest possible membership, the Council stresses, is essential for the system to work. All member states are urged to take an active part, so diamonds from war zones can be kept out of the legal world market.

Lebanon's sovereignty took center stage in the autumn of 2004. On 2 September, the Council adopted Resolution 1559. A contested presidential vote loomed in Beirut. Many saw Syria's hand behind it. The Council voiced grave concern at armed militias beyond Beirut's control.

The text calls on all foreign forces left in Lebanon to withdraw. That meant Syrian troops above all. It also calls for all militias, Lebanese or not, to disband and disarm. Beirut's control must extend over all its land. The coming vote must be free and fair, under Lebanese rules, with no foreign say. Syria pulled out within a year. The militia clause stayed unmet and disputed.

A republic born from a broken union took its seat in 1960. On 28 September, the Council adopted Resolution 159 without dissent. The Republic of Mali had formed weeks before. Senegal had walked out of the short-lived Federation of Mali in August. Mali then proclaimed its own republic in September.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the Republic of Mali. The Assembly seated it the same day. The two-step path tells the story in paper form. A federation was backed in June, then a lone republic in September. West Africa's map was redrawn at speed that year. This text is one small proof of the pace.

Resolution 1659, adopted on 15 February 2006, puts the Council's weight behind the Afghanistan Compact. The compact had been launched in London on 31 January, setting shared goals between Afghanistan's government and its international backers after the Bonn process ended. Afghanistan's foreign minister wrote to tell the Secretary-General of the launch.

The Council endorsed the compact. The text around that endorsement pledges continued support as Afghans rebuild their country, strengthen constitutional democracy, and take their place among nations. It stresses that security, governance, and development reinforce one another, and that the fight against terrorism and narcotics remains central. Regional cooperation is named as a real tool for Afghan security and growth.

Six more months for the Golan Heights force are approved on 20 June 2007. UNDOF is renewed until 31 December 2007, still watching the separation between Israeli and Syrian forces. The parties are called on to carry out resolution 338 of 1973 at once. The force's work on the zero-tolerance policy against sexual exploitation and abuse is welcomed. The Secretary-General is asked to report at the end of the period.

Iraq's oil-money protections are extended by Resolution 1859, adopted on 22 December 2008. The multinational force mandate was ending on 31 December 2008, and security had improved. Iraq's government asked in an annexed letter for another year of the arrangements. The arrangements shielded oil revenues from old regime-era debts and claims while Iraq worked to settle them. A transition to Iraqi-run oversight was being prepared.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the deposit of oil and gas export proceeds into the Development Fund for Iraq until 31 December 2009. It extends the monitoring role of the International Advisory and Monitoring Board and the legal immunities of Resolution 1483 (2003). The deal is reviewable by 15 June 2009 at Iraq's request. The Council also starts a review of its Iraq resolutions back to 661 (1990), seeking the facts needed to restore Iraq's international standing from before that resolution.

Burundi's UN office is scaled down in Resolution 1959, adopted on 16 December 2010. Five elections held through 2010 had passed without large-scale violence, a milestone for peace and democracy, and the integrated office BINUB was credited for its recovery work. Reports of extrajudicial killings, torture, and curbs on opposition parties and civil society remained a serious concern.

The Council asks the Secretary-General to replace BINUB with a smaller United Nations Office in Burundi, BNUB, for 12 months from 1 January 2011. BNUB must strengthen judicial and parliamentary institutions, promote political dialogue, back the creation of transitional justice mechanisms, protect human rights, and help tie economic policy to peacebuilding and fair growth. The government is urged to investigate rights abuses, bring those responsible to justice, and set up an independent national human rights commission. Reports are due every six months.

Syria's civil war had made the work of United Nations observers almost impossible by the summer of 2012. Resolution 2059 concerns UNSMIS, the United Nations Supervision Mission in Syria. Its unarmed observers had been sent to watch a cease-fire that was failing. The security situation grew more dangerous week by week.

The Council renewed the mission's mandate for a final period of thirty days. Plans to reshape the mission would guide that last period. All sides had to keep the observers safe and let them move and work freely. The main duty for their safety lay with the Syrian authorities. Any further renewal would come only if heavy weapons fell silent. Violence also had to drop enough for the mission to do its job. A report was due within fifteen days.

Resolution 259 passed on 27 September 1968. Twelve members backed it, and three did not vote either way. It tries to send a UN envoy into the Arab lands Israel held after the June 1967 war. The Council feared for the safety of the Arabs who lived there. A 1967 text had set out their rights as wards of war. Israel kept naming terms for the envoy's visit, and the visit kept slipping.

The Council asked the UN chief to send the envoy at once. He was to report on how the 1967 rights text was being kept. Israel was asked to take him in, work with him, and ease his task. Other states were urged to help as well.

United Nations peacekeepers in Cyprus were killed and wounded during the fighting of the summer of 1974. The force stood on the island with the full consent of Cyprus, Turkey, and Greece. Resolution 359, adopted on 15 August 1974, speaks directly to the safety of that force.

The Council deeply deplored the deaths and injuries among the peacekeepers. All parties had to respect the international status of the United Nations force in full. Nothing could be done that put the lives of its members at risk. Full cooperation with the force was required in all its tasks. That included its humanitarian work across Cyprus. The text stressed a wider point: the safety of any United Nations peacekeeping force must be respected under all circumstances.

Lebanon's request keeps UNIFIL in the south in Resolution 459, adopted on 19 December 1979 by twelve votes to none with two abstentions. The Secretary-General's report on the force was before the Council. Members noted with concern that the ceasefire kept being violated, that UNIFIL itself was attacked, and that obstacles blocked the force from deploying fully and moving freely.

The Council renewed UNIFIL's mandate for a further period, into June 1980. It restated its call for strict respect for Lebanon's territorial integrity, unity, sovereignty, and political independence within its recognized borders. It also welcomed the Lebanese government's efforts to reassert its authority in the south, a goal the force existed to serve.

The assassination of the UN mediator in Palestine drives Resolution 59, adopted on 19 October 1948. Count Folke Bernadotte and French observer Colonel André Sérot had been murdered on 17 September. A month later, the Council noted with concern, Israel's provisional government had still sent no report on how the investigation was progressing.

The Council asked that government to report at an early date on the inquiry and on any negligence by officials that bore on the crime. It reminded all governments and authorities in Palestine that their duties under the summer's truce resolutions had to be carried out in full and honestly. It also pressed the acting mediator to spread UN observers fairly across both parties' territory.
